<page url="https://aureauds.dev/getting-started.html">
# Introduction

An open-source design system with one look for the web and for React Native, made to be read by people with low vision.

Aurea is a design system with two outputs: the **web** (React components and plain CSS) and **mobile** (React Native components). The look is the same on both sides.

On the web, the interactive behavior comes from [Base UI](https://base-ui.com): focus trapping, Esc to close, focus return and scroll lock in dialogs, drawers, menus, popovers and tooltips. Aurea adds the look, the tokens and the components on top.

## Why Aurea?

**Readable first.** The typeface is Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, designed for low vision. Contrast is measured by tests in both themes, focus is always visible, and touch targets are at least 44px on touch screens.

**One look, two platforms.** The web and the native packages share the same tokens. A button on a phone and a button in a browser have the same color, shape and spacing.

**Every value is a token.** Color, radius, type and space come from tokens in the DTCG format, and the components read their values from them.

**Two themes, three densities.** Light and dark are equal citizens. Each one comes in compact, comfortable and spacious.

**Typed.** The React and React Native packages ship TypeScript types. On the web, even icon names are checked by the compiler.

**Light to import.** The web package is ESM. Components with a heavy engine (charts, data grid, code editor, calendar, QR code, dependency graph) live in their own entry points, with optional peer dependencies, so importing a `Button` never pulls them in.

## The identity

- Floating, independent surfaces. Cards, dialogs and panels have a 22px radius; the bottom sheet has 32px.
- Buttons with text, fields, filters and tabs are capsules.
- The primary color is a yellow that stays the same in light and dark.
- No borders around components: pieces are set apart by fill. The one exception is the outline card.
- No gradients.
- Icons from Phosphor, with the filled form on the selected item.

## The packages

| Package | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `@aurea-uds/react` | The React components, typed |
| `@aurea-uds/core` | The CSS (tokens and components) and a small plain-JavaScript behavior layer |
| `@aurea-uds/fonts` | Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Mono, for the web and for React Native |
| `@aurea-uds/icons` | The Phosphor icon sprite |
| `@aurea-uds/tokens` | The tokens in DTCG format, as CSS, JSON and a native module |
| `@aurea-uds/native` | The React Native components |
| `@aurea-uds/contracts` | The contract and the API surface of every component |

All seven packages are released together, with the same version number. What changed in each release is in the [changelog](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## FAQ

**Is Aurea free?**
Yes. It is open source under the Apache License 2.0, free for everyone. The fonts are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 and the icons under MIT.

**Is it stable?**
Aurea is still in `0.x`. A minor release can break the API, and every break is written in the changelog. The road to `1.0` is on the [Roadmap](./docs-roadmap.html).

**Can I use it without React?**
Yes. Install `@aurea-uds/core` and `@aurea-uds/fonts` and use the CSS classes in plain HTML. See [Frameworks](./docs-frameworks.html).

**Does it work with Server Components?**
Yes. The main entry point can be imported from a Server Component, and the interactive modules carry `"use client"` themselves. Two proof apps, one with Server Components and one client-only, are built on every check.

**Is React Native the same package?**
No. `@aurea-uds/native` is a separate package with its own list of components and its own dependencies. It is not the web list with fewer items.

**What language are the built-in texts in?**
English by default. A Portuguese table ships with the packages, and any single sentence can be replaced through the provider.

## Get involved

- Questions, requests and bugs: [open an issue](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/issues). Every issue is read; what makes sense joins the queue, with no promised date.
- Contributing: read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- Security: follow [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/blob/main/SECURITY.md) and do not open a public issue.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-quick-start.html">
# Quick Start

Install the packages, load the fonts before the core, and wrap the app in the provider.

## Requirements

- React 19 or newer, with `react-dom` 19 or newer. Components take `ref` as a plain prop, which is React 19 behavior.
- A bundler that reads the `exports` map of a package and imports CSS files, such as Vite or Next.js.

The packages are ESM. Using React Native? Skip to [React Native](#react-native): it is a different package.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/react @aurea-uds/core @aurea-uds/fonts @aurea-uds/icons
```

No React? `@aurea-uds/core` and `@aurea-uds/fonts` are enough. See [Frameworks](./docs-frameworks.html) for plain HTML.

## Import the styles

Import the fonts **before** the core. The core embeds no font.

```tsx
import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css";
import "@aurea-uds/core/css";
```

Put these two lines once, in the entry file of your app (for example `src/main.tsx` in Vite, or `app/layout.tsx` in Next.js).

## Add the provider

Wrap the app in `AureaProvider`. It hands out the default sentences, tells the components where the icon sprite is, and mounts what tooltips and toasts use.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export default function App() {
  return <AureaProvider><Screen /></AureaProvider>;
}
```

The default sentences are in English. For Portuguese, pass the table that ships with the package, or replace single sentences:

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, ptBR} from "@aurea-uds/react";

<AureaProvider strings={ptBR}>…</AureaProvider>
<AureaProvider strings={{close: "Fechar"}}>…</AureaProvider>
```

## Set up the icons

The icons are one static SVG sprite. Copy `node_modules/@aurea-uds/icons/dist/aurea-icons.svg` to the folder your app serves as static files (`public/` in Vite and in Next.js).

By default the components look for it at `/aurea-icons.svg`, which only works when the app is served at the root of the domain. If yours is not, set the address once in the provider:

```tsx
<AureaProvider spriteUrl="/assets/aurea-icons.svg">…</AureaProvider>
```

Without the sprite, every icon of every component fails silently. More in [Icons](./docs-icons.html).

## Your first component

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";

<Button variant="primary">Save</Button>
```

Every component is also available by category, for example `@aurea-uds/react/actions` or `@aurea-uds/react/inputs`. Browse them all in [Components](./components.html).

## Theme and density

Aurea reads two attributes on the `html` element: `data-theme` (`light` or `dark`) and `data-density` (`compact`, `comfortable` or `spacious`). Write them in your markup so the first paint already has the right theme:

```html
<html data-theme="dark" data-density="comfortable">
```

To change them at runtime, use the `useAureaTheme()` hook or the [ThemeToggle](./themetoggle.html) component. More in [Dark Mode](./docs-dark-mode.html) and [Density](./docs-density.html).

## React Native

Mobile is another package, `@aurea-uds/native`, with its own list of components and its own dependencies. It is not the web list with fewer items. Do not install `@aurea-uds/react` or `@aurea-uds/core` in a React Native app.

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/native react-native-svg react-native-safe-area-context
```

It needs React 19 or newer and React Native 0.76 or newer. For the text to use Atkinson Hyperlegible, add `@aurea-uds/fonts` and load its native files. The example below uses `useFonts` from Expo:

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, Button, Screen} from "@aurea-uds/native";
import {AUREA_FONTS, FONT_FAMILIES} from "@aurea-uds/fonts/native";
import {useFonts} from "expo-font";

export default function App() {
  const [ready] = useFonts(AUREA_FONTS);
  if (!ready) return null;
  return (
    <AureaProvider fontFamilies={FONT_FAMILIES}>
      <Screen scroll>
        <Button tone="brand">Save</Button>
      </Screen>
    </AureaProvider>
  );
}
```

The date, photo and file pickers need optional dependencies of their own. The package README lists them: [packages/native](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/tree/main/packages/native).

## After you upgrade

Restart the dev server (`vite`, `next dev`) after upgrading Aurea. A server that was already running keeps serving the previous version, and the symptoms mislead: icons requested by old names, or components without the new feature. A restart is enough; there is no cache to delete.

## What's next

- [Frameworks](./docs-frameworks.html): Next.js, Vite, plain HTML and React Native.
- [Components](./components.html): every component, with its props table.
- [Theming](./docs-theming.html): tokens, themes and densities.
- [Blocks](./blocks.html): ready sections to drop into a page.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-design-principles.html">
# Design Principles

The ten rules behind every Aurea component, and how each one is checked.

Aurea is a design system for React on the web and React Native. It follows ten principles. Each one comes from a recorded decision, and most of them are enforced by a test or a build check, not by convention.

## Core principles

### 1. Low vision first

Aurea is designed for people who see poorly, and that choice shapes the rest of the system. The text font is Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, made to be legible for low-vision readers. Focus is always visible. Touch targets are at least 44px. Contrast is measured in the browser, not estimated.

Where the identity and legibility pull in different directions, the trade-off is written down, with its numbers. See [Accessibility](./docs-accessibility.html).

### 2. Tokens are the single source

Every colour, radius, font, weight, line height and space comes from a token. The tokens live in one file in the DTCG format (`$value` and `$type`). The CSS is one output of that file. The object the native package reads is another.

A raw number in a component is treated as a defect. The build ratchets raw pixel, radius, font and weight values, so a new one fails.

```css
.my-panel {
  border-radius: var(--radius-card);
  padding: var(--space-4);
  background: var(--card);
}
```

See [Tokens](./tokens.html).

### 3. A shape you can recognise

The geometry is fixed and shared by every component.

- Surfaces float. Cards, dialogs and panels have a 22px corner (`--radius-card`).
- The sheet that rises from the bottom has a 32px corner (`--radius-sheet`).
- Text buttons, fields, filters and tabs are capsules (`--radius-control`).
- A button that holds only an icon is a circle, at every size, on both targets.

Nothing is square.

### 4. No lines

Aurea components do not draw borders. Every border colour is transparent. The border width stays, so no measurement changes.

What a line used to separate is separated by a fill instead. The fills are the text colour, made translucent: `--fill-1` at 6%, `--fill-2` at 10%, `--fill-3` at 20%. Because they are translucent, they stay visible on any surface. Where something passes behind a piece, the opaque version is used (`--fill-2-solid`, `--fill-3-solid`).

Two lines remain, by decision:

- the outline card, `Card variant="outline"`, with a light line;
- the full-width line under the area tabs of a site header (`Header` with `tabs` and `divider`).

The focus ring is not a border. It stays.

### 5. No gradients

Aurea uses no gradients, including functional ones such as progress bars. Depth comes from surface and space. Gradients also disappear when a user forces high-contrast colours.

There is one exception: the colour pickers paint the colours you choose from (the `ColorArea` and the colour track of the `Slider`). That code lives in one file. The validator fails the build if a gradient appears in the stylesheet, the site or any other component file.

### 6. The yellow does not change

The brand yellow is `oklch(0.795 0.184 86.047)`. It is the same in the dark and the light theme.

A brand (`data-brand`) is a separate axis from the theme. A brand redefines colour and nothing else: type, radius, density, spacing and icons stay Aurea's. Without `data-brand`, nothing changes.

See [Colors](./docs-colors.html) and [Theming](./docs-theming.html).

### 7. Meaning before appearance

A button has two independent axes. `appearance` says how it is drawn. `tone` says what it means.

```tsx
<Button appearance="solid" tone="brand">Save</Button>
<Button appearance="outline" tone="neutral">Edit</Button>
<Button appearance="ghost" tone="danger" leadingIcon="trash">Delete</Button>
```

| Axis | Values |
|---|---|
| `appearance` | `solid`, `outline`, `ghost`, `link`, `nav`, `soft` |
| `tone` | `neutral`, `brand`, `danger`, `success`, `warning`, `info` |

If two different intentions end up looking the same, the meaning wins and gets its own token. The API does not degrade in silence: a value you ask for is the value you get.

### 8. Behaviour from a proven engine, skin from Aurea

Aurea does not reimplement focus, keyboard or ARIA. On the web, behaviour comes from Base UI and the skin is entirely Aurea's: no engine style reaches the core stylesheet. On native, components are built on React Native primitives, with a plain `StyleSheet` and Aurea's own theme provider.

Presentation is CSS first. When a prop changes semantics, keyboard or ARIA (for example, the orientation of `Tabs`), JavaScript resolves it, so the drawing and the behaviour never disagree.

### 9. One API across web and native

Props that exist on both targets have the same name and the same values. `tone`, `appearance` and `size` mean the same thing in `@aurea-uds/react` and `@aurea-uds/native`.

```tsx
// Web
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
<Button appearance="solid" tone="brand" size="md">Save</Button>

// React Native
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/native";
<Button appearance="solid" tone="brand" size="md" onPress={save}>Save</Button>
```

The scale is adapted to each target. Web controls are 32, 36 and 40px tall (`sm`, `md`, `lg`, comfortable density). Native controls use a scale made for the finger: 40, 48 and 56 (`--touch-control-h-sm`, `-md`, `-lg`). Both scales move with the three densities: compact, comfortable and spacious. See [Density](./docs-density.html).

### 10. Grow by variation, never by removal

A component is corrected, never removed. A new need enters as a variant or a prop of a component that already exists. When a component is renamed, the old name keeps working: `Topbar` still works next to `Header`.

This keeps upgrades additive. Code written against an earlier version keeps compiling, except where a release note says otherwise.

## How the principles are kept

Each principle has a check behind it, so it cannot drift quietly.

| Principle | Checked by |
|---|---|
| Tokens only | the validator's raw-value ratchet |
| No lines | a unit test that reads the code in every state, and a browser sweep of every page in both themes |
| No gradients | the validator, on the stylesheet, the site and the component code |
| Round icon-only buttons | a geometry test, in the three densities |
| One focus line | a sweep that tabs through every preview |
| Measured contrast | axe on every page, in both themes |

The site sweeps run in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-frameworks.html">
# Frameworks

Use Aurea with Next.js, Vite, plain HTML or React Native.

Two proof apps are built on every check of the repository: one in Next.js with Server Components, one in Vite with client rendering only. The examples on this page follow what they do. If a `"use client"` directive goes missing or shows up where it is not needed, those builds fail.

## Next.js

The App Router works with Server Components out of the box. You do not add `"use client"` to use Aurea.

### 1. Install the packages

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/react @aurea-uds/core @aurea-uds/fonts @aurea-uds/icons
```

Copy `node_modules/@aurea-uds/icons/dist/aurea-icons.svg` to `public/`. Next.js serves it at `/aurea-icons.svg`, which is where the components look by default.

### 2. Set up the root layout

The layout stays a Server Component. Import the fonts before the core, write the theme on the `html` element, and wrap the content in the provider.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import type {ReactNode} from "react";
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/react";
import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css";
import "@aurea-uds/core/css";

export default function RootLayout({children}: {children: ReactNode}) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" data-theme="dark">
      <body>
        <AureaProvider>{children}</AureaProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

### 3. Use your first component

A page can import from the main entry point without any directive.

```tsx
// app/page.tsx
import {Button, Card, Stack} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <main>
      <Card>
        <Stack>
          <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>
        </Stack>
      </Card>
    </main>
  );
}
```

### What runs where

- The main entry point is a server module, so importing from it in a Server Component works.
- The interactive modules carry `"use client"` themselves.
- Components that are only markup, such as `Card`, `Stack`, `Cluster` and `Grid`, render on the server and send no JavaScript.
- The helpers `cx`, `defaultStrings`, `ptBR` and `defaultSpriteUrl` can be called on the server.

A Server Component cannot pass a function to a client component. When you need state or an event handler, move that part to a file of your own marked `"use client"`:

```tsx
// app/save-toggle.tsx
"use client";

import {useState} from "react";
import {Toggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function SaveToggle() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  return <Toggle pressed={on} onPressedChange={setOn}>Autosave</Toggle>;
}
```

## Vite

### 1. Install the packages

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/react @aurea-uds/core @aurea-uds/fonts @aurea-uds/icons
```

Copy `node_modules/@aurea-uds/icons/dist/aurea-icons.svg` to `public/`.

### 2. Set up the entry file

```tsx
// src/main.tsx
import {StrictMode} from "react";
import {createRoot} from "react-dom/client";
import {AureaProvider, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css";
import "@aurea-uds/core/css";

function App() {
  return <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>;
}

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <AureaProvider><App /></AureaProvider>
  </StrictMode>
);
```

Write the theme in `index.html`, on the `html` element, so the first paint is already right:

```html
<html lang="en" data-theme="dark" data-density="comfortable">
```

In a client-only bundler the `"use client"` directives are plain text and are dropped. Nothing else changes.

If the app is not served at the root of the domain, set `spriteUrl` on the provider to where the sprite really is.

## Plain HTML

Without React, install the CSS and the fonts:

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/core @aurea-uds/fonts
```

Load the fonts **before** the core. Plain HTML does not understand package names, so point to the installed files (adjust the path) or serve them through a bundler.

```html
<html data-theme="dark" data-density="comfortable">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@aurea-uds/fonts/dist/fonts.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@aurea-uds/core/dist/aurea.css">
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
</html>
```

With a bundler, use the entry points instead: `import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css"` and `import "@aurea-uds/core/css"`.

The core also ships a small plain-JavaScript file, `@aurea-uds/core/js`, for behavior the markup cannot do alone, such as tabs that move with the arrow keys and the copy and share buttons. It does nothing when there is no page, so it is safe to import during server rendering.

```html
<script src="node_modules/@aurea-uds/core/dist/aurea.js"></script>
```

## React Native

React Native uses its own package, `@aurea-uds/native`, with its own components. It works with Expo and needs React Native 0.76 or newer.

```bash
pnpm add @aurea-uds/native react-native-svg react-native-safe-area-context
```

The setup, with fonts and the provider, is in [Quick Start](./docs-quick-start.html#react-native).

## Next steps

- [Quick Start](./docs-quick-start.html)
- [Components](./components.html)
- [Dark Mode](./docs-dark-mode.html)
- [Styling](./docs-styling.html)
</page>

# Showcase

What is built with Aurea today, and how to get your project listed here.

## This site

The site you are reading is built only with Aurea. Every page, from the header and the side navigation to the code blocks and the live examples, uses the same components and tokens that are published on npm.

This is enforced, not just intended: a check in the repository fails the build when the site imports anything from outside Aurea or loads a resource from another address. When the site needs a piece that does not exist, the piece is created in Aurea first.

Use the theme switch in the header to see every page in light and in dark.

## Blocks

The [Blocks](./blocks.html) area holds ready sections, larger than a pattern and smaller than a screen: sign-in panel, settings form, members table, stats row, pricing row, activity panel, analytics workbench, media library and more. Each one is built with the components of this site, and its code is on its page.

## Patterns and recipes

- [Patterns](./patterns.html): components already assembled in one specific way, ready to copy.
- [Recipes](./recipes.html): product archetypes, with the patterns to use and the rules to hold for a whole kind of application.

## Your project here

Built something with Aurea and want it listed? [Open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/issues) with the name, a link and one sentence about it.

Only public projects are listed, and only with the owner's permission.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-roadmap.html">
# Roadmap

Where Aurea stands, and what has to be true before version 1.0.

Aurea is in `0.x`. No dates are promised here: each step ships when it is done and checked. What changed in each release is in the [changelog](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## What 0.x means

- A minor release can break the API.
- Every break is written in the changelog. `0.x` is not a license to break things silently.
- All seven packages move together, with the same version number.

## What 1.0 will promise

From `1.0` on, Aurea follows [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org) without the `0.x` exception: the public API does not break without a new major version.

## Already in place

- The web packages (React and plain CSS) and the React Native package, on the public npm registry.
- Server Components support, proven on every check by two apps that are built from the packages: one in Next.js, one in Vite.
- Tests in three browser engines: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
- Pixel snapshots of the site, and an accessibility sweep of every page in both themes.
- A check that installs the published packages in a clean folder and builds them on both sides of the server and client boundary.
- A props table on the component pages, checked against the TypeScript types.

## Before 1.0

1. **Finish the open requests.** The requests from apps that use Aurea today are worked through first.
2. **Review every component, variant by variant.** Anatomy, sizes, states and keyboard behavior are checked one component at a time, and corrected where they fall short.
3. **Run the native package on iOS devices.** It has been tested on Android devices; iPhone runs come before `1.0`.
4. **More brand palettes.** The brand axis changes color only, and the yellow of the default brand stays fixed. Two more ready-made palettes come before `1.0`.
5. **An independent audit.** Everything is reviewed by someone who did not write the code, and what the audit finds is fixed before the release.
6. **A final visual review** of every page, in both themes.

## Decided not to build

- **A rich text engine.** The block editor gives the frame; the text engine stays with your app. The reason is security: whoever owns the editing surface owns the safety of pasted HTML, and only your app can decide what is safe to render.
- **Routing in React Native.** Aurea gives the look of the navigation; the router is your app's choice.
- **Gradients.** They are not part of the identity. The one exception is inside the color pickers, where the gradient is the content itself.

## Ask for something

Missing a component or a feature? [Open an issue](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/issues). Every issue is read; what makes sense joins the queue, with no promised date.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-colors.html">
# Colors

The color roles of Aurea, what each one is for, and their values in the light and dark themes.

Aurea names colors by role, not by hue. A component asks for "the card" or "the text on the primary button", and each theme answers with its own value.

Every role is a CSS custom property. The values come from the token file (DTCG format) and are written in hex or OKLCH. The same roles exist in React Native, with camelCase names.

The page always has a theme: `data-theme="light"` or `data-theme="dark"` on `<html>`. Without it, the color roles are not defined. See [Dark Mode](./docs-dark-mode.html).

```css
.my-panel {
  background: var(--card);
  color: var(--card-foreground);
}

.my-action {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: var(--primary-foreground);
}
```

## Accent

The accent is the brand yellow, `oklch(0.795 0.184 86.047)`. It is the same in both themes. It marks the main action, the current item and the chosen control.

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--primary` | The yellow fill: the primary button, the brand card, full bars |
| `--primary-foreground` | Text and icons on the yellow. Dark gray in both themes |
| `--primary-hover` | The yellow fill under the pointer |
| `--primary-active` | The yellow fill while pressed |
| `--primary-emphasis` | Yellow used as text or icon: the current item, the primary badge |
| `--primary-outline` | Yellow used as a stroke or a thin mark |
| `--primary-mark` | The small brown mark on the yellow: the switch knob, the slider thumb center |
| `--link` | Link text |
| `--link-hover` | Link text under the pointer |
| `--control-selected` | A checked checkbox, radio, switch or slider |
| `--control-selected-foreground` | The check mark on a checked control |
| `--control-selected-dot` | The white dot of a checked radio |

In the light theme the yellow is also the text color for emphasis and links. It measures 1.75:1 on the light page background, below the 4.5:1 that body text needs. Use it for emphasis, never for long text.

## Neutrals

Neutrals are the grays that fill quiet controls and hover states.

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--secondary` | The neutral fill of secondary and tertiary buttons, and of a list item under the pointer |
| `--secondary-foreground` | Text on `--secondary` |
| `--secondary-hover` | `--secondary` under the pointer |
| `--muted` | A quiet neutral fill |
| `--accent` | The hover fill of outline and ghost buttons. In Aurea it is a gray, not the brand color |
| `--accent-foreground` | Text on `--accent` |
| `--segment` | The chosen tab in tabs and segmented controls |

## Fills

Aurea draws no borders around components. A piece that needs to stand apart from what is behind it gets a fill instead. The fills are the text color at a low opacity, so they show on any background.

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--fill-1` | The text color at 6% |
| `--fill-2` | The text color at 10%: fields, outline buttons, toolbars, code blocks |
| `--fill-3` | The text color at 20%: the box of a checkbox or radio, the track of a switch |
| `--fill-2-solid` | `--fill-2` mixed opaque over the page color |
| `--fill-3-solid` | `--fill-3` mixed opaque over the page color |

Use the `-solid` versions when something passes behind the piece, or when one piece covers another. A see-through fill would let it show.

## Status colors

There are four status colors: success, warning, danger and info. Each one has three roles, and they are never swapped.

| Role | Success | Warning | Danger | Info |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full fill | `--success` | `--warning` | `--destructive` | `--info` |
| Text on the fill | `--success-foreground` | `--warning-foreground` | `--destructive-foreground` | `--info-foreground` |
| Fill under the pointer | `--success-hover` | `--warning-hover` | none | `--info-hover` |
| Text, icon or bar on the page | `--success-400` | `--warning-400` | `--danger-400` | `--info-400` |
| Soft background | `--success-bg` | `--warning-bg` | `--danger-bg` | `--info-bg` |

- The full fill is the **same color in both themes**. A solid success button looks the same in light and dark.
- Text on the warning fill is dark gray. Text on the other three fills is white.
- Text, icons and progress bars on the page use the `-400` role. Each theme sets it so it reads on its own surfaces.
- **Never paint text with a full fill color.** In the dark theme, the fills used as text fall below 4.5:1.

## Foreground

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--foreground` | Body text |
| `--foreground-strong` | Text that must stand out a little more |
| `--muted-foreground` | Secondary text: hints, descriptions, metadata |
| `--subtle-foreground` | Quiet text |
| `--text-muted` | Another name for `--muted-foreground` |

## Background

`--background` is the page. The `<body>` gets it, with `--foreground` as its text color, as soon as the Aurea CSS loads.

## Surface

Surfaces float over the page: cards, dialogs, menus, panels.

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--card` | Cards, dialogs and panels |
| `--card-foreground` | Text on a card |
| `--popover` | Menus, popovers and tooltips |
| `--popover-foreground` | Text on a popover |
| `--surface-1` | The first level of surface. Same as `--card` |
| `--surface-2` | The second level |
| `--surface-3` | The third level |
| `--surface-inset` | A recessed area, below the page |
| `--surface-hover` | A surface under the pointer |
| `--sidebar` | The application sidebar |
| `--sidebar-foreground` | Text in the sidebar |
| `--sidebar-primary` | The current item in the sidebar |
| `--sidebar-accent` | A sidebar item under the pointer |

## Form field

Fields (input, textarea, select, number field) are filled with `--fill-2`. They have no border.

An invalid field turns its fill to `--danger-bg`, and its focus ring to `--danger-400`. No red line is drawn.

The `secondary` look of a field uses `--secondary` instead.

## Separator

`--border` is the color of the [Separator](./separator.html), a 1px drawn line between groups. It is a fill, not a border around a piece.

The outline card is the only component with a border. Its line is the text color at 10%.

## Category colors

Eight colors mark a **group**, not a status: "Cars" and "Bikes", not "done" or "failed". They are `red`, `orange`, `green`, `teal`, `cyan`, `blue`, `violet` and `pink`.

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--category-red` | Text and icon of the category |
| `--category-red-bg` | The soft background of the category |

The other seven follow the same pattern. Yellow is not a category: it belongs to the brand.

- Category colors do not change with the brand. The name says the color.
- Neighbors on the color wheel alternate two lightness levels, so they differ by more than hue.
- Each one passes 4.5:1 in both themes.
- The color never goes alone. Put the word on it, and an icon if you can.

The [Badge](./badge.html) takes them as `variant` on the web and as `tone` in React Native.

## Other

| Token | Use |
|---|---|
| `--focus-strong` | The focus ring. The yellow in the dark theme, the text color in the light theme |
| `--selection` | Selected text |
| `--overlay` | The veil behind dialogs and drawers |
| `--chart-1` to `--chart-5` | The chart scale. In the default brand, five steps of one blue |

## Primitives

Primitives are the raw values behind the roles. They are the same in both themes. Prefer the roles.

| Token | Value |
|---|---|
| `--brand-yellow` | `oklch(0.795 0.184 86.047)` |
| `--brand-yellow-ink` | `#242424`, the text on the yellow |
| `--brand-yellow-foreground` | `oklch(0.421 0.095 57.708)`, the brown mark on the yellow |
| `--white` | `oklch(1 0 0)` |
| `--black` | `oklch(0 0 0)` |

## How to use colors

Pair each fill with its own text color. `--card` goes with `--card-foreground`, `--primary` with `--primary-foreground`.

```css
.notice {
  background: var(--warning-bg);
  color: var(--foreground);
}

.notice-icon {
  color: var(--warning-400);
}

.save {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: var(--primary-foreground);
}

.save:hover {
  background: var(--primary-hover);
}
```

In React Native, read the roles from `useAureaTokens()`. Colors come as hex strings, because React Native does not read OKLCH.

```tsx
import {View, Text} from "react-native";
import {useAureaTokens} from "@aurea-uds/native";

export function Panel() {
  const t = useAureaTokens();
  return (
    <View style={{backgroundColor: t.color.card}}>
      <Text style={{color: t.color.cardForeground}}>Saved</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

## Default theme

The main roles, side by side.

| Token | Light | Dark |
|---|---|---|
| `--background` | `#f5f5f5` | `#1f1f1f` |
| `--foreground` | `#242424` | `#ffffff` |
| `--card` | `#ffffff` | `#292929` |
| `--secondary` | `#ebebeb` | `#333333` |
| `--muted-foreground` | `#616161` | `#adadad` |
| `--border` | `#e0e0e0` | `#525252` |
| `--primary` | the brand yellow | the brand yellow |
| `--primary-foreground` | `#242424` | `#242424` |
| `--success` | `#107c10` | `#107c10` |
| `--success-400` | `#0e700e` | `#54b054` |
| `--warning` | `#f7630c` | `#f7630c` |
| `--warning-400` | `#8a3707` | `#faa06b` |
| `--destructive` | `#c50f1f` | `#c50f1f` |
| `--danger-400` | `#b10e1c` | `#eeacb2` |
| `--info` | `#0078d4` | `#0078d4` |
| `--info-400` | `#006cbf` | `#5caae5` |
| `--overlay` | black at 40% | black at 50% |

Every token, with its value in each theme, is on the [Tokens](./tokens.html) page.

## Customizing colors

The yellow is Aurea's identity and stays the same in every theme. Another palette comes in as a **brand**, with `data-brand`. You can also override a single role in your own CSS. Both are explained in [Theming](./docs-theming.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-theming.html">
# Theming

How Aurea's tokens become CSS custom properties, the three attributes that switch them, and how to change a value.

Aurea's look comes from tokens. The tokens live in one file, in the DTCG format, and a build turns them into CSS custom properties for the web and a JavaScript module for React Native.

Components never hold a color or a size of their own. They read the tokens. Change a token and every component that uses it follows.

## How it works

Three attributes switch the tokens. Each one is independent of the others.

| Attribute | Values | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| `data-theme` | `light`, `dark` | Every color role |
| `data-density` | `compact`, `comfortable`, `spacious` | Control heights, table rows, card padding |
| `data-brand` | `lory` | The color palette, in both themes |

Everything else (type, space, radius, motion, shadows) is set once on `:root` and is the same in every theme, density and brand.

Each group of tokens is emitted under its own selector:

```css
:root { /* type, space, radius, motion: the same everywhere */ }
[data-theme="dark"] { /* the dark color roles */ }
[data-theme="light"] { /* the light color roles */ }
[data-density="compact"] { /* the compact sizes */ }
[data-brand="lory"][data-theme="dark"] { /* the brand palette, dark */ }
```

```html
<html data-theme="dark" data-density="comfortable">
  <body>
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
  </body>
</html>
```

## Quick start

Load the fonts, then the Aurea CSS, and put a theme on `<html>`.

```tsx
import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css"; // before the core
import "@aurea-uds/core/css";
```

```html
<html data-theme="light" data-density="comfortable">
```

`data-theme` is required: without it the color roles are not defined. `data-density` is optional: without it you get the comfortable sizes.

To switch the theme at run time, see [Dark Mode](./docs-dark-mode.html). For the density, see [Density](./docs-density.html).

## Naming pattern

- A name without a suffix is a fill: `--primary`, `--card`, `--success`.
- `-foreground` is the text on that fill: `--primary-foreground`, `--card-foreground`.
- `-hover` and `-active` are the fill under the pointer and while pressed.
- `-400` is a status color used as text, icon or bar on the page: `--success-400`.
- `-bg` is a soft status background: `--success-bg`.
- `-solid` is an opaque version of a see-through fill: `--fill-2-solid`.

The full list of color roles is on [Colors](./docs-colors.html).

## Brands

A brand is a second palette. It is set with `data-brand`, next to `data-theme`.

```html
<html data-brand="lory" data-theme="light">
```

- **A brand changes color only.** Type, radius, density, space and icons stay Aurea's in every brand.
- **A brand has a light and a dark palette.** The theme still works inside it.
- **Without `data-brand`, nothing changes.** You get Aurea as it is.
- **Inside Aurea's own palette, the yellow never changes.** It is the same in light and dark.

The package ships one brand, `lory`. A brand lives in the token file, next to the themes, and the build emits it with them. Brands are web only today: the React Native package has no brand axis.

## A theme for one part of the page

The selectors are attributes, not `:root`, so `data-theme` works on any element. Everything inside follows it.

```html
<html data-theme="light">
  <body>
    <section data-theme="dark">A dark band inside a light page</section>
  </body>
</html>
```

The components do the same for you:

- [Section](./section.html) takes `theme="dark"` or `theme="light"` for one band of a page.
- [Card](./card.html) with `variant="contrast"` puts the dark theme inside the card.

A brand set on an ancestor reaches a nested theme too: `[data-brand="lory"] [data-theme="dark"]` is part of the brand's selector.

## Overriding a token

All of Aurea's CSS sits in one cascade layer, named `aurea`. Any rule you write outside a layer wins over it, whatever the order of the files.

To change a role, redefine the custom property under the same selector:

```css
[data-theme="dark"] {
  --background: #181818;
  --card: #222222;
}
```

To change it in one place only, scope it:

```css
.landing-banner {
  --card-pad: 1.5rem;
}
```

Keep the pairs together. If you change a fill, check the text that sits on it. Aurea measures the contrast of its own values in both themes; it cannot measure yours.

## Token formats

The `@aurea-uds/tokens` package ships the same tokens in three forms.

| Import | What it is |
|---|---|
| `@aurea-uds/tokens/css` | The CSS custom properties alone, without the component styles |
| `@aurea-uds/tokens/json` | The DTCG source file |
| `@aurea-uds/tokens/native` | The JavaScript module that the React Native package reads |

You do not need `@aurea-uds/tokens/css` if you load `@aurea-uds/core/css`: the core already includes the tokens.

## In React Native

React Native has no CSS cascade, so the tokens come from the provider. Wrap the app in `AureaProvider` from `@aurea-uds/native`, then read the resolved tokens with `useAureaTokens()`.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, useAureaTokens} from "@aurea-uds/native";
import {View} from "react-native";

function Box() {
  const t = useAureaTokens();
  return <View style={{backgroundColor: t.color.card, padding: t.size.cardPad}} />;
}

export function App() {
  return (
    <AureaProvider defaultTheme="light" defaultDensity="comfortable">
      <Box />
    </AureaProvider>
  );
}
```

- Names are camelCase: `--card-foreground` becomes `t.color.cardForeground`.
- `t.color` holds hex strings. React Native does not read OKLCH, so the hex form is the one that works.
- `t.size` holds every number in dp: space, radius, type, heights.
- Outside an `AureaProvider`, the hooks throw. There is no cascade to fall back on.

## Variables reference

Every token, with its value in each theme, brand and density, is on the [Tokens](./tokens.html) page.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-dark-mode.html">
# Dark Mode

Switch between the light and dark themes, follow the system, and save the choice.

Aurea's themes are CSS. The page reads its colors from the `data-theme` attribute on `<html>`: `light` or `dark`. Both themes are complete: light and dark are equal.

```html
<html data-theme="dark">
```

The attribute is required. Without it, the color roles are not defined and the page has no colors.

Put the theme in the markup that the server sends. Then the first paint is already right, with no flash.

```tsx
import {ThemeToggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function Toolbar() {
  return (
    <>
      <ThemeToggle />
      <ThemeToggle mode="light-dark-system" />
    </>
  );
}
```

## The theme switch

[ThemeToggle](./themetoggle.html) is the ready-made switch. It has two modes.

| Mode | What it is |
|---|---|
| `light-dark` | The default. One round button that flips the theme. It shows where it goes: a dark moon in the light theme, a yellow sun in the dark theme |
| `light-dark-system` | Three options in a row: light, dark and system. System follows the computer and changes with it |

The button's accessible name says what it does: "Switch to dark theme" or "Switch to light theme". The three-option mode is a radio group named "Theme", moved with the arrow keys.

ThemeToggle changes the theme. It does not save the choice. See [Saving the choice](#saving-the-choice).

## With AureaProvider

[AureaProvider](./aureaprovider.html) can own the theme. It writes `data-theme` on `<html>` for you.

| Prop | What it does |
|---|---|
| `theme` | The theme, controlled: `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` |
| `defaultTheme` | The first theme, uncontrolled |
| `onThemeChange` | Called with the theme on screen: `"light"` or `"dark"` |
| `onThemePreferenceChange` | Called with what was chosen, which can be `"system"` |

- With `"system"`, the provider follows the computer's light or dark setting, and changes when it changes. The page still gets `light` or `dark`: the CSS knows only those two.
- With neither `theme` nor `defaultTheme`, the provider adopts the `data-theme` already in the markup. It does not overwrite it.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function App({children}: {children: React.ReactNode}) {
  return <AureaProvider defaultTheme="system">{children}</AureaProvider>;
}
```

## Reading the theme

`useAureaTheme()` reads the theme and the density straight from `<html>`. It follows the attribute, whoever changes it.

| Field | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `theme` | `"light"`, `"dark"` or `null` | The theme on screen |
| `preference` | `"light"`, `"dark"`, `"system"` or `null` | What was chosen. Outside a provider, the theme on screen |
| `density` | `"compact"`, `"comfortable"`, `"spacious"` or `null` | The density on screen |
| `setTheme` | function | Sets `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` |
| `toggleTheme` | function | Flips what is on screen |
| `setDensity` | function | Sets the density |

`theme` is `null` on the server, because the server cannot know it. While it is `null`, do not render anything that depends on the theme.

Inside an `AureaProvider`, `setTheme` goes through the provider. Outside one, it writes the attribute directly. Outside a provider, `"system"` writes the computer's current theme once; it does not follow later changes.

`useTheme()` is the other hook. It reads the theme from the provider instead of the page. Use it only inside an `AureaProvider` that owns the theme. See [useAureaTheme](./useaureatheme.html) and [useTheme](./usetheme.html).

## Saving the choice

Aurea stores nothing, on purpose. Remembering a person's choice is the application's job.

Save the value from `onThemePreferenceChange`, and give it back as `defaultTheme` on the next visit.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, ThemeToggle, type AureaThemePreference} from "@aurea-uds/react";

const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme") as AureaThemePreference | null;

export function App() {
  return (
    <AureaProvider
      defaultTheme={saved ?? "system"}
      onThemePreferenceChange={(choice) => localStorage.setItem("theme", choice)}
    >
      <ThemeToggle mode="light-dark-system" />
    </AureaProvider>
  );
}
```

This example runs in the browser only. With server rendering, the saved theme has to reach `<html>` before the page paints. The next section does that.

## Next.js with next-themes

[next-themes](https://github.com/pacocoursey/next-themes) saves the choice, follows the system and sets the theme before the first paint. It writes `data-theme` on `<html>` by default: the same attribute Aurea reads. No glue code is needed.

```bash
pnpm add next-themes
```

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import {ThemeProvider} from "next-themes";
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/react";
import "@aurea-uds/fonts/css";
import "@aurea-uds/core/css";

export default function RootLayout({children}: {children: React.ReactNode}) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body>
        <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="system" enableSystem>
          <AureaProvider>{children}</AureaProvider>
        </ThemeProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

Leave `theme` and `defaultTheme` off the `AureaProvider`. Then next-themes is the only one writing the attribute.

Switch the theme with the `setTheme` of next-themes. ThemeToggle writes through Aurea, which next-themes does not see, so the choice would not be saved.

```tsx
"use client";
import {useTheme} from "next-themes";
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function ThemeButtons() {
  const {setTheme} = useTheme();
  return (
    <>
      <Button onClick={() => setTheme("light")}>Light</Button>
      <Button onClick={() => setTheme("dark")}>Dark</Button>
      <Button onClick={() => setTheme("system")}>System</Button>
    </>
  );
}
```

To read the theme in a component, `useAureaTheme()` works next to next-themes, because it reads the attribute.

## Plain HTML

Without React, set the attribute yourself, or use the small script in `@aurea-uds/core/js`:

```html
<script src="node_modules/@aurea-uds/core/dist/aurea.js"></script>
<script>
  window.Aurea.setTheme("light");
</script>
```

## A dark part in a light page

`data-theme` works on any element, not only `<html>`. A [Section](./section.html) with `theme="dark"` makes a dark band in a light page, and a [Card](./card.html) with `variant="contrast"` puts the dark theme inside one card. See [Theming](./docs-theming.html).

## Styling for both themes

Use the color roles, and your own styles follow the theme with no extra rule:

```css
.my-panel {
  background: var(--card);
  color: var(--card-foreground);
}
```

Avoid fixed colors. A hex value that reads well on one theme is usually wrong on the other. The roles are listed on [Colors](./docs-colors.html).

## In React Native

The native `AureaProvider` owns the theme. It is required: without it, the components have no colors.

- With no `theme` and no `defaultTheme`, it follows the device's light or dark setting, until `setTheme` is called. From then on, the choice wins.
- If the device does not report a setting, the theme is dark.
- `theme` is controlled. `defaultTheme` is the first value. `onThemeChange` reports a change.
- `useAureaTheme()` from `@aurea-uds/native` returns `theme`, `density`, `setTheme`, `setDensity` and `toggleTheme`. On the device the theme is never `null`.
- The native theme accepts `"light"` and `"dark"`. There is no `"system"` value: leaving the theme unset is how it follows the device.
- The native ThemeToggle is the round button that flips the theme. It draws the `moon` and `sun` icons from your icon registry, in their filled form. Register them, or the icon does not draw.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, ThemeToggle, criarRegistroDeIcones} from "@aurea-uds/native";
import MoonFill from "@aurea-uds/native/icons/moon-fill";
import SunFill from "@aurea-uds/native/icons/sun-fill";

const icons = criarRegistroDeIcones({"moon-fill": MoonFill, "sun-fill": SunFill});

export function App() {
  return (
    <AureaProvider icons={icons}>
      <ThemeToggle />
    </AureaProvider>
  );
}
```

Like on the web, the native provider saves nothing. Store the choice yourself and pass it back as `defaultTheme`.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-styling.html">
# Styling

Style Aurea with props first, then with a class name, plain CSS and the tokens.

Aurea ships one stylesheet, `@aurea-uds/core/css`. Every component draws itself with class names from it. You change the look in four ways, from the most to the least preferred: props, a class name, your own CSS, and the tokens.

## Start with props

Most changes are already a prop. A button has two axes: `appearance` (how much weight the box has) and `tone` (what the color means). `variant` is a shortcut for common pairs, and `size` picks a step of the scale.

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>
  <Button appearance="outline" tone="success">Approve</Button>
  <Button appearance="soft" tone="danger">Delete</Button>
  <Button appearance="ghost" size="sm">Cancel</Button>
</Cluster>
```

A prop keeps the component inside the system. It also keeps both themes, the three densities and high contrast working. Reach for CSS only when no prop does the job.

## Basic styling

Components accept `className`. Your class is added after Aurea's own classes, never in place of them.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" className="checkout-save">Save</Button>
```

The button above renders `class="btn btn-primary checkout-save"`. Components also accept `style` for inline values:

```tsx
<Card style={{maxInlineSize: "32rem"}}>Summary</Card>
```

## How your CSS wins

The whole stylesheet, tokens included, sits inside one cascade layer named `aurea`. A rule outside any layer beats a rule inside a layer, whatever the specificity. So plain CSS in your app overrides Aurea without `!important` and without long selectors.

```css
.checkout-save {
  min-inline-size: 12rem;
}
```

If your app puts its own CSS in layers too, declare the order once, with `aurea` first:

```css
@layer aurea, app;
```

## Use the tokens

In Aurea every color, radius, font size and space comes from a token. The tokens are CSS custom properties on `:root`. Use them in your own CSS, and your additions follow the theme and the density for free.

```css
.order-summary {
  padding: var(--space-4);
  border-radius: var(--radius-card);
  background: var(--fill-1);
  color: var(--foreground);
  font-size: var(--text-sm);
}
```

Two rules of the system apply to your CSS as well:

- **No gradients.** Aurea uses flat color only.
- **No lines.** Components draw no visible border; the `outline` card and the `Header` divider are the only lines. A piece that needs to stand out from the page gets a translucent fill (`--fill-1`, `--fill-2`, `--fill-3`) instead of an outline. The focus ring stays.

All tokens, with their values in each theme, are on the [Tokens](./tokens.html) page. To change the tokens themselves, see [Theming](./docs-theming.html).

## State-based styling

Interactive components built on Base UI expose their state as `data-*` attributes. Aurea's stylesheet styles these attributes, and you can target them the same way.

| Attribute | Where you see it |
|---|---|
| `data-pressed` | a `Toggle` that is on |
| `data-highlighted` | the menu item under the pointer or the keyboard |
| `data-selected` | the selected tag, tree node or calendar day |
| `data-disabled` | a disabled slider, menu item or tag |
| `data-popup-open` | a menu trigger while its menu is open |
| `data-starting-style` / `data-ending-style` | a dialog, popover, tooltip or toast while it enters or leaves |

Navigation and fields use ARIA attributes instead, because a screen reader reads the same attribute: `aria-current` marks the current page, `aria-pressed` a pressed button, `aria-invalid` a field with an error.

```css
.toggle[data-pressed] {
  color: var(--primary);
}

.sidebar-item[aria-current] {
  font-weight: var(--weight-semibold);
}
```

Some components wrap a native element and use its own state. A `Switch` is a checkbox with `role="switch"`, so its state is `:checked`.

## Responsive design

`size` and other scale props take a responsive value. Give a `base` and the steps that change it. The `viewport` steps react to the window width:

```tsx
<Button size={{base: "sm", viewport: {md: "lg"}}}>Save</Button>
```

The `container` steps react to the width of the nearest `ContainerScope` instead. Use them for a component that lives in panels of different widths:

```tsx
<ContainerScope>
  <Button size={{base: "sm", container: {md: "lg"}}}>Save</Button>
</ContainerScope>
```

| Step | Viewport from | Container from |
|---|---|---|
| `2xs` | 360px | 360px |
| `xs` | 480px | 480px |
| `sm` | 640px | 640px |
| `md` | 768px | 768px |
| `lg` | 1024px | 1024px |
| `xl` | 1280px | none |
| `2xl` | 1536px | none |

A value reacts to the viewport or to the container, never to both. For anything else, write a media query or a container query in your own CSS.

## Class names

Class names are short and flat: the block, then a modifier joined by a hyphen. These are the names the components emit, and the names you use in plain HTML.

| Component | Classes |
|---|---|
| `Button` | `.btn`, `.btn-primary`, `.btn-outline`, `.btn-tone-success`, `.btn-sm`, `.btn-icon` |
| `Card` | `.card`, `.card-raised`, `.card-interactive`, `.card-header`, `.card-title`, `.card-content`, `.card-footer` |
| `Icon` | `.icon`, `.icon-sm`, `.icon-lg`, `.icon-xl` |

To see the classes of any component, open its page and read the rendered markup, or search the stylesheet in `@aurea-uds/core/dist/aurea.css`.

## Plain HTML

The stylesheet works without React. Load the fonts first, then the core, and write the classes yourself:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@aurea-uds/fonts/dist/fonts.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="node_modules/@aurea-uds/core/dist/aurea.css">
<button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
```

The core also ships a small script, `@aurea-uds/core/js`. It is safe on any page and adds a few behaviors to plain markup:

- arrow keys, Home and End on an element with `role="tablist"`;
- copy to the clipboard for any trigger marked `data-aurea-copy`;
- `window.Aurea.setTheme`, `window.Aurea.setDensity` and `window.Aurea.toggleTheme`, which write the `data-theme` and `data-density` attributes;
- `window.Aurea.showToast` for a toast.

The React package does not need this script.

## Next steps

- Learn how components move in [Animation](./docs-animation.html).
- Change the tokens in [Theming](./docs-theming.html).
- Build bigger pieces in [Composition](./docs-composition.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-animation.html">
# Animation

The motion Aurea ships, the tokens behind it, and how it stops when the user asks for less movement.

Aurea moves little, and only to explain a change: a window that opens, a button that is pressed, something that is still loading. All of it is plain CSS in the core stylesheet. There is no animation library to install.

## Built-in motion

These components move on their own:

| What | How it moves |
|---|---|
| `Button` and `IconButton` | colors change smoothly; the button shrinks a little while pressed |
| `Dialog` | the backdrop fades in; the window fades in from slightly larger, and leaves slightly smaller |
| `Drawer` | slides in from its side |
| `Popover` and `Tooltip` | fade and grow in, fade and shrink out |
| `Toast` | slides in, and slides out in the direction it was swiped |
| `Accordion` | the chevron turns when an item opens |
| `Spinner`, `Skeleton`, `Progress`, `ProgressCircle` | loop while the wait has no end |

A tooltip opened from the keyboard, or moved to a neighbor, appears at once, without the entry animation.

```tsx
<Popover trigger={<Button>Open popover</Button>} title="Popover">
  It grows in and shrinks out.
</Popover>
```

## Motion tokens

Every transition in the core reads its timing from a token. Use the same tokens in your own CSS, and your motion matches the rest of the interface.

| Token | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `--duration-fast` | 120ms | color changes, presses, and dialogs, popovers and tooltips that leave |
| `--duration-base` | 180ms | the switch, popovers and tooltips that enter |
| `--duration-slow` | 280ms | dialogs, drawers and toasts that enter |
| `--ease-standard` | `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` | the default curve |
| `--ease-emphasized` | `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` | the drawer and the toast sliding in |

```css
.result-row {
  transition: background var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-standard);
}

.result-row:hover {
  background: var(--fill-1);
}
```

The loops (the spinner, the skeleton pulse and the indeterminate progress) keep their own timing, because they repeat.

## Entering and leaving

Dialogs, drawers, popovers, tooltips and toasts are built on Base UI. While one of them enters, it carries `data-starting-style`. While it leaves, it carries `data-ending-style`. The core sets the start and end look on these attributes, and the transition does the rest.

Change the movement by writing your own rule for the same attributes. Your CSS sits outside the `aurea` cascade layer, so it wins:

```css
.popover[data-starting-style],
.popover[data-ending-style] {
  opacity: 0;
  scale: 1;
}
```

This popover now only fades. See [Styling](./docs-styling.html) for the other state attributes.

## Reduced motion

Aurea follows the system setting. When the user turns on "reduce motion", the media query `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` matches, and the stylesheet acts on its own. It has eight rules for it:

- **One global rule.** It cuts every animation and every transition on the page to almost zero, plays each animation once, and turns smooth scrolling off.
- **Seven rules for single parts.** They remove the transition of the slider thumb, the color area thumb, the color swatch, the progress circle fill and the accordion chevron. The skeleton stops pulsing.
- **The indeterminate progress bar** does not freeze as a short piece, which would read as a value. It shows the whole bar, dimmed.

CSS cannot reach motion you start from JavaScript. Check the same setting before you animate:

```ts
const reduce = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;
```

## React Native

React Native has no stylesheet cascade, so there is no global rule. The native components that animate ask the system first, and stay still when the user asked for less movement ("Reduce Motion" on iOS, "Remove animations" on Android).

The same question is public for your own animations: `useReduceMotion()`. It returns `true`, `false`, or `null` while the system has not answered yet. Wait for the answer, so not even one frame plays for someone who asked for none. The durations come from the tokens, as numbers in milliseconds.

```tsx
import * as React from "react";
import {Animated} from "react-native";
import {useAureaTokens, useReduceMotion} from "@aurea-uds/native";

export function FadeIn({children}: {children: React.ReactNode}) {
  const t = useAureaTokens();
  const reduce = useReduceMotion();
  const opacity = React.useRef(new Animated.Value(0)).current;
  React.useEffect(() => {
    if (reduce === null) return;
    if (reduce) { opacity.setValue(1); return; }
    Animated.timing(opacity, {toValue: 1, duration: t.size.durationBase, useNativeDriver: true}).start();
  }, [reduce, opacity, t.size.durationBase]);
  return <Animated.View style={{opacity}}>{children}</Animated.View>;
}
```

## Next steps

- Target state attributes in [Styling](./docs-styling.html).
- See every token on the [Tokens](./tokens.html) page.
- Read how Aurea serves low vision in [Accessibility](./docs-accessibility.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-composition.html">
# Composition

Build bigger pieces from parts, slots, item lists and the render prop.

Aurea components fit together in a few fixed ways. A component can have parts, take other elements in named slots, draw a list from data, or hand its look to an element you choose. This page shows each one.

## Parts

Some components come in parts that you arrange yourself. The parts hang from the main component, with a dot.

```tsx
<Card>
  <Card.Header>
    <Card.Title>Weekly report</Card.Title>
    <Card.Description>Sent every Monday at 9:00.</Card.Description>
  </Card.Header>
  <Card.Content>12 people receive it.</Card.Content>
  <Card.Footer>
    <Button variant="primary">Edit</Button>
    <Button>Pause</Button>
  </Card.Footer>
</Card>
```

| Component | Parts |
|---|---|
| `Card` | `Card.Media`, `Card.Header`, `Card.Title`, `Card.Description`, `Card.Content`, `Card.Footer` |
| `RadioGroup` | `RadioGroup.Item` |
| `Grid` | `Grid.Item`, which takes a `span` of 1 to 12 columns |

Each part is optional. Use the ones you need, in the order the design asks for. `Card.Title` is an `h3`.

## Slots

Many components take other elements through named props. The component places them and spaces them; you choose what goes in.

```tsx
<AppShell
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  navItems={[
    {id: "home", label: "Home", href: "/", icon: "house"},
    {id: "reports", label: "Reports", href: "/reports", icon: "chart-bar"},
  ]}
  currentNavId="reports"
  topbar={<SearchField aria-label="Search" placeholder="Search" />}
>
  <Reports />
</AppShell>
```

| Component | Slots |
|---|---|
| `AppShell` | `brand`, `navigation`, `topbar`, `aside`, `children` |
| `Header` | `brand`, `actions`, `menuActions`, `children` |
| `Button` | `leadingIcon`, `trailingIcon`, `kbd` |
| `Badge` | `leading`, `trailing` |
| `Popover` | `trigger` |
| `Tooltip` | its single child is the trigger |

## Lists from data

Navigation and lists take an `items` array and draw the markup themselves: `Sidebar`, `Header`, `Breadcrumb`, `Timeline`, `Accordion`, `TreeView` and others. You pass data, Aurea keeps the structure, the keyboard behavior and the current-item marker right.

```tsx
<Breadcrumb
  items={[
    {label: "Home", href: "/"},
    {label: "Reports", href: "/reports"},
    {label: "Weekly"},
  ]}
/>
```

## The render prop

A button that navigates should be your router's link, not a `button` with a click handler. The `render` prop does that. Pass an element, and Aurea draws its own look and content on it.

```tsx
import {RouterLink} from "./router";

<Button variant="primary" leadingIcon="chart-bar" render={<RouterLink to="/reports" />}>
  Reports
</Button>
```

The element receives the classes, the content (icons, text, shortcut) and the attributes of the button. The destination stays yours. When the button is disabled or loading, the click is blocked on your element too.

These accept `render`:

- `Button` and `IconButton`;
- `Card`, which needs it with `variant="interactive"`, so a whole card can be a link;
- navigation items: the items of `Sidebar`, `AppShell`, `Header` (and its `tabs`), `NavList` and `Breadcrumb`, and the action items of `DropdownMenu`;
- `Image`.

```tsx
<Card variant="interactive" render={<RouterLink to="/reports/weekly" />}>
  <Card.Title>Weekly report</Card.Title>
</Card>
```

Follow two rules so behavior and accessibility stay right:

- Render the element that matches the job: a link for navigation, a button for an action.
- Your element's own props win over Aurea's, and its `className` is added after Aurea's. Do not drop the props it receives.

For a plain link you do not need `render`. A `Button` with `href` already renders an `a`.

## Your own components

Wrap an Aurea component to fix the props your app repeats. Keep the rest open.

```tsx
import {Button, type ButtonProps} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function SaveButton(props: Omit<ButtonProps, "variant">) {
  return <Button variant="primary" leadingIcon="floppy-disk" {...props} />;
}
```

Aurea itself grows the same way. A new need becomes a variation of an existing component, a new `variant` value or a new prop, before it becomes a new component. When you miss something, look for the variation first.

## Entry points

Everything is exported from `@aurea-uds/react`. The same components are also grouped by category, matching the catalog:

```tsx
import {Button, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react/actions";
import {Input, Select} from "@aurea-uds/react/inputs";
```

The categories are `actions`, `inputs`, `navigation`, `overlays`, `disclosure`, `feedback`, `data-display`, `identity`, `media`, `code`, `communication`, `layout`, `system` and `agents`. The package is tree-shaken either way. The categories help you read and adopt Aurea one area at a time.

Six heavier modules live only on their own entry point, so you install their engine only if you use them: `code-editor`, `data-grid`, `qrcode`, `calendar`, `chart` and `graph`.

## Next steps

- Change the look in [Styling](./docs-styling.html).
- Browse every component in [Components](./components.html).
- See full screens built from these pieces in [Patterns](./patterns.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-density.html">
# Density

Three sizes for the same interface, compact, comfortable and spacious, switched with one attribute.

Density sets how tall the controls are and how much room the content gets. Aurea has three: `compact`, `comfortable` and `spacious`.

Density is its own axis. It does not depend on the theme or the brand: each theme comes in all three densities.

Colors, type, radius and icons do not change with the density. Only sizes do.

```html
<div data-density="compact">
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
</div>
<div data-density="comfortable">
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
</div>
<div data-density="spacious">
  <button class="btn btn-primary" type="button">Save</button>
</div>
```

## Set the density

Put `data-density` on `<html>`:

```html
<html data-theme="dark" data-density="compact">
```

Without the attribute, the page gets the comfortable sizes. They are the default values of the tokens.

In React, [AureaProvider](./aureaprovider.html) can own the density:

| Prop | What it does |
|---|---|
| `density` | The density, controlled |
| `defaultDensity` | The first density, uncontrolled |
| `onDensityChange` | Called with the new density |

To read or change it from a component, use `useAureaTheme()`, which returns `density` and `setDensity`. Inside a provider, `useDensity()` does the same through the provider. See [useAureaTheme](./useaureatheme.html) and [useDensity](./usedensity.html).

```tsx
import {Button, useAureaTheme} from "@aurea-uds/react";

export function DensityButtons() {
  const {setDensity} = useAureaTheme();
  return (
    <>
      <Button onClick={() => setDensity("compact")}>Compact</Button>
      <Button onClick={() => setDensity("comfortable")}>Comfortable</Button>
      <Button onClick={() => setDensity("spacious")}>Spacious</Button>
    </>
  );
}
```

Without React, the script in `@aurea-uds/core/js` has `window.Aurea.setDensity("compact")`.

Aurea does not save the density. Like the theme, remembering it is the application's job.

## The tokens

These tokens change with the density. Every other token stays the same.

| Token | Compact | Comfortable | Spacious |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--control-h-xs` | `1.5rem` | `1.625rem` | `1.75rem` |
| `--control-h-sm` | `1.75rem` | `2rem` | `2.25rem` |
| `--control-h-md` | `2rem` | `2.25rem` | `2.5rem` |
| `--control-h-lg` | `2.25rem` | `2.5rem` | `2.75rem` |
| `--control-h-xl` | `2.75rem` | `3.125rem` | `3.5rem` |
| `--row-h` | `2.625rem` | `3rem` | `3.375rem` |
| `--card-pad` | `0.75rem` | `1rem` | `1.25rem` |
| `--section-gap` | `1.125rem` | `1.5rem` | `2rem` |
| `--touch-control-h-sm` | `2.25rem` | `2.5rem` | `2.75rem` |
| `--touch-control-h-md` | `2.75rem` | `3rem` | `3.25rem` |
| `--touch-control-h-lg` | `3.25rem` | `3.5rem` | `3.75rem` |

## What follows the density

- **Controls**, through `--control-h-*`: buttons, icon buttons, inputs, selects, textareas, tabs, segmented controls, menu items, list box items, pagination, sidebar items and switches.
- **Table rows**, through `--row-h`: the height of each cell.
- **Cards**, through `--card-pad`: the padding inside a card.
- **Your own layout**, through `--section-gap`: the space between sections. No web component uses it, so it is there for you.
- **React Native controls**, through `--touch-control-h-*`: the touch scale of the native buttons.

To size something of your own with the density, read the same tokens:

```css
.my-toolbar {
  min-height: var(--control-h-md);
  padding: var(--card-pad);
}
```

## Touch screens

On a touch screen, buttons, tabs, segmented controls, pagination and navigation list rows are at least 44px tall, whatever the density. The compact density never makes a target smaller than a finger.

This minimum is the token `--target-min` (`2.75rem`).

## A different density for one part

The selectors are attributes, so `data-density` works on any element, not only `<html>`. Everything inside follows it.

```html
<html data-theme="light" data-density="comfortable">
  <body>
    <aside data-density="compact">A dense side panel</aside>
  </body>
</html>
```

## In React Native

The native `AureaProvider` from `@aurea-uds/native` takes `density`, `defaultDensity` and `onDensityChange`. Without them, the density is comfortable.

- `useAureaTheme()` returns `density` and `setDensity`.
- `useAureaTokens()` returns the sizes of the current density in dp: `t.size.controlHMd`, `t.size.rowH`, `t.size.cardPad`, `t.size.touchControlHMd`.
- The native buttons use the touch scale, `touchControlH*`, which is taller than the web scale.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/native";

export function App({children}: {children: React.ReactNode}) {
  return <AureaProvider defaultDensity="compact">{children}</AureaProvider>;
}
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-icons.html">
# Icons

The Phosphor icon set, how to serve its sprite, the filled form for the selected item, and how to add your own drawing.

Aurea draws its icons from Phosphor Icons: 1,433 glyphs, each in a regular and a filled form. On the web they live in one SVG sprite, in the `@aurea-uds/icons` package. On React Native each glyph is its own module.

## Serve the sprite

The sprite is a static file. Copy it to where your app serves static files:

```bash
cp node_modules/@aurea-uds/icons/dist/aurea-icons.svg public/
```

Then tell the provider where it is, once:

```tsx
<AureaProvider spriteUrl="/aurea-icons.svg">
  <App />
</AureaProvider>
```

The default is `/aurea-icons.svg`, which only works when the app is served from the root of the domain. Under any other path, set `spriteUrl`, or every icon of every component fails without an error. If your bundler emits the file, pass the URL it gives you. A page that inlines the symbols itself passes `spriteUrl=""`, so the reference stays local.

## The Icon component

`Icon` draws one glyph. Its size follows the icon scale (`sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`), which stays the same in every density. It takes the color of the text around it.

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <Icon name="house" />
  <Icon name="house" weight="fill" />
  <Icon name="bell" size="lg" />
  <Icon name="bell" size="lg" weight="fill" />
</Cluster>
```

An `Icon` is always decorative: it renders with `aria-hidden="true"`. The meaning goes in text next to it, or in the `label` of an `IconButton`:

```tsx
<IconButton icon="gear" label="Settings" />
```

Most components take an icon by name too: `leadingIcon` and `trailingIcon` on `Button`, `icon` on `IconButton` and on navigation items, `leadingIcon` on menu items.

## The filled form

`weight="fill"` draws the filled form. Aurea uses it for the selected item, such as the active tab or the current menu item, and in alerts. The components switch it on their own, so you seldom set it by hand.

`weight="bold"` exists only for `x`, the glyph of `CloseButton`. Any other name asked in `bold` draws the regular form.

## Names are checked

The name is the Phosphor name, exactly as Phosphor writes it. TypeScript checks it in `Icon` and in the props that take an icon. A wrong name does not compile:

```tsx
<Icon name="caret-down" />   // compiles
<Icon name="chevron-down" /> // does not compile: the Phosphor name is caret-down
```

The full API is on the [Icon](./icon.html) page.

## Your own icons

There are two ways to add a glyph that the set does not have, such as your logo.

### Pass a drawing

`Icon`, the icon props of `Button` and `IconButton`, and the node icons of `DependencyGraph` also accept a component that returns an `svg`. It receives Aurea's class and size, and inherits the color through `currentColor`. It has no filled form.

```tsx
import type {SVGAttributes} from "react";

function Router(props: SVGAttributes<SVGSVGElement>) {
  return (
    <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth={2} {...props}>
      <rect x="3" y="13" width="18" height="7" rx="2" />
      <path d="M7 13V8M17 13V8" />
    </svg>
  );
}

<Button leadingIcon={Router}>Add router</Button>
```

### Add names to a sprite

If you serve your own sprite, declare its names once. From then on they type-check like the Phosphor names:

```tsx
declare module "@aurea-uds/react" {
  interface AureaIconNames { brand: true }
}

<Icon name="brand" />
```

The symbol id in the sprite is `i-` followed by the name. To mix two sprites on one page, pass `spriteUrl` on the single `Icon` that reads the second one.

## Plain HTML

Without React, point straight at the symbol. The id is `i-` plus the name, and `-fill` for the filled form:

```html
<svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="/aurea-icons.svg#i-magnifying-glass"></use></svg>
<svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="/aurea-icons.svg#i-house-fill"></use></svg>
```

## React Native

`@aurea-uds/native` has one module per glyph and per form, with the same names as the web sprite. Import each icon by its own path, so only the icons you use enter the bundle:

```tsx
import House from "@aurea-uds/native/icons/house";
import HouseFill from "@aurea-uds/native/icons/house-fill";
import {AureaProvider, criarRegistroDeIcones} from "@aurea-uds/native";

const ICONS = criarRegistroDeIcones({house: House, "house-fill": HouseFill});

<AureaProvider icons={ICONS}>
  <App />
</AureaProvider>
```

Components look icons up by name in this registry. Register the filled form under the `-fill` key; when it is missing, the regular form is drawn. A name that is not registered draws nothing, and a warning names it during development.

Color does not inherit on React Native. `Icon` uses the text color of the theme unless you pass `color`. For your own glyph, `criarGlifo` builds one from rectangles, circles and paths, and you declare its name in `AureaIconNames` from `@aurea-uds/native`.

## What is left out

Phosphor's brand logos (the names that end in `-logo`) are not in the set. Third-party trademarks do not belong in an Apache-2.0 library. The glyphs themselves are under the MIT license, with the notice in the package's `NOTICE` file.

## Next steps

- See the icon sizes on the [Tokens](./tokens.html) page.
- Learn how icons flip, or do not, in [RTL](./docs-rtl.html).
- Read about labels and contrast in [Accessibility](./docs-accessibility.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-rtl.html">
# RTL

Mirror Aurea for right-to-left languages with two settings, and know what stays in place on purpose.

Aurea supports right-to-left writing, such as Arabic and Hebrew. The stylesheet is written with logical properties along the line, so the layout mirrors itself. You set the direction in two places, and that is all.

## Turn it on

1. Put `dir="rtl"` on the `html` element. This mirrors the CSS. It is the app's job: Aurea does not touch the document.
2. Pass `direction="rtl"` to `AureaProvider`. This tells the components that place popups and read arrow keys.

```tsx
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <body>
    <AureaProvider direction="rtl">
      <App />
    </AureaProvider>
  </body>
</html>
```

Set `lang` to the language of the page as well. Screen readers need it.

```tsx
<div dir="rtl">
  <Timeline
    items={[
      {title: "Created", description: "Draft opened", time: "10:02"},
      {title: "Reviewed", time: "11:40"},
    ]}
  />
</div>
```

## What each setting does

The `dir` attribute drives the CSS. Margins, paddings, positions and text alignment are written as start and end, not left and right, so they flip with the direction. It works on any element, which is why the example above mirrors inside a page that reads left to right.

The `direction` prop drives behavior. It goes to Base UI, which uses it for the side a popup opens on and for the meaning of the left and right arrow keys. A few Aurea components also read it: the `TreeView` arrow points the other way, the arrow of the `AppShell` collapse button follows the direction, and the horizontal axis of the color area and the color slider runs from the right.

## What stays in place

Some things do not mirror, on purpose:

- **The check mark of `Checkbox`.** It is a drawn mark, not a direction.
- **The `Spinner`.** It is a drawn glyph too, and keeps its shape.
- **`Drawer side="left"` and `side="right"`.** The names promise a physical side, so the drawer keeps it.
- **Icons.** The glyphs are not flipped. Where an arrow means "next" or "back", pass the glyph that points the right way for the direction, for example `caret-left` instead of `caret-right`.

## Your own CSS

Write your additions the same way, and they mirror with the rest:

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| `margin-left` | `margin-inline-start` |
| `padding-right` | `padding-inline-end` |
| `left: 0` | `inset-inline-start: 0` |
| `text-align: left` | `text-align: start` |

```css
.order-total {
  margin-inline-start: auto;
  padding-inline: var(--space-4);
  text-align: end;
}
```

## Known limit

Six rules in the stylesheet still use the `:dir(rtl)` selector: the corner position of an anchored `Badge`, the arrow of `Select`, and the thumb of `Switch`. Some build tools rewrite `:dir()`, and after the rewrite these rules can stop matching. New rules in the core resolve direction with logical properties instead, and these six are on the list to move.

## React Native

On React Native, the right-to-left layout is switched on by the app, through React Native itself. Aurea has no prop for it. `Heading`, `Paragraph` and `Code` take `align="start"` and `align="end"`, which follow the direction instead of a fixed side.

## Next steps

- Read the rest of the CSS rules in [Styling](./docs-styling.html).
- Choose the right arrow glyphs in [Icons](./docs-icons.html).
- Check keyboard and screen reader support in [Accessibility](./docs-accessibility.html).
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-accessibility.html">
# Accessibility
