What Aurea does for people with low vision, keyboard and screen-reader users, and how each part is checked.

Low vision is the first audience Aurea designs for. This page lists what the components do on their own, what the test suite checks, and the two places where Aurea knowingly falls short of WCAG.

## At a glance

| Area | What Aurea does | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Atkinson Hyperlegible Next for text, the Mono for code | the fonts package |
| Contrast | measured in the browser, in both themes | axe on every page, a contrast matrix for buttons |
| Focus | one visible ring, 2px, on every focusable piece | a sweep that tabs through every preview |
| Touch | 44px targets on touch screens and on native | geometry tests, native unit tests |
| Keyboard | behaviour from Base UI, focus order follows the document | engine and focus-order tests |
| Screen readers | names, states and descriptions wired by the components | axe, native state tests |
| Motion | animations stop when the system asks for less motion | a global CSS rule, a native hook |
| Forced colours | focus and icons repaint in system colours | a forced-colours test |
| Text size | no page scrolls sideways with text at 200% | the site sweep |

## Readable type

The text font is **Atkinson Hyperlegible Next**. Code uses **Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono**. Both ship in `@aurea-uds/fonts`: WOFF2 for the web, TTF for React Native.

The family was made to increase legibility for readers with low vision. Letters that are easy to confuse, such as `I`, `l` and `1`, or `O` and `0`, have distinct shapes.

The selected item of a navigation (a tab, the current menu item, the bottom bar) switches its icon to the filled weight. The state changes shape, not only colour.

## Contrast

### Measured, not assumed

Contrast is checked on the colour the browser actually paints, after every token and colour mix is resolved.

- **axe** runs on every page of this site, in the dark and the light theme, with the WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 A and AA rules plus best practices. It runs in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
- A **contrast matrix** checks every `appearance` and `tone` of the button, in both themes.
- A unit test fails if text is ever painted with the background colour of a state. Filled state backgrounds (`--success`, `--info`, `--warning`, `--destructive`) are for fills; text, icons and bars on the page use their `-400` pair.
- Text on the brand yellow is dark grey (`brand-yellow-ink`, `#242424`), at 8.13:1, in both themes.

### Known trade-offs

Aurea has two documented gaps against WCAG. Both are deliberate project decisions, made with the numbers in front of them.

**1. Accent text in the light theme.** In the light theme, accent text and icons use the brand yellow itself: the current sidebar item, links, the primary badge, the current page of a pagination, the "today" of a calendar, and similar accents. The yellow measures **1.75:1** on the light page background, 1.91:1 on the white of a card and 1.60:1 on the grey of a field. WCAG asks for 4.5:1 for text (1.4.3) and 3:1 for icons (1.4.11). It does not pass.

The exception is exactly one colour in one theme: `--primary` used as text in the light theme. Any other colour that fails still fails the build, and the dark theme has no exception. Brands (`data-brand`) keep their own accent colours.

**2. Field boundaries.** Aurea draws no lines (see [Design Principles](./docs-design-principles.html)). Fields and controls are separated from the page by a translucent fill instead of a border. That boundary measures 1.34:1 for fields and 1.92:1 for controls in the dark theme, and 1.21:1 and 1.49:1 in the light theme. WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1, so fields do not meet it.

If your product must meet WCAG AA in full, account for both points.

## Focus

Every focusable piece shows one focus line. It is never a border plus a separate ring.

- Width: `--focus-width`, 2px. Gap from the piece: `--focus-offset`, 2px.
- Inside a clipped container (a table row, a tree item), the ring is drawn inward so it is not cut off.
- In the light theme, the ring is the text colour (`--focus-strong`): 14.24:1 on the page and 8.13:1 around the yellow button. In the dark theme, it is the brand yellow.
- On an invalid field, the ring takes the danger colour, so the error stays visible while it is being fixed.
- React Native has no outline. There, focus is shown as a border in the focus colour.

A sweep tabs through every component preview on this site and fails if a focused piece draws two lines.

## Touch targets

The minimum target is `--target-min`: 2.75rem, which is 44px at a 16px root.

- **Web.** On a touch screen (`pointer: coarse`), buttons, tabs, segmented controls, pagination, media controls and navigation rows grow to at least 44px. Small close and remove buttons keep their drawing and get an invisible 44px hit area around it.
- **Native.** `Button` and `IconButton` always keep a 44-point target, even when the drawing is smaller. The target is real layout, not an extended hit zone, so the screen reader sees it too. Native buttons, fields and selects are 48 tall by default (`--touch-control-h-md`, comfortable density).

## Keyboard

On the web, keyboard behaviour comes from Base UI. Aurea does not reimplement it. A test checks that each component's documentation declares every key the engine handles.

- Focus order follows the document. Nothing is reordered visually without being reordered in the markup, and a sweep checks that visual order equals focus order on every page.
- The date picker and the colour picker open with focus inside and return focus to the trigger on `Esc`. The colour picker keeps `Tab` inside while it is open.
- `AppShell` renders a "Skip to content" link at the start of the shell.

## Screen readers

Components wire names, descriptions and states themselves.

```tsx
<Field label="Email" hint="We never share it." error="Enter a valid address.">
  <Input type="email" />
</Field>

<IconButton icon="trash" label="Delete" />
```

- `Field` connects the label, the hint and the error to the control, and marks it invalid when there is an error.
- `IconButton` requires `label`. On both targets the type does not compile without it, because a button with only an icon has no text to announce.
- On native, every state a component reports to assistive technology (checked, selected, disabled) is also written as the matching `aria-*` attribute, so it reaches screen readers in the browser too.
- axe also runs on overlays while they are open.

### Language

Every built-in label (close, loading, pagination, skip to content) comes from a set of strings. English is the default. Portuguese is included, and any label can be replaced.

```tsx
import {AureaProvider, ptBR} from "@aurea-uds/react";

<AureaProvider strings={ptBR}>{app}</AureaProvider>
```

## Motion

- **Web.** Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, one global rule in the core stylesheet cuts animations, transitions and smooth scrolling to near zero. Components do not need to opt in.
- **Native.** React Native has no global rule, so Aurea asks the system. `useReduceMotion()` returns `true`, `false`, or `null` while the system has not answered yet. Aurea's animations wait for the answer, so not a single frame plays for someone who asked for less motion.

```tsx
import {useReduceMotion} from "@aurea-uds/native";

const reduce = useReduceMotion();
if (reduce !== false) return; // skip the animation until we know it is allowed
```

See [Animation](./docs-animation.html).

## Forced colours

When the system forces its own colours (`forced-colors: active`), the focus ring uses the system text colour. Icons drawn as masks would vanish, so they repaint in the system colour of the text next to them. Colour swatches keep their colour, because the colour is their content. A dedicated test checks each of these.

Aurea does not change its design under `prefers-contrast: more`.

## Text size and reflow

A sweep sets the root text size to 200% on every page of this site and fails any page that then scrolls sideways. A second sweep checks that no page scrolls sideways at any width.

## Right-to-left

Set `dir="rtl"` on the `html` element and `direction="rtl"` on `AureaProvider`. The stylesheet uses logical properties, so layouts mirror on the inline axis. A test checks that components mirror, and that what must not mirror stays in place. See [RTL](./docs-rtl.html).

## What stays with your app

Aurea cannot check content it does not own.

- Write meaningful labels, alt text (`imageAlt` on `Badge`, for example) and headings in order.
- Check the contrast of your own colours and images.
- Content you place inside a component is your responsibility. On native, do not put a pressable element inside a piece that is marked as one accessible element: on iOS, VoiceOver hides what is inside.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-llms-txt.html">
# LLMs.txt

Files that let AI coding assistants read the Aurea documentation.

Aurea publishes its documentation in the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) format, so an AI coding assistant can read it directly.

## Available files

- [llms.txt](https://aureauds.dev/llms.txt): the index. One line per page, with a link to the page as Markdown.
- [llms-full.txt](https://aureauds.dev/llms-full.txt): the whole documentation in one file. It holds the Getting Started pages, every component, every hook, the patterns, the blocks and the recipes.
- [aurea-agents.md](https://aureauds.dev/aurea-agents.md): short rules for AI coding agents. See [AGENTS.md](./docs-agents-md.html).

Every page of this site is also Markdown, next to its HTML: change `.html` to `.md` in the address. The "View as Markdown" item, in the menu next to "Copy Markdown", opens it.

## Integration

Most assistants can read documentation from an address. Give it the index:

```bash
https://aureauds.dev/llms.txt
```

For a tool that loads a whole file into its context, give it the full text:

```bash
https://aureauds.dev/llms-full.txt
```

The full file is large. When the context window is small, give the index, and let the assistant open only the pages it needs.

The "Copy Prompt" button at the top of every page copies a ready setup text: it tells the assistant to install the [Aurea skill](./docs-agent-skills.html) and to read the index.

## Contributing

Found an answer from an assistant that the documentation got wrong? [Open an issue](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/issues) with the page and the question.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-agent-skills.html">
# Agent Skills

Give your AI coding assistant the rules for building interfaces with Aurea.

The Aurea skill gives an AI coding assistant what it needs to build with Aurea: how to install it on the web and on React Native, the rules the look depends on, and where to read each component.

It follows the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) format: one `SKILL.md` file that the assistant loads when the task calls for it.

## Installation

```bash
npx skills add victor1mor/aurea-uds
```

The installer finds the assistants you use (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode and others) and puts the skill where each one reads skills from. It comes from the open `skills` package.

### Install scope

By default the skill goes into the project, next to your code, so the whole team gets it. Add `-g` to install it for your user instead, in every project:

```bash
npx skills add victor1mor/aurea-uds -g
```

## Usage

The assistant finds the skill on its own when the work involves Aurea: a project that depends on `@aurea-uds/react`, `@aurea-uds/core` or `@aurea-uds/native`, or a request for Aurea components, tokens or themes.

Ask it, for example, to:

- build a settings page with Aurea components;
- add a dark mode switch;
- move a screen from raw CSS values to Aurea tokens.

## What's included

- Installation and setup, for the web and for React Native.
- The rules the look depends on: tokens only, no lines, no gradients, the yellow that does not change, Phosphor icon names.
- The accessibility the app must keep.
- Where to read each component: the [LLMs.txt](./docs-llms-txt.html) files.

## Structure

```bash
skills/aurea-uds/
└── SKILL.md
```

The file is in the [repository](https://github.com/victor1mor/aurea-uds/tree/main/skills/aurea-uds), under the Apache 2.0 license.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/docs-agents-md.html">
# AGENTS.md

Short Aurea rules to put in your project's AGENTS.md, for AI coding agents.

[AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) is a file at the root of a project with instructions for AI coding agents. Aurea publishes its rules in a form you can put there.

## Usage

Download the file and save it at the root of your project:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://aureauds.dev/aurea-agents.md -o AGENTS.md
```

If your project already has an `AGENTS.md`, add the Aurea rules to the end of it instead:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://aureauds.dev/aurea-agents.md >> AGENTS.md
```

Some assistants read a file with another name, such as `CLAUDE.md`. Use the name your assistant reads.

## What it contains

- Where to read the documentation: the [LLMs.txt](./docs-llms-txt.html) files.
- To ask whether the app is for the web or React Native before installing anything.
- The setup for each target.
- The rules the look depends on, and the accessibility the app must keep.

It is the same text as the [Aurea skill](./docs-agent-skills.html). Use the skill when your assistant supports skills; use this file when it does not.

## Keeping it current

The file does not update itself. Download it again after upgrading Aurea.
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/accessgate.html">
# AccessGate

Hides an action the user cannot take, or shows it inert with the reason.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AccessGate} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AccessGate allowed={can("publish")}>
  <Button variant="primary">Publish</Button>
</AccessGate>

<AccessGate allowed={can("publish")} mode="disable" reason="Only an editor can publish">
  <Button variant="primary">Publish</Button>
</AccessGate>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allowed` | `boolean` | — | REQUIRED, and it is an ANSWER, not a question: Aurea holds no rules, roles or policies. You decide, from whatever your app uses, and pass the result. THIS IS NOT SECURITY — hiding a button stops nobody from calling the API. The server is what refuses; this only avoids offering what would be refused. |
| `children` | `ReactElement` | — | REQUIRED. A single element — the action being gated. When allowed, it comes through untouched, with no wrapper. |
| `mode` | `hide \| disable` | hide | hide removes the action from the DOM, which is what an authorization library does and the right default when the action would mean nothing to this user. disable keeps it visible and inert, for when they should know it exists — an admin-panel kit is the reference that lets you pick, and the pick is the whole reason this component exists. |
| `reason` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED when mode is disable, and the type enforces it: an action that says "no" without saying why is worse than one that is simply absent. It is shown in a Tooltip on the inert control. |
| `fallback` | `ReactNode` | — | Only in hide mode: what takes the place of the action. Use it for a read-only rendering of the same information, not for a second "you cannot do this" message. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/accordion.html">
# Accordion

Accordion stacks questions that open to show their answer. One opens at a time, like the reference's: opening one closes the other. It is built on the browser's own <details>, so it opens without JavaScript.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Accordion} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Accordion items={[
  {id: "ship", title: "How do I install it?", content: "Install the packages…"},
  {id: "theme", title: "Can I change the colours?", content: "Every visual value is a token…"},
]} />
```

- No box around it: a hairline between the items, none after the last.

- The question has 16 on every side; the arrow at the end turns when it opens.

- The hover highlight is a capsule — Aurea's corner on the reference's measures.

- multiple lets several stay open; defaultValue opens items from the start.

- variant="surface" puts it in a card. A disabled item is announced and skipped by Tab.

## Examples

### Surface

In a card, with the line at 94% and the hover on the neutral fill.

```tsx
<Accordion variant="surface" items={items} />
```

### Several open

multiple keeps each item independent.

```tsx
<Accordion multiple defaultValue={["ship", "native"]} items={items} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `Array<{id: string; title: ReactNode; content: ReactNode}>` | — | The sections. Built on native <details>/<summary>, so opening, closing, keyboard and find-in-page come from the browser and the component ships no JavaScript at all. Several can be open at once: exclusivity would need the `name` attribute, and hiding what someone just opened is rarely what they wanted. |
| `variant` | `default \| surface` | default | surface puts the items in a card, with the line at 94% and the neutral hover. |
| `multiple` | `boolean` | false | Lets several items stay open. Without it, opening one closes the other, as in the reference. |
| `defaultValue` | `string[]` | — | The ids of the items that start open. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/agentcard.html">
# AgentCard

Who an agent is, what state it is in, and what it can do.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AgentCard} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AgentCard
  name="Curator"
  model="opus-5"
  state="running"
  description="Keeps the reference library tidy."
  capabilities={[{name: "search", icon: "magnifying-glass"}, {name: "summarise"}]}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `string` | — | Required. Also feeds the avatar fallback, so a card never shows an empty circle. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | One line about what the agent is for. |
| `avatarSrc` | `string` | — | Optional portrait; without it the initials stand in. |
| `model` | `string` | — | Which model is behind it, shown as secondary text. A string and not an enum: the list changes faster than this library ships. |
| `state` | `AgentState` | — | Renders an AgentStatus in the header. Omit it and the header simply has no state. |
| `capabilities` | `AgentCapability[]` | — | What the agent can do, as pills. `description` becomes the tooltip; the icon is optional. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` | — | Your buttons, in the footer. The reference dispatches actions by STRING (`onAction(action: string)`), which trades the compiler for a verbal agreement — here whoever builds the button already knows what it does. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the card. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/agentinspector.html">
# AgentInspector

The detail of one agent: configuration, tools, instructions.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AgentInspector} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AgentInspector
  title="Curator"
  sections={[{label: "Configuration", items: [{term: "Model", value: "opus-5"}]}]}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Names the panel, and names the region for a screen reader when it is a string. |
| `sections` | `Array<{ label: string; items: Array<{ term: string; value: ReactNode }> }>` | — | Labelled groups of term and value, each one a DataList — the anatomy of the reference's DetailsView, using the component that already exists here. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Free body under the sections, for inspecting what the record did not foresee. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the panel. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/agentstatus.html">
# AgentStatus

The state of an agent, in one fixed vocabulary.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AgentStatus} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AgentStatus state="running" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `state` | `"idle" \| "thinking" \| "running" \| "paused" \| "error" \| "completed"` | "idle" | The six states come measured from the reference, not invented here. Each maps to a Status variant instead of a loose colour: the reference writes `text-yellow-500` inside the component, and colour inside a component is what this design system forbids. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | Overrides the built-in wording. The default is translated; replace it when your domain calls the state something else. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the status element. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/alert.html">
# Alert

Inline message that stays in context.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Alert} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Alert variant="info" title="Heads up">Contextual information.</Alert>
<Alert variant="danger" title="Upload failed">The file exceeds 10 MB.</Alert>
<Alert title="You have 2 credits left" action={<Button variant="tertiary">Upgrade</Button>}>
  Get a paid plan for more credits
</Alert>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `info \| success \| warning \| danger \| accent` | info | Tone and, with it, the live region: `danger` renders role="alert", which interrupts the screen reader; the others render role="status", which waits for a pause. `accent` is the reference library's accent, in Aurea's link colour. The state colour paints the icon and the title, on the card surface. Colour is never the only signal — what carries the meaning is the text. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Rendered as a <strong> above the body. Optional on purpose: a one-line alert reads better without one. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The message. An Alert stays in the reading flow, in context — a page-width warning is a Banner and a transient one is a Toast. |
| `state` | `waiting_user \| waiting_approval \| waiting_dependency \| offline \| stale \| partial \| degraded` | — | Universal state (Part J) — an axis of its own alongside `variant`, because the two answer different questions: `variant` is how serious this is, `state` is what is happening. Merging them would put “out of date” next to “danger” and force the caller to pick one. It sets `data-state`, derives the severity when no `variant` is given — waiting states inform, the rest warn, and none of the seven is `danger`, because in all seven the screen still works — and supplies the message when there are no children. |
| `icon` | `IconName` | — | Overrides the glyph. The icon is a FUNCTION of the variant by default, because a system that makes you remember which glyph means "danger" ends up with four answers to the same question. |
| `action` | `ReactNode` | — | The alert's button (Upgrade, Undo), as the reference: after the text and before the X, in the middle; on a phone (below 640) it goes under the text, in the same column. |
| `onDismiss` | `() => void` | — | Shows the X (the CloseButton) and is called when it is pressed. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/appshell.html">
# AppShell

Application frame: sidebar, topbar and main content.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AppShell} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AppShell
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  navigation={<nav aria-label="Contents"><a href="/inbox" aria-current="page">Inbox</a><a href="/archive">Archive</a></nav>}
  topbar={<Button variant="primary" size="sm">New</Button>}
>
  <h1>Inbox</h1>
</AppShell>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `brand` | `ReactNode` | — | Logotype and product name. Lives in the topbar, beside the navigation toggle. |
| `navigation` | `ReactNode` | — | The sidebar content, usually a <nav>. The shell never invents one, so the landmark and its label are yours. |
| `navItems` | `SidebarItem[]` | — | The sidebar list, handed to the Sidebar the shell already creates — same shape as Sidebar items. Use this instead of passing a second <Sidebar> as navigation: that nests two panels, two borders and two 22px radii, and the inner one clips its text. When navigation is also given, the list comes first. |
| `currentNavId` | `string` | — | The id of the current item in navItems. Marked with aria-current="page" and the selected skin. |
| `navLabel` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the <nav> built from navItems. Falls back to the sidebarLabel string. |
| `topbar` | `ReactNode` | — | What sits in the topbar next to the brand: sections, search, actions. |
| `topbarVariant` | `"floating" \| "flush"` | "floating" | Skin of the topbar. flush removes the outer gap, and the sidebar rises to meet it. |
| `sidebarVariant` | `"floating" \| "flush" \| "plain"` | "floating" | Skin of the sidebar, forwarded to it. flush is the one exception this design system makes to its floating surfaces: the panel sits against the edges, takes the full height and is separated from the content by a single rule. Without this prop the variant would be unreachable for anyone composing through the shell, which is the normal path. |
| `sidebarScrollbar` | `hover \| visible` | hover | The left sidebar's scrollbar, forwarded to it: hover (light, shown with the pointer over it, with focus inside and on touch screens) or visible (always on screen). |
| `sidebarCollapsed` | `boolean` | false | Narrows the sidebar panel to --sidebar-rail. A floating panel keeps its two outer margins in the grid track; flush uses the token as the raw track width. Controlled by you, like the palette's open: the shell does not decide when to collapse. Without sidebarCollapsible it draws no button; with it, the button calls onSidebarCollapsedChange and you decide. Below 1024px the drawer is never a rail, controlled or not: collapsed inside the drawer it was a column of unnamed icons. |
| `sidebarCollapsible` | `boolean` | false | Draws the collapse button at the top of the junction between the sidebar and the content — centred on the gap, level with the first item, sticky with the sidebar — and turns the sidebar into the rail on its own between 1024 and 1279px. Off by default: without it the shell is exactly the one before, and an app that already drives sidebarCollapsed with its own button does not get a second one. Behaviour read from the sidebar that one of the references uses (the main reference library has no app frame). |
| `defaultSidebarCollapsed` | `boolean` | — | Starts collapsed without controlling it. The person's choice holds until the window crosses 1280px; then the width decides again. |
| `onSidebarCollapsedChange` | `(collapsed: boolean) => void` | — | Called on every change — the button, or the width crossing 1280px. Keeping the preference is the app's job, as before. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Page content. Rendered inside the <main> the shell owns. |
| `topbarDivider` | `boolean` | false | Passes Topbar's `divider` to the flush bar the shell builds. |
| `layout` | `"app" \| "docs"` | "app" | The arrangement. docs is the one of the reference documentation: one block of 1400 in the middle of the screen with the sidebar (220), the text and, from 1280 up, the table of contents (240 at the start of a 268 column); the bar on top is the small one, on the same block. Both columns start 16 below the bar and stop 32 above the bottom of the screen; inside the sidebar, 16 on both sides and 8 inside each item; the table of contents shows no scrollbar. From 768 up the sidebar is a column; below, it is a drawer that opens from the end of the bar, where its button goes (after the bar's actions). Below 1280 the table of contents is a sticky bar under the top bar, 40 high, with the name of the section in view; it opens the list as a drawer. On a phone the text keeps 24 from the edge and 32 below that bar. |
| `topbarTabs` | `HeaderTab[]` | — | The second row of the bar on top: the site's areas, forwarded as the Header's tabs. |
| `topbarCurrentTab` | `string` | — | The id of the current area, forwarded as the Header's currentTab. |
| `topbarTabsLabel` | `string` | "Sections" | The accessible name of the second row, forwarded as the Header's tabsLabel. |
| `contentVariant` | `"surface" \| "plain"` | "surface" | `plain` removes the box around the content area. `.content` is a card — same background, border and radius as `.card` — so a Card inside it would be a box inside an identical box. The margin stays. |
| `aside` | `ReactNode` | — | The right-hand column — a documentation page's "On this page" (a TableOfContents). From 1280 up it is the third column; below, it follows the content. With the docs layout, below 1280 it is the drawer of the table-of-contents bar instead. |
| `asideLabel` | `string` | strings.tocLabel | The right column's name for screen readers. |
| `asideVariant` | `"floating" \| "flush" \| "plain"` | sidebarVariant | Skin of the right-hand column. Without it, the same as the left sidebar. plain removes the box — the items sit loose on the page, like a documentation page's "On this page". |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/aspectratio.html">
# AspectRatio

A box that keeps its proportion, whatever the width.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AspectRatio} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio={16 / 9}>
  <img src="/cover.jpg" alt="" />
</AspectRatio>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ratio` | `number` | 1 | Width over height, as a number — 16/9 is 1.777…. It becomes the CSS aspect-ratio, so the box keeps the proportion at any width. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/aureaprovider.html">
# AureaProvider

Root provider: strings, icon sprite, text direction, toasts and where popups mount.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AureaProvider} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AureaProvider spriteUrl="/assets/aurea-icons.svg" direction="ltr" strings={{close: "Fechar"}}>
  <App />
</AureaProvider>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Your application. Put the provider once, at the root — everything below it reads the context. |
| `strings` | `Partial<AureaStrings>` | English defaults | Overrides for the built-in accessible names and labels. Merged over the defaults, so you translate only what you need. `ptBR` ships as a ready locale. |
| `spriteUrl` | `string` | "/aurea-icons.svg" | Where the icon sprite lives. Application configuration, so it belongs here and not on every Icon — an app served from a sub-path used to lose every glyph and had to be fixed component by component. |
| `direction` | `ltr \| rtl` | ltr | Tells the engine which way the inline axis runs, so popup sides and arrow keys mirror. The CSS mirrors on its own through logical properties — but you still have to put dir="rtl" on your <html>; the provider does not touch the DOM. |
| `portalContainer` | `HTMLElement \| null` | — | Where every popup mounts: dialog, drawer, tooltip, popover, hover card, both menus, notification panel, combobox list and toasts. Unset, they mount on document.body — which is what lets them stack and position without inheriting overflow or transform from anything. Point it at a node inside one of your landmarks when you need popup content to satisfy the "all content in a landmark" check. |
| `theme` | `AureaThemePreference` | — | Controlled theme. Pass it to command; the provider then never writes it on its own. "system" follows the computer's light/dark (prefers-color-scheme) and changes with it. |
| `defaultTheme` | `AureaThemePreference` | — | Seeds the theme without controlling it. With NEITHER of the two, the provider adopts whatever the document already carries on <html> — the data-theme in the markup exists so the page does not flash, and a provider that overwrote it on first paint would bring the flash back. "system" follows the computer's light/dark (prefers-color-scheme) and changes with it. |
| `onThemeChange` | `(theme: AureaTheme) => void` | — | Fires with the new theme, whether it changed from here or from useTheme. |
| `onThemePreferenceChange` | `(preference: AureaThemePreference) => void` | — | Called with what was CHOSEN, which can be "system" (onThemeChange gets the theme on screen). The moment to save the choice. |
| `density` | `AureaDensity` | — | Controlled density. Same convention as theme. |
| `defaultDensity` | `AureaDensity` | — | Seeds the density without controlling it. |
| `onDensityChange` | `(density: AureaDensity) => void` | — | Fires with the new density. |
| `toastPlacement` | `"top" \| "top-start" \| "top-end" \| "bottom" \| "bottom-start" \| "bottom-end"` | "bottom" | Where the toasts of useToast() appear. bottom (the middle of the bottom edge) is the reference library's default. 460 wide from 640 up; the screen minus 16 on each side on a phone. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/automationcard.html">
# AutomationCard

A rule that runs on its own: when this, then that — and a switch.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AutomationCard} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AutomationCard
  name="Nightly reindex"
  trigger="Every day at 02:00 UTC"
  action="Run the indexer on changed documents"
  enabled
  onToggle={setEnabled}
  lastRun="yesterday, 02:00"
  lastResult="success"
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `ReactNode` | — | What the rule is called. |
| `trigger` | `ReactNode` | — | The WHEN. Rendered as the term/value pair the house already uses, not as prose: whoever reads this needs to find the condition without scanning a paragraph. |
| `action` | `ReactNode` | — | The THEN. A rule is a condition and a consequence — that pair is what separates this card from AgentCard, which is identity, and from TaskQueue, which is queued work. |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | — | Whether the rule is live. A disabled rule does not disappear and does not change colour: it recedes. Hiding it would hide the very rule someone is looking for in order to switch it back on. |
| `onToggle` | `(enabled: boolean) => void` | — | Without it there is no switch — a read-only card stays read-only instead of showing a control that does nothing. |
| `lastRun` | `ReactNode` | — | When it last fired. |
| `lastResult` | `"success" \| "failure"` | — | How it went, as a Status — so the outcome is a word and not only a colour. |
| `details` | `Array<{term: string; value: ReactNode}>` | — | Extra rows appended after WHEN and THEN in the same list. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` | — | Buttons for the footer. They enter as nodes, so whoever builds the button knows what it does — the reference dispatches by string, which trades the compiler for a verbal agreement. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the card. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | One line under the name, saying what the automation does. It is separate from name so the card can lay the two out on its own grid. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/avatar.html">
# Avatar

Represents a user or entity with image or initials.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Avatar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Avatar fallback="AU" />
<Avatar fallback="VM" size="lg" />
<Avatar fallback="B" tone="info" emphasis="soft" />
<Avatar fallback={<Icon name="floppy-disk" />} tone="warning" emphasis="soft" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src` | `string` | — | The picture. A broken URL falls back instead of showing the browser's broken-image glyph — measured, it did not before. |
| `alt` | `string` | "" | Empty by default, because an avatar usually sits beside the name it stands for and repeating it is noise. Fill it when the avatar is the only identification. |
| `fallback` | `ReactNode` | — | What shows with no src, or when src fails: initials, an icon, anything. Without it the circle is empty, which is a legitimate placeholder. |
| `size` | `sm \| md \| lg` | md | Token scale, not pixels. It shares --control-h-* with the controls, so an avatar next to a button of the same size lines up by construction, and density reaches it. |
| `tone` | `"neutral" \| "brand" \| "danger" \| "success" \| "warning" \| "info"` | "neutral" | The colour of the fallback letter or icon — what it means (the reference's color). |
| `emphasis` | `"default" \| "soft"` | "default" | soft drops the ring and gives the tone's light background, as the reference's soft avatar (the yellow floppy disk of its showcase). |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/avatargroup.html">
# AvatarGroup

Overlapping stack of avatars, with a count for the ones that do not fit.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AvatarGroup} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AvatarGroup max={3} total={9} label="Reviewers">
  <Avatar fallback="AM" />
  <Avatar fallback="CT" />
  <Avatar fallback="RS" />
  <Avatar fallback="JP" />
</AvatarGroup>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | none | REQUIRED. The Avatar elements. They overlap in source order. |
| `max` | `number` | none | How many to show. The rest become a single count. Without it, every avatar is shown. |
| `total` | `number` | the number of children | Use when the real total lives on the server and only a page of avatars was sent. |
| `label` | `string` | none | Whose faces these are. A row of portraits with no name says nothing. |
| `size` | `sm \| md \| lg` | md | Size of the count bubble, so it matches the avatars beside it — pass the same value you passed them. The scale is Avatar's. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/badge.html">
# Badge

Badge is short metadata in a pill — and, with `anchor`, the counter that rides on the corner of something else. One component covers both because they are the same object: a small mark that qualifies what is next to it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Badge variant="success">Ready</Badge>
<Badge variant="success" emphasis="outline">Ready</Badge>
<Badge variant="success" emphasis="solid">Ready</Badge>
```

- Three emphases — `soft` (the tinted pill), `outline`, and `solid`. All 36 combinations of variant × emphasis × theme were measured for contrast; the lowest is 5.6:1.

- Three sizes. `md` is the historical one and did not move, so nothing that already used Badge changed by a pixel.

- Accessories: a status `dot`, a round `image`, and `leading`/`trailing` nodes.

- Numbers: `count` with `max` (over it, `99+`) and `showZero` — zero hides itself, because an empty inbox does not deserve a mark. `formatBadgeCount` is exported so your accessible name can say the same string the eye sees.

- `anchor` hangs it on a corner of any child, with `anchorShape="circle"` pulling it 14% back for round parents. A cutout ring in the surface colour keeps it from melting into the icon; override `--badge-ring` when the surface is not the page background.

- An anchored badge is aria-hidden ON PURPOSE: the count belongs in the accessible name of the thing it decorates. A bell announced as "bell 8" tells nobody what the 8 is.

## Examples

### Flat

The soft tone without the line around it — the reference's release badge at the top of this site.

```tsx
<Badge tone="primary" emphasis="flat" leading={<Icon name="rocket" />}>What's new</Badge>
<Badge tone="success" emphasis="flat">Ready</Badge>
```

### Sizes, and what goes inside

A status dot, a round picture, or a glyph before and after the text.

```tsx
<Badge size="sm" dot variant="success">Online</Badge>
<Badge size="md" image="/ana.jpg" imageAlt="">Ana</Badge>
<Badge size="lg" trailing={<Icon name="arrow-right" />}>Next</Badge>
```

### Counting, and the ceiling

Over `max` it reads `99+`. Zero hides itself unless you ask for it — that is the same rule the reference implementations settled on.

```tsx
<Badge count={5} emphasis="solid" variant="danger" />
<Badge count={100} emphasis="solid" variant="danger" />
<Badge count={1000} max={999} emphasis="solid" variant="danger" />
```

### anchor — the counter on the corner

Pass the thing being decorated as children. The count goes in ITS accessible name; the badge itself is hidden from screen readers.

```tsx
<Badge anchor="top-end" count={8} emphasis="solid" variant="danger">
  <IconButton icon="bell" label="Notifications, 8 unread" />
</Badge>
```

### anchorShape — square corner, or round

On a circle the badge is pulled 14% back into the corner. Without that it floats off the edge, which is the giveaway of a counter glued on by hand.

```tsx
<Badge anchor="bottom-end" anchorShape="circle" dot variant="success">
  <Avatar name="Ana Prado" />
</Badge>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `neutral \| primary \| info \| success \| warning \| danger \| running \| paused \| offline \| review \| red \| orange \| green \| teal \| cyan \| blue \| violet \| pink` | neutral | Tone of the label. The four operational ones exist because the state of a job is metadata as often as it is a condition; when it is a condition standing on its own, use Status. The eight colour names (red, orange, green, teal, cyan, blue, violet, pink) are CATEGORIES, not states — they mark a group (a section, a type of item) and say nothing about health. They skip yellow, which belongs to the brand, and pass AA in both themes in all three emphases. Pair the colour with a word or a leading icon: colour alone is never the label. |
| `tone` | `BadgeVariant` | — | The colour, with the native package's name — the same names on web and native. The same axis as variant; it wins when both are given. |
| `emphasis` | `soft \| outline \| solid \| flat` | soft | How loud the tone is. `soft` is the tinted pill you already know; `outline` is contour only; `solid` fills with the accent and is what a notification counter wants. All 36 combinations of variant × emphasis × theme were measured for contrast — the lowest is 5.6:1, and the skin spec keeps it that way. flat is the soft tone without the line around it, as the reference's chip. |
| `size` | `xs \| sm \| md \| lg` | md | `md` is the historical size and did not move, so nothing that already uses Badge changed. `xs` (16px, borderless) is the counter that rides on an icon — it is what BottomNav asks for; `sm` sits between them; `lg` is for a standalone label. Every size is its OWN class, never a contextual override: `geometry.spec` holds `.badge` to one height per page, and a rule that shrank it by context reproved — correctly. |
| `dot` | `boolean` | false | A status dot before the text, inheriting the current colour. With `anchor` and nothing to show, the dot IS the badge — the plain 8px mark that means "something new". |
| `leading / trailing` | `ReactNode` | — | A glyph before or after the text. They take a NODE, not an icon name, and that is a boundary decision, not laziness: Icon reads the sprite through a hook, so importing it here would drag this module to the client and undo the 118.5 KB that ADR-0026 saved. |
| `image / imageAlt` | `string` | — | A round picture at the start — an avatar or a flag. Empty alt when it is decorative, which is the usual case beside a name. |
| `count / max / showZero` | `number / number / boolean` | — / 99 / false | Numeric content. Over `max` it reads `99+`. Zero hides itself unless `showZero`, because an empty inbox does not deserve a mark. `formatBadgeCount(count, max)` is exported so the accessible name can say the same string the eye sees. |
| `fit` | `"auto" \| "content"` | "auto" | `content` keeps the badge as wide as its text even inside a column. The default follows the container, and that was measured: `.stack` declares no `align-items`, so a badge inside it stretches (300 px in a 300 px column, 55 px loose in a block). Implemented as `inline-size: fit-content`, not `align-self`, so a badge in a row keeps its vertical centring. Ignored with `anchor`. The native Badge takes the same prop. |
| `anchor` | `top-end \| top-start \| bottom-end \| bottom-start` | — | Switches to the OVERLAY shape: `children` becomes the thing being decorated (a bell, an avatar, a menu row) and the badge hangs off that corner. Without it, `children` is the pill's content and nothing about the old usage changes. |
| `anchorShape` | `square \| circle` | square | `circle` pulls the badge 14% back into the corner — the `overlap` of one of the references, and the number is theirs, measured in their source. Without it a counter on a round avatar floats off the edge. |
| `invisible` | `boolean` | false | Hides the overlay without moving the child. Use it when the count is loading rather than absent. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The label — or, with `anchor`, the element being decorated. Short by construction: it is a pill, and a badge that wraps to a second line is a sentence in the wrong component. |
| `badgeContent` | `ReactNode` | — | What the overlay shows when it is not a number. Named after a reference library's prop and not `content`, which collides with the HTML attribute of that name. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/banner.html">
# Banner

Prominent message spanning a wide region. variant="consent" is the cookie notice, with the preferences window.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Banner} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Banner variant="success" title="Saved" icon="check" onDismiss={() => setShown(false)}>
  Your changes are live.
</Banner>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `info \| success \| warning \| danger \| consent` | info | Tone, and the same live-region rule as Alert: `danger` is role="alert", the rest role="status". `consent` is the cookie notice: a region named by its h2, the text, and three buttons of the SAME weight — reject the non-essential, accept all, choose — then the confirmation, which takes the focus. Put it at the top of the page, before the skip link, and do not fix it to the screen. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Rendered as a <strong> above the body. On consent it is the h2 that names the region; without it, the strings' consentTitle. |
| `icon` | `IconName` | — | Glyph in the leading column. Leave it out and the column still holds its place — an empty span keeps the three-column grid — so banners stacked together stay aligned. |
| `onDismiss` | `() => void` | — | Passing it is what draws the close button. Without it the banner cannot be dismissed, which is the right default for something the reader has to see. On consent it is the "Hide this message" button of the confirmation; without it the notice hides itself. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The body, under the title. |
| `state` | `waiting_user \| waiting_approval \| waiting_dependency \| offline \| stale \| partial \| degraded` | — | Universal state (Part J) — same axis and same derivation as on Alert: `variant` is severity, `state` is the condition. It sets `data-state`, picks the severity when no `variant` is given, and supplies the message when there are no children. A banner is the page-width place to say “no connection” or “working with reduced capability”, which is why it carries the same vocabulary as the inline alert instead of a second one. |
| `categories` | `ConsentCategory[]` | [] | Only on consent: the categories of the preferences window, in order — {id, label, description?, required?}. Required ones are always on and have no switch; the others start OFF. |
| `value` | `ConsentChoice` | — | Only on consent: the choice already stored, {[id]: boolean}, so the person can come back and change it — show the notice again from a "Cookie settings" link. Without it, only the required categories are on. |
| `onConsent` | `(choice: ConsentChoice, action: "accept-all" \| "reject" \| "custom") => void` | — | Only on consent: the choice made, for the app to store and obey. Required categories always come as true. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/blockeditor.html">
# BlockEditor

The frame around content blocks — order, handle, removal, and the slot where your own editor goes. Aurea does not own the rich text.

## Usage

```tsx
import {BlockEditor} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [blocks, setBlocks] = useState([
  {id: "t", kind: "Heading", children: <h2>The joke tax</h2>},
  {id: "p", kind: "Text", children: <Textarea aria-label="Paragraph" defaultValue="…" />},
  {id: "i", kind: "Image", children: (
    <figure><Image src={photo} alt="The king" ratio="16/9" /><figcaption>The king</figcaption></figure>
  )},
]);

<BlockEditor
  label="Article"
  blocks={blocks}
  onReorder={(from, to) => setBlocks(prev => {
    const next = [...prev];
    next.splice(to, 0, ...next.splice(from, 1));
    return next;
  })}
  onRemove={i => setBlocks(prev => prev.filter((_, n) => n !== i))}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `blocks` | `Array<{id, kind?, children}>` | — | The blocks, in the order they are shown. `children` is your block — a textarea, your rich text editor, a figure with a caption. `kind` names it for a screen reader ("Image", "Quote"); it falls back to a generic "Block". |
| `onReorder` | `(from: number, to: number) => void` | — | Called with the two indexes. The editor is controlled and keeps no order of its own — the keyboard path and the pointer path call this same callback, so there are never two sources of truth. |
| `onRemove` | `(index: number) => void` | — | Optional. Omit it and no remove button is rendered — a button that cannot do anything is a focus target that lies to whoever uses the keyboard, which is the defect the Gallery measured in item L2. |
| `label` | `string` | Content blocks | Accessible name of the list. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/bottomnav.html">
# BottomNav

BottomNav is the bar an application's top-level navigation lives in on a phone. It takes the SAME item type as Sidebar, on purpose: one list feeds the sidebar on a desktop and the bar on a phone, and two lists of one menu drift apart.

## Usage

```tsx
import {BottomNav} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const items = [
  {id: "garage", label: "Garage", icon: "car", href: "/"},
  {id: "fuel", label: "Fuel", icon: "gas-pump", href: "/fuel",
    badge: <Badge size="xs" variant="primary" emphasis="solid">3</Badge>},
  {id: "service", label: "Service", icon: "wrench", href: "/service"},
  {id: "me", label: "Profile", icon: "user", href: "/me"},
];

<BottomNav variant="edge" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

- TWO AXES, and they do not mix. `variant` says where the bar sits — `edge` against the screen, `floating` as a loose pill. `indicator` says what SHAPE marks the current item. The meaning never changes with the shape: current is always gold.

- Nine indicators: none, subtle, pill, circle, circle-raised, circle-bold, circle-outline, capsule, expand. Everything else is shared — touch target, icon frame, typography, badge anchoring, safe area. That is what makes them variants of one component instead of nine.

- The bar stands still when you pick another destination. No size depends on which item is current — not the item, not the label weight — so only the paint moves. The one item that grows is the current one in `expand`, and it grows into a FIXED slot: the buttons shift, the bar does not.

- Every item keeps its label, in every indicator but `expand`. Icon-only navigation only works when the symbols are unmistakable, and Garage/Fuel/Service are not. In `expand` the other items keep their name for the screen reader only.

- The container is a <nav> landmark and each item is a link — not a tab. A tab swaps a panel inside the page; a bottom bar changes page. Giving role="tablist" to a menu makes the screen reader promise arrow keys that lead nowhere.

- The counter hangs off the icon's top corner and is smaller than it — 16px on a 24px icon, the ratio measured in four apps that ship. With no number it is a plain dot: `badge: ""`.

- The current item is marked with aria-current="page" — the same attribute the screen reader announces and the skin paints, so they cannot drift apart.

- One list, two chromes: pass your Sidebar `items` straight in. A nested `items` is ignored here, because a bottom bar is flat.

- It reserves room for the iPhone home indicator with env(safe-area-inset-bottom). That needs viewport-fit=cover in YOUR meta viewport; without it the bar just gets its normal spacing.

- Positioning is sticky, not fixed: it stays inside its container, so it cannot cover a page it does not own, and it falls back to static when there is nothing to scroll.

- The four names of 17/08/2026 — flat, surface, pill, dock — still work and map onto the pair. They are deprecated, not removed.

## Examples

### Floating subtle — a soft container

The bar floats, and the current item gets a soft brand-tinted container around icon and label. The lightest of the filled indicators.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="subtle" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating pill — the same container, fully rounded

Identical to subtle except for the radius. Nothing else changes, which is the point of separating layout from indicator.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="pill" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating circle — the fill wraps only the icon

The label stays below the circle, outside it. This is what a messaging app does, and it is the shape that survives long names.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="circle" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating circle raised — depth instead of colour

The circle becomes a surface of its own, lifted off the bar. The only indicator that separates by elevation rather than by fill.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="circle-raised" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating circle bold — solid gold

The only indicator that fills with the brand colour, so it is the only one that flips the whole foreground — icon, label and counter inside the shape.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="circle-bold" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating circle subtle — a ring, no fill

A soft disc behind the icon frame (no line since 0.34.0). It marks position without adding mass, which is what a navigation bar wants.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="circle-outline" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating capsule — a wide pill behind the icon

A 56 × 32 gold capsule behind the icon only, the active indicator of the design reference. The label stays below it, so the shape never stretches with a long name.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="capsule" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### Floating expand — only the current item says its name

The other items show the icon alone; the current one becomes a gold capsule with the name beside the icon. Its slot is fixed, so the bar never changes size.

```tsx
<BottomNav indicator="expand" label="Garage" current={route} items={items} />
```

### A dot, when there is no number

An empty badge is the plain dot that means "something new". It has no accessible name — there is nothing to read — so put the meaning in the label.

```tsx
<BottomNav
  variant="edge"
  label="Garage"
  current={route}
  items={[
    {id: "garage", label: "Garage", icon: "car", href: "/"},
    {id: "fuel", label: <>Fuel <span className="sr-only">(new)</span></>, icon: "gas-pump", href: "/fuel", badge: ""},
  ]}
/>
```

### Driven by a router

An item without href is a <button>. Same skin, same aria-current — what changes is who performs the navigation. Three to five destinations is the range this component is for; with two, a segmented control usually says it better.

```tsx
<BottomNav
  label="Garage router"
  current={route}
  items={[
    {id: "garage", label: "Garage", icon: "car", onClick: () => go("/")},
    {id: "fuel", label: "Fuel", icon: "gas-pump", onClick: () => go("/fuel")},
    {id: "service", label: "Service", icon: "wrench", onClick: () => go("/service")},
  ]}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `SidebarItem[]` | — | The navigation, as data — the SAME type Sidebar takes, on purpose: one list feeds the sidebar on desktop and the bar on the phone, and two lists of one menu drift apart. Each item is {id, label, href?, icon?, badge?, onClick?}. A nested `items` is ignored here: a bottom bar is flat. `badge` hangs off the icon's top corner and is sized against it (16px on a 24px icon, the ratio measured in shipping apps); pass an EMPTY badge (`badge: ""`) to get the plain dot that means "something new". An item may carry render (a ReactElement, your router's link) instead of href — it receives the item's skin, the current-page state and the item's content. |
| `current` | `string` | — | The id of the item you are on. It gets aria-current="page", which is also what the skin paints — one source for both, so they cannot drift apart. |
| `variant` | `"floating" \| "edge"` | "floating" | Where the BAR sits: floating as a loose pill, or edge against the screen with a hairline above it. It says nothing about how the current item is marked — that is `indicator`, and keeping the two apart is the point. The older names (flat, surface, pill, dock) are still accepted and map onto the pair; they are deprecated, not removed. |
| `indicator` | `"none" \| "subtle" \| "pill" \| "circle" \| "circle-raised" \| "circle-bold" \| "circle-outline" \| "capsule" \| "expand"` | "none" | The SHAPE that marks the current item. The meaning never changes with the shape: current is always the brand gold. `none` marks by colour alone; `subtle` and `pill` wrap icon and label in a tinted container and differ only in radius; `circle`, `circle-raised` and `circle-outline` wrap only the icon, by fill, by elevation or by a ring; `circle-bold` is a solid disc around icon and label, the only one that flips the whole foreground; `capsule` is the 56 × 32 active indicator of the design reference, behind the icon; `expand` draws only icons and grows the current item into a gold capsule with its label — the others keep theirs for the screen reader. Every other indicator keeps every label visible. No measure depends on which item is current, so the bar never moves (ADR-0055). |
| `width` | `"full" \| "content"` | "full" | How wide the floating pill is. `full` spans the screen minus the margin, as it always has; `content` sizes the pill to its items and centres it. Items then measure their own content instead of sharing the width equally, with the item's own touch target (--control-h-lg) as the minimum. Ignored on `edge`, which sits against the screen edge and stays full width. |
| `label` | `string` | "Main" | Accessible name of the <nav>. Two navigation landmarks with the same name fail axe, and a page with a bottom bar usually has a Topbar or Sidebar too — name it. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/breadcrumb.html">
# Breadcrumb

Trail showing the current location in a hierarchy.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Breadcrumb} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Breadcrumb items={[
  {label: "Home", href: "/"},
  {label: "Patterns", href: "/patterns"},
  {label: "QR code"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `Array<{label: ReactNode; href?: string; render?: ReactElement}>` | — | The trail, in order. An item with no href renders as a <strong> carrying aria-current="page" instead of a link — the last crumb is where you already are, and a link to the current page is one more thing to skip. An item may carry render (a ReactElement, your router's link) instead of href — it receives the item's skin, the current-page state and the item's content. |
| `label` | `string` | "Breadcrumb" | Accessible name of the <nav>. Two navigation landmarks sharing a name fail axe. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/button.html">
# Button

Buttons trigger an action or navigate. Keep one primary button per view so the main action is unmistakable; everything else recedes to secondary, outline, ghost or link.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button variant="primary">Publish</Button>
<Button variant="secondary">Edit</Button>
<Button variant="tertiary">Cancel</Button>
<Button variant="outline">Preview</Button>
<Button variant="ghost">Skip</Button>
<Button variant="danger">Delete</Button>
```

- Variants over two axes — appearance (solid, outline, ghost, link) and tone (neutral, brand, destructive) — plus secondary, the neutral fill with the brand-coloured label.

- Five sizes (xs / sm / md / lg / xl) from density tokens; the pill shape is invariant.

- type="button" by default: a Cancel button inside a <form> never fires submit by accident.

- Loading shows a spinner and sets aria-busy; the label stays for context.

- With href it renders an anchor — same skin, link semantics. Disabled becomes aria-disabled.

- share opens the device's share sheet when the browser has one; otherwise it copies the link and says "Link copied" under the button, at the button's own size, and to the screen reader.

- Stretch with fullWidth, announce a shortcut with kbd. For a button that STAYS on, the component is Toggle — `pressed` here is deprecated since 0.4.0 and goes away in 1.0.

## Examples

### Sizes

Five heights from density tokens. On a coarse pointer every size floors at 44px, so xs never becomes an impossible target.

```tsx
<Button size="xs">Extra small</Button>
<Button size="sm">Small</Button>
<Button>Medium</Button>
<Button size="lg">Large</Button>
<Button size="xl">Extra large</Button>
```

### Destructive hierarchy

Deleting is not always the loudest action on the screen. Same tone, three weights.

```tsx
<Button variant="danger">Delete</Button>
<Button variant="danger-outline">Delete</Button>
<Button variant="danger-ghost">Delete</Button>
```

### Soft

The pale fill of the tone with the tone's letter — the reference's soft button. danger-soft is the shortcut for the destructive one that should not shout.

```tsx
<Button appearance="soft" tone="brand">Upgrade</Button>
<Button appearance="soft" tone="success">Approve</Button>
<Button variant="danger-soft">Remove</Button>
```

### Quiet

The muted letter, one step smaller: a secondary control that sits beside the main ones without competing, like the Theme button at the top of this site.

```tsx
<Button size="sm" quiet leadingIcon="paint-bucket">Theme</Button>
```

### Link appearance

Text with no capsule, for inline actions. The underline is there at rest — revealing it on hover would hide the affordance.

```tsx
<Button variant="link">Learn more</Button>
<Button variant="link-primary">Upgrade plan</Button>
<Button variant="link-danger">Delete account</Button>
```

### Loading

Busy and blocked, with the label kept: aria-busy is set and the spinner replaces nothing.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" loading>Publishing…</Button>
```

### Disabled

Unavailable, not hidden — the reason has to be reachable somewhere on the screen.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" disabled>Publish</Button>
<Button disabled>Save draft</Button>
<Button variant="outline" disabled>Preview</Button>
```

### With icons

Glyphs on either side. The icon never replaces the label — it repeats it.

```tsx
<Button leadingIcon="plus">New item</Button>
<Button variant="outline" trailingIcon="caret-down">Sort by</Button>
<Button variant="danger" leadingIcon="trash">Delete</Button>
```

### With shortcut

The key that fires it, shown and announced: kbd renders a Kbd inside the button and sets aria-keyshortcuts. Pass a list for a combination: one cap per key, and the reader hears Control+K.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" kbd="⌘K">Command</Button>
<Button variant="outline" kbd="/">Search</Button>
<Button leadingIcon="magnifying-glass" kbd={["Ctrl", "K"]}>Search</Button>
```

### As a link

With href it renders an anchor wearing the same skin: a button that navigates is a link, and the reader announces it as one.

```tsx
<Button variant="outline" href="/docs" trailingIcon="arrow-right">Read the docs</Button>
```

### Share

share asks the browser whether it can share this link — feature detection, not device guessing. On a phone (and in Chrome, Edge or Safari on a computer) the device's share sheet opens, and closing it is not an error. Where the browser cannot share, the link is copied and "Link copied" appears under the button, at the button's own size. If copying fails, the link is shown selected for Ctrl+C.

```tsx
<Button share={{url: "https://example.com/report", title: "Weekly report"}} leadingIcon="share-network">Share</Button>
<IconButton icon="share-network" label="Share link" variant="secondary" share={{url: "https://example.com/report"}} />
```

### Full width

Stretched to the container for a form footer or a narrow screen — only the width changes.

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" fullWidth>Continue</Button>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `primary \| secondary \| tertiary \| outline \| ghost \| primary-outline \| primary-ghost \| danger \| danger-outline \| danger-ghost \| link \| link-primary \| link-danger \| nav \| danger-soft` | tertiary | A shortcut for the (appearance, tone) pair; the two-axis API is appearance + tone. `secondary` is the neutral fill with the brand-coloured label; `tertiary` the neutral fill with the plain label (the default). |
| `appearance` | `solid \| outline \| ghost \| link \| nav \| soft` | solid | How much weight the box carries. nav is an appearance of its own (a navigation item), not a tone. soft is the tone's light background with the tone's text (the reference's danger-soft). |
| `tone` | `neutral \| brand \| danger \| success \| warning \| info` | neutral | What the colour means. Every tone works with every appearance, filled included — each has its own colour and text pair per theme. |
| `size` | `xs \| sm \| md \| lg \| xl` | md | Height comes from the density tokens; the pill radius never changes. |
| `href` | `string` | — | Renders an <a> with the same skin. A button that navigates is a link. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | false | Shows the spinner, sets aria-busy and blocks interaction. The label stays. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled: the control leaves the tab order entirely. With href it becomes aria-disabled, since a link has no disabled state. USE IT WHEN THERE IS NOTHING TO EXPLAIN — measured on 2026-08-13, a disabled button cannot be focused, so a Tooltip hung on it is never read by anyone navigating with a keyboard, and wrapping it in a span (what other libraries document) fixes the pointer and not the keyboard, because the span comes in at tabIndex -1. |
| `aria-disabled` | `boolean` | — | Inert but REACHABLE: the control keeps its place in the tab order and announces itself as disabled, and this component blocks activation — the attribute is semantics only, so leaving it to the browser would announce "disabled" on a button that still acts. Use it when there IS a why to tell, and put the why in a Tooltip, which now reaches. There is no permission component in Aurea and there will not be one: hiding an action is {can ? … : …} in your own code, and hiding a button is not security — see ADR-0023. |
| `leadingIcon` | `AureaIcon` | — | Glyph before the label — a name from the allowlist, or the app’s own drawing (a component that returns its <svg>), as Icon and IconButton take. |
| `trailingIcon` | `AureaIcon` | — | Glyph after the label — a name, or the app’s own drawing, as leadingIcon. |
| `type` | `button \| submit \| reset` | button | Deliberately not submit: a Cancel inside a form must not fire the main action. |
| `fullWidth` | `boolean` | false | Stretches to the container. Only the width changes — the pill radius is invariant. |
| `quiet` | `boolean` | false | Less weight: muted text one step smaller (12 on sm) — a site header's tool button, as the reference's "Theme". The box and the background stay the appearance's. |
| `pressed` | `boolean` | — | DEPRECATED, removed in 1.0 — use <Toggle>. It only paints and announces (aria-pressed) and YOU keep the state; Toggle owns the state, returns onPressedChange and demands an accessible name when it is icon-only. On, it shows the raised capsule with a yellow underline. |
| `kbd` | `string \| string[]` | — | Shortcut shown as a Kbd inside the button and announced with aria-keyshortcuts. A list (["Ctrl", "K"]) shows one key cap per key and announces the combination (Control+K). |
| `grow` | `boolean` | false | In a row (Cluster), takes an equal share with the other buttons that also grow. `fullWidth` asks for the whole line instead. |
| `target` | `HTMLAttributeAnchorTarget` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `rel` | `string` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `download` | `boolean \| string` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `render` | `ReactElement` | — | The element drawn instead of the <button>/<a> — your router's link, e.g. render={<Link href="/reports" />}. It receives the button's skin, content (icons, label, shortcut) and attributes; the destination is its own. Disabled or loading, its click is blocked too, like the disabled link. |
| `share` | `{ url?: string; title?: string; text?: string }` | — | The button shares. It asks the browser whether it can share this link (navigator.canShare) — detecting the capability, not guessing the device. If it can (phones; Chrome, Edge and Safari on desktop), the device's share sheet opens, and cancelling is not an error. If it cannot, it copies the link and shows "Link copied" anchored to the button, at the button's size. If the copy fails, it says so and shows the link selected. The notice speaks to the screen reader. Without url, it is the page's address. Needs the AureaProvider (or aurea.js on the page) to give the notice; it emits [data-aurea-share], which aurea.js also reads. Only on a <button> (ignored with href or render). On native, the same name opens the system share sheet. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/buttongroup.html">
# ButtonGroup

ButtonGroup binds buttons of the same kind into one coordinated set. It groups visually and semantically — every button stays tabbable, which is exactly what separates it from a Toolbar. Pick by the keyboard behaviour you want, never by how it looks.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ButtonGroup, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Range">
  <Button>Day</Button>
  <Button>Week</Button>
  <Button>Month</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

- role="group" with an accessible name: a set with no name is a pile of buttons to a screen reader.

- Every button keeps its own tab stop. For arrow-key navigation with a single tab stop use Toolbar.

- Joined into one capsule: no gap, rounded only at the ends, a hairline between buttons. `detached` keeps them as loose pills with a small gap.

- variant, size and disabled set on the group reach every button; a button may still set its own.

- fullWidth stretches the group and shares the width equally.

- Selection: one-of-many is SegmentedControl; many-of-many is ToggleGroup.

- Disabling one item does not disable the set, and the disabled item keeps its place.

## Examples

### With leading icons

The glyph repeats the verb of each button; the group still reads as one unit.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Export">
  <Button leadingIcon="download">Download</Button>
  <Button leadingIcon="share">Share</Button>
  <Button leadingIcon="link-simple">Copy link</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

### Variant and size from the group

Set once on the group; every button follows. Here the outline look in the small size.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Zoom" variant="outline" size="sm">
  <Button leadingIcon="minus">Out</Button>
  <Button>100%</Button>
  <Button leadingIcon="plus">In</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

### Detached

Loose pills with a small gap, for buttons that belong together but are not one control.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Actions" detached>
  <Button>Duplicate</Button>
  <Button>Move</Button>
  <Button>Archive</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

### Single selection

The same job with the right component: SegmentedControl carries one value and one tab stop.

```tsx
<SegmentedControl label="View" value="board" onChange={setView}
  items={[{value: "list", label: "List"}, {value: "board", label: "Board"}]} />
```

### Disabled item

One unavailable option does not disable the set, and it keeps its place so the row never shifts.

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Plan">
  <Button>Monthly</Button>
  <Button>Yearly</Button>
  <Button disabled>Lifetime</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `string` | Options | Accessible name of the group. Falls back to the i18n string, but a real name beats a generic one. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Buttons of the same kind. Mixing controls here breaks the promise of a group. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the wrapper. |
| `orientation` | `Responsive<Orientation>` | horizontal | Stacks the buttons instead of lining them up. Visual only — it changes no order, no semantics and no keyboard — so it resolves in the CSS layer and costs no observer. |
| `variant` | `ButtonVariant \| danger-soft` | — | The look of every button inside; a button may set its own. |
| `size` | `xs \| sm \| md \| lg \| xl` | — | The size of every button inside; a button may set its own. Accepts a responsive value. |
| `fullWidth` | `boolean` | false | Fills the parent's width, and the buttons share it equally. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Disables every button inside. |
| `detached` | `boolean` | false | Loose capsules with a 4 gap that wrap, instead of joined. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/calendar.html">
# Calendar

Month grid for picking a day, a range, or several days.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Calendar} from "@aurea-uds/react/calendar";
```

```tsx
<Calendar
  mode="range"
  label="Stay"
  defaultMonth={new Date(2026, 7, 1)}
  selected={{from: new Date(2026, 7, 12), to: new Date(2026, 7, 18)}}
  disabled={{before: new Date(2026, 7, 6)}}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `"single" \| "range" \| "multiple"` | none | What a click does. `single` picks one day, `range` picks a start and an end, `multiple` collects days that need not touch. |
| `selected` | `Date \| DateRange \| Date[]` | none | The current selection. Its shape follows `mode`. |
| `onSelect` | `(value) => void` | none | Called with the new selection. Without it the calendar is read-only, which is a legitimate use: a month with days marked. |
| `disabled` | `Matcher \| Matcher[]` | none | Days that cannot be picked — a date, a range, `{before}`/`{after}`, weekdays, or a function. This is what a native date input cannot do, and the reason this component exists. |
| `label` | `string` | none | Names the whole calendar, for when the month name is not enough to tell it apart — two of them side by side would both announce "August 2026". Inside a popover the trigger already says it, so leave it out. |
| `showOutsideDays` | `boolean` | true | Fills the first and last week with the neighbouring month's days. On by default: a grid with holes at the edges shifts shape when the month changes. |
| `className` | `string` | none | Added to the calendar box. |
| `…DayPicker` | `ComponentProps<typeof DayPicker>` | none | Everything else goes to the engine — `numberOfMonths`, `month`, `locale`, `weekStartsOn`, `fromDate`/`toDate`, `modifiers`. `classNames` merges over the Aurea names instead of replacing them. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/card.html">
# Card

Floating surface that groups related content.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <Card.Header>
    <Card.Title>A floating surface</Card.Title>
    <Card.Description>Radius 22px, no line, no shadow stack.</Card.Description>
  </Card.Header>
  <Card.Content>
    <p>The parts are optional: a card can hold anything.</p>
  </Card.Content>
  <Card.Footer>
    <Button variant="primary">Save</Button>
    <Button>Cancel</Button>
  </Card.Footer>
</Card>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `base \| raised \| interactive \| inset \| outline \| selected \| danger \| contrast` | base | Which surface it is. `interactive` is the only one that answers the pointer, so use it only when the whole card really is a target; `inset` recesses instead of floating, which is what a panel inside a card wants. `contrast` stands out from the screen in both themes: in the light theme it is the dark theme's card, with no outline; in the dark theme it is the regular card with a yellow outline. Inside it the whole dark theme applies (data-theme="dark" on the card), so every child adjusts by itself. Do not use it in a list of choices: in the dark theme its outline is close to `selected`. `outline` has no fill of its own — it takes the colour of whatever it sits on — and keeps only the line around it: the big showcase box of a documentation home page. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The content. Padding comes from --card-pad and the 22px radius from --radius-card; neither is a prop, because the floating surface is the identity of the system. |
| `render` | `ReactElement` | — | The ELEMENT the card renders as, with the Aurea surface merged into it. Required when variant is "interactive": a card that is a target has to be a real target — <button> for an action, <a href> for navigation — and only you know which. tabIndex on a <div> would give focus with no role, no key and no accessible name. |
| `accent` | `brand \| success \| info \| warning \| danger` | — | A colour stroke on the top edge, --accent-width (4) tall, in the tone's FILL colour, the same in both themes. It is decoration: the card's own title says the subject, so the stroke carries no information of its own. The other sides keep the regular 1px border, and the stroke wins over `selected`, `danger` and the `contrast` outline. |
| `padding` | `"normal" \| "none"` | "normal" | none removes the inner padding so media bleeds to the edge; the 22 radius stays and clips the media. |
| `orientation` | `"vertical" \| "horizontal"` | "vertical" | `horizontal` is the list mode: Card.Media on the left at thumbnail width (96, --space-24) and the content beside it. |
| `Card.Media` | `component` | — | The card's media part. Vertical, as first child, it bleeds to the top and side edges; horizontal, it sits on the left inside the padding, with the house's concentric radius (ADR-0033). |
| `Card.Header` | `component` | — | The header: the title and the description, together. 12 between the parts. |
| `Card.Title` | `component` | — | The card's title — an h3, 14/24 medium, as the reference. 12 between the parts. |
| `Card.Description` | `component` | — | The line under the title, 14/20 muted. 12 between the parts. |
| `Card.Content` | `component` | — | The body: a column with 4 between the items. 12 between the parts. |
| `Card.Footer` | `component` | — | The footer: a row (the buttons), 8 between them. 12 between the parts. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/carousel.html">
# Carousel

Slides that snap, with arrows and dots. The scroll container is the engine.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Carousel} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

