| `poster` | `string` | — | Still image for the facade. With it, nothing from the provider loads until the play button is pressed; without it, the frame loads lazily right away. |
| `ratio` | `string` | 16/9 | Box proportion in CSS syntax. Reserved before anything loads, so the page does not jump. |
| `href` | `string` | — | The video on its own site. Shown as a link under the frame — the way out when the owner blocks embedding, which the page cannot detect. |
| `autoplay` | `boolean` | true | With a poster, start playing after the click by adding autoplay=1 to the address (YouTube and Vimeo read the same key). The person already asked to play. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/mediaplayer.html">
# MediaPlayer

Video/audio player with full controls.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayer} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayer
  kind="audio"
  src="/media/episode-14.mp3"
  title="Episode 14"
  subtitle="Measuring instead of counting"
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src` | `string` | — | The media. Any <video> attribute is accepted and forwarded. |
| `kind` | `video \| audio` | video | Audio swaps the picture for a placeholder with the title, and drops the full-screen button — there is nothing to enlarge. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Shown over the video and used as the accessible name of the control group when it is a string. It deliberately shadows the HTML title attribute: a tooltip on a player is not what you want. |
| `subtitle` | `ReactNode` | — | Second line under the title. |
| `poster` | `string` | — | Still frame before playback. Video only. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Where <track> elements go. Captions are read from the element's textTracks, so the CC button appears only when a track actually exists. |
| `onPlay` | `(e: SyntheticEvent) => void` | — | Your media handlers are COMPOSED with the internal ones, never replacing them — the same holds for onPause, onEnded, onTimeUpdate, onLoadedMetadata, onDurationChange, onProgress and onVolumeChange. An external onPlay that replaced ours would leave the button reading "Play" during playback. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/mediaplayershell.html">
# MediaPlayerShell

Layout shell hosting a media player and its chrome.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayerShell} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayerShell role="group" aria-label="Camera 3">
  <div className="media-viewport">
    <div className="media-placeholder"><Icon name="video-camera" /><strong>Standing by</strong></div>
  </div>
  <div className="media-overlay-title">
    <div><strong>Camera 3</strong><span>Loading dock</span></div>
    <Badge variant="danger">on air</Badge>
  </div>
  <div className="media-controls">
    <div className="media-control-row">
      <div className="media-control-group">
        <button className="media-control" type="button" aria-label="Play"><Icon name="play" /></button>
        {/* sem barra de busca: ao vivo não tem para onde voltar */}
        <span className="media-time">LIVE</span>
      </div>
      <div className="media-control-group">
        <button className="media-control" type="button" aria-label="Mute"><Icon name="speaker-high" /></button>
        <button className="media-control" type="button" aria-label="Full screen"><Icon name="arrows-out" /></button>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</MediaPlayerShell>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The chrome you compose, hosted by the frame. What the frame gives you is worth naming, because rebuilding it by hand is where players go wrong: the dark canvas that stays dark in both themes, overflow clipping so nothing escapes the rounded corner, an isolated stacking context so .media-overlay-title and .media-controls layer above the picture without z-index fights, and a fixed aspect-ratio so the page does not jump before the media has measured itself. Slots it is built for: .media-viewport (picture or placeholder), .media-overlay-title, .media-controls. Use it when the default chrome would be WRONG — a live stream has no duration and nothing to seek, so a seek bar there is a control that lies. For a player that plays, use MediaPlayer. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the surface. Every other div attribute passes through. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/memoryledger.html">
# MemoryLedger

What the agent stored, recalled or forgot — and where it came from.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MemoryLedger} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MemoryLedger records={[
  {id: "1", content: "Prefers metric units", scope: "semantic",
   operation: "added", time: "10:02", source: "conversation"},
  {id: "2", content: "Old shipping address", scope: "episodic",
   operation: "forgotten", time: "10:41"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `records` | `MemoryRecord[]` | — | One entry per posting, not per memory. A ledger is append-only: "forgotten" does not drop the row, it records the forgetting — and that row is exactly what you go looking for when an agent stops knowing something. |
| `label` | `string` | "Memory ledger" | Accessible name of the list. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the list. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/menubar.html">
# Menubar

The application menu row — File, Edit, View — where an open menu hands over to its neighbour.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Menubar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Menubar label="Main" menus={[
  {label: "File", items: [{label: "New"}, {label: "Open"}, "separator", {label: "Quit"}]},
  {label: "Edit", items: [{label: "Undo"}, {label: "Redo"}]},
  {label: "View", items: [{label: "Zoom in"}, {label: "Zoom out"}]},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `menus` | `Array<{ label: ReactNode; items: MenuEntry[]; disabled?: boolean; }>` | — | The bar, as data: one entry per top-level menu, each with its own MenuEntry list. Passing them together is what lets an open menu hand over to its neighbour on the arrow key. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the bar. |
| `orientation` | `Responsive<MenubarOrientation>` | horizontal | A vertical menubar is the side-panel shape. Responsive. |
| `loopFocus` | `boolean` | true | The arrow wraps from the last menu back to the first. |
| `modal` | `boolean` | true | While a menu is open the rest of the page is inert. Turn it off for a bar that stays usable with a menu down. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Turns the whole bar off. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/messagecomposer.html">
# MessageComposer

Input surface for composing a message.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MessageComposer} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MessageComposer
  icon="chat"
  placeholder="Message the team…"
  onSend={text => send(text)}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `onSend` | `(text: string, details?: {files: File[]; replyToId?: string; editingId?: string}) => void` | — | Called with the trimmed text, then the field clears itself. Empty or whitespace-only never sends, and the send button stays disabled until there is something to send. The second argument exists only when attach, replyTo or editing is in use, so a call checked as onSend(text) still is exactly that. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | — | Hint inside the field. It is not the name — a placeholder disappears the moment you type. |
| `label` | `string` | "Message" | Accessible name of the input, which is what a screen reader reads. |
| `icon` | `IconName` | — | Glyph inside the field, before the text. |
| `sendLabel` | `string` | "Send" | Accessible name of the send button, which shows only an icon. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Disables the field and the button together. |
| `attach` | `boolean \| {accept?: string; maxSize?: number; multiple?: boolean}` | — | A paperclip inside the field opens the file picker. The chosen files sit above the field, inside the same frame, with FileInput's row (.file-item: name, size, a thumbnail for images, remove) and FileInput's filter and messages. Uploading is the app's: the files go out in onSend. With a file, an empty text can be sent. Hidden while editing. |
| `replyTo` | `{id: string; author?: ReactNode; body: ReactNode} \| null` | — | The message being answered, shown above the field as a quote (who, and its first line). The field takes focus. The id goes out in onSend as replyToId. |
| `onCancelReply` | `() => void` | — | The X on the quote, and Escape in the field. The app clears replyTo. |
| `editing` | `{id: string; body: string} \| null` | — | Edit mode: the old text fills the field, Send becomes Save, and the id goes out in onSend as editingId. When editing ends, the field is cleared — the old text does not stay as a draft. |
| `onCancelEdit` | `() => void` | — | The X on the quote, and Escape in the field. The app clears editing. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the <form>. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/messagelist.html">
# MessageList

Scrolling list of conversation messages.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MessageList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MessageList messages={[
  {id: "1", author: "Analyst", time: "09:12", body: "The sweep is green.", avatar: {fallback: "AN"}},
  {id: "2", author: "You", time: "09:14", body: "Shipping it.", status: {label: "sent", variant: "success"}},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `messages` | `ChatMessage[]` | — | The conversation, as data: {id, body, author?, time?, avatar?, status?}. Transport and state are yours; this renders. A message may also carry direction ("incoming" \| "outgoing"), forwardedFrom, replyTo {id, author?, body}, attachments [{id, kind: "image" \| "video" \| "file", src?, alt?, name?, bytes?, duration?, href?}], edited and day. Photos and videos become an album in the Gallery (zoom included); files become FileInput's row, with a download link when href is given. A day separator appears whenever day changes from one message to the next; its text is the app's. |
| `hasMoreBefore` | `boolean` | false | There are older messages above. A row at the top (the measure of the reference library's load-more table row) calls onReachStart when it enters the screen. |
| `onReachStart` | `() => void` | — | Load older messages. When they arrive on top, the message that was at the top of the screen stays exactly where it was. Turns the window on. |
| `loadingBefore` | `boolean` | false | Older messages are on their way: the top row shows the Spinner, the list is aria-busy, and onReachStart is not called again until it ends. |
| `hasMoreAfter` | `boolean` | false | There are newer messages below that the app dropped to keep its window small (about a thousand). The bottom row calls onReachEnd. |
| `onReachEnd` | `() => void` | — | Bring newer messages back. Turns the window on. |
| `loadingAfter` | `boolean` | false | Newer messages are on their way: the bottom row shows the Spinner. |
| `onOpenAttachment` | `(message: ChatMessage, attachment: MessageAttachment) => void` | — | Called when a photo or video of an album is clicked, instead of the built-in zoom — for a player, or the app's own viewer. |
| `label` | `string` | "Conversation" | Accessible name of the log region. Name it when a page holds more than one conversation. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the container, which is also the live region. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/modelusage.html">
# ModelUsage

Consumption split by model: which one took how much.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ModelUsage} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ModelUsage metric="tokens" entries={[
  {id: "1", model: "opus", provider: "anthropic", tokens: 1_840_000},
  {id: "2", model: "haiku", provider: "anthropic", tokens: 620_000},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `entries` | `ModelUsageEntry[]` | — | One row per model: model, optional provider, and the three measures (tokens, cost, requests). Rows are sorted descending by the active metric, on a copy — the caller's array is not mutated. |
| `metric` | `"tokens" \| "cost" \| "requests"` | "tokens" | Which measure the bars compare. The reference exposes the same choice as four tabs because each one is a separate query in its product; here the data arrives ready and the dimension is a prop. |
| `currency` | `string` | "USD" | ISO currency code, used only when metric is "cost". |
| `locale` | `string` | "en-US" | Passed to Intl.NumberFormat. The default is fixed on purpose: a locale read from the environment would make the rendered text differ between a developer machine and CI, and the catalogue is rendered ahead of time. |
| `label` | `string` | "Model usage" | Accessible name of the region. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the card. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/multicombobox.html">
# MultiCombobox

MultiCombobox is the many-of-many Combobox: the picked options stay as chips inside the field, and typing filters what is left. It takes flat options or groups, and it accepts a remote search — you filter on your side, the component only shows and announces the result.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MultiCombobox} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [tags, setTags] = useState([]);

<MultiCombobox label="Tags" placeholder="Add a tag…" value={tags}
  onValueChange={setTags}
  items={[{value: "a11y", label: "Accessibility"}, {value: "perf", label: "Performance"}]} />
```

- Selected options live as removable chips in the field, each with its own remove control.

- Flat items or grouped items ({label, items}) for a long, sectioned list.

- onInputChange plus loading: the search can be remote and the wait is announced, not silent.

- Base UI keyboard: arrows, Enter, Escape, and Backspace removing the last chip.

- disabled reaches the chips too: no removing what you cannot add.

- The previews show the CLOSED field; the popup lives in a portal and only exists in a real app.

## Examples

### Remote search

You own the query; the component shows the state of it.

```tsx
<MultiCombobox label="People" loading={isFetching}
  onInputChange={q => search(q)}
  items={results} value={picked} onValueChange={setPicked} />
```

### Grouped options

Sections with headings, for a list long enough to need them.

```tsx
const items = [
  {label: "Actions", items: [{value: "button", label: "Button"}]},
  {label: "Inputs", items: [{value: "input", label: "Input"}]},
];

<MultiCombobox label="Components" items={items} value={picked} onValueChange={setPicked} />
```

### Disabled

The chips stay readable, and nothing can be added or removed.

```tsx
<MultiCombobox label="Tags" items={tags} value={picked} disabled />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `ComboboxOption[] \| ComboboxOptGroup[]` | — | Flat options or groups with headings. |
| `value` | `ComboboxOption[]` | — | The selected options, as chips inside the field. |
| `onValueChange` | `(v) => void` | — | Fires with the new selection. |
| `onInputChange` | `(text: string) => void` | — | For a remote search: you filter, the component only shows. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | false | Announces "Loading…" while your search is in flight. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the field. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Turns off the field, the buttons and the chip removals at once. |
| `empty` | `ReactNode` | "No results" | What the list shows when nothing matches. `loading` still wins over it, so the list never flashes 'No results' while a query is in flight. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | — | Shown while nothing is selected. With chips in the field it only shows on an empty selection. |
| `id` | `string` | — | Id of the INPUT, not of the container — it is what a <label htmlFor> has to point at. Without it one is generated. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the field wrapper, not onto the input. |
| `aria-describedby` | `string` | — | Goes to the input, which is the focusable node. It is spelled out because this component unpacks a fixed list of props and silently drops anything else — that is what kept Field from reaching the input (AUD-0001). |
| `aria-invalid` | `boolean \| "true" \| "false"` | — | Same route and same reason as aria-describedby: the input carries it, the wrapper would not announce it. |
| `aria-label` | `string` | — | Accessible name when there is no visible label — a filter in a grid without labels. With `label`, prefer `label`. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/navlist.html">
# NavList

NavList is the list of tappable rows that open something: leading icon, label, an optional second line, an optional trailing value, and the chevron that says the row goes somewhere. It is the brick every settings screen is built from.

## Usage

```tsx
import {NavList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <NavList items={[
    {id: "profile", label: "Profile", description: "Name, photo, handle", icon: "user", href: "/profile"},
    {id: "alerts", label: "Notifications", description: "Push, email", icon: "bell", value: "On", href: "/alerts"},
    {id: "plan", label: "Plan", icon: "wallet", value: <Badge size="xs">Free</Badge>, href: "/plan"},
    {id: "sync", label: "Sync", icon: "cloud", value: <Status tone="success">Live</Status>, href: "/sync"},
  ]} />
</Card>
```

- It is a plain <ul> of links — NOT a landmark. Sidebar and BottomNav are app chrome and live in a <nav>; this is content inside the page, and a third <nav> on one screen only adds noise for anyone navigating by landmark.

- There is no current item, on purpose. aria-current would promise a current page in a list you enter and come back from — that is Sidebar's job, not this one.

- The trailing value takes any node, so Badge, Status or plain text compose in without this component knowing they exist. That is why there is no `badge` prop here.

- The text is the only track that shrinks. The value and the chevron never do: a clipped value lies ("R$ 1.2" for "R$ 1.234") and a clipped chevron stops saying the row opens.

- `href` decides the element AND the chevron. With it the row is a link and gets the arrow; without it the row is a button and has no arrow — because the arrow promises the row opens something, and signing out opens nothing.

- A disabled row stays FOCUSABLE and inert (aria-disabled), because :disabled drops a control out of the tab order and keyboard users never find out the row is there.

- On a coarse pointer the whole row grows to 44px — WCAG 2.5.5, and the size the iOS and Android guidelines both land on. The target is the row, never the chevron.

- The list paints no surface and draws no divider: Card already gives the grouped panel, and the row highlight here is the pill — a pill with a rule under it contradicts itself.

## Examples

### A list of conversations

AN-04: a photo at the start, in place of the icon, and small signs before the value — pinned, muted. Each sign has a name the screen reader reads; it is not drawn.

```tsx
<Card>
  <NavList items={[
    {id: "ana", label: "Ana", description: "See you tomorrow", avatar: {src: ana, fallback: "AN"},
      indicators: [{icon: "push-pin", label: "Pinned"}], value: <Badge size="xs">3</Badge>, href: "/chat/ana"},
    {id: "team", label: "Design team", description: "Bia: the new deck is up", avatar: {fallback: "DT"},
      indicators: [{icon: "bell-slash", label: "Muted"}], href: "/chat/team"},
  ]} />
</Card>
```

### Just label and chevron

The second line, the value and the icon are all optional. A row that only goes somewhere carries only the name and the arrow.

```tsx
<Card>
  <NavList items={[
    {id: "terms", label: "Terms of service", href: "/terms"},
    {id: "privacy", label: "Privacy", href: "/privacy"},
    {id: "about", label: "About", href: "/about"},
  ]} />
</Card>
```

### Rows that act, and rows that cannot

No href means the row is a <button> — and it carries NO chevron, because the arrow promises the row opens something and signing out opens nothing. A disabled row is a button too (a disabled link does not exist in HTML) and it stays focusable, so a keyboard user still hears that it is unavailable.

```tsx
<Card>
  <NavList items={[
    {id: "export", label: "Export data", description: "Sends a copy by email", icon: "download", onClick: startExport},
    {id: "beta", label: "Beta features", description: "Not on your plan", icon: "lightning", disabled: true},
    {id: "out", label: "Sign out", icon: "sign-out", onClick: signOut},
  ]} />
</Card>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `NavListItem[]` | — | The rows, as data — the house idiom, the same one Sidebar, BottomNav, Timeline and Breadcrumb use. Each item is {id, label, description?, value?, icon?, avatar?, indicators?, href?, onClick?, disabled?}. `description` is the second line and it is optional on purpose: a settings row often needs it ("Notifications" / "Push, email") and a plain destination row does not. `value` is the trailing accessory and takes any node, so Badge, Status or plain text compose in without this component knowing about them. `href` decides the element AND the chevron: with it the row is a link and gets the arrow, without it the row is a button and carries none — an arrow promises the row opens something. `disabled` forces the button form and marks it aria-disabled. An item may carry render (a ReactElement, your router's link) instead of href — it receives the item's skin, the current-page state and the item's content. `avatar` ({src?, fallback?}, the same shape as ChatMessage.avatar) puts a photo at the start of the row, in place of the icon. `indicators` ([{icon, label}]) are small muted signs before the value — pinned, muted — and each label is read by the screen reader, not drawn. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the <ul>. The list paints no surface of its own — wrap it in Card when the design calls for a grouped panel. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/notificationcenter.html">
# NotificationCenter

Inbox surface aggregating notifications.

## Usage

```tsx
import {NotificationCenter} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<NotificationCenter
  onMarkAllRead={markAll}
  items={[
    {id: "1", title: "Build passed", time: "2m", group: "Today"},
    {id: "2", title: "New member", time: "1h", group: "Today", read: true},
  ]}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `NotificationItem[]` | — | The feed, as data: {id, title, description?, time?, icon?, read?, group?, onClick?}. Read and unread are yours — the panel is presentational. So is the order: groups are formed in order of first appearance and never re-sorted. |
| `onItemClick` | `(item: NotificationItem) => void` | — | Fires for every item. An item that has neither this nor its own onClick renders as a <div>, not a button — nothing that does nothing is focusable. |
| `onMarkAllRead` | `() => void` | — | Draws the mark-all action, and only while something is unread. |
| `label` | `string` | "Notifications" | Accessible name of the trigger and of the panel. The unread count is appended to the trigger's name, so it is heard and not only seen. |
| `icon` | `IconName` | notification | Glyph on the trigger. |
| `side` | `top \| right \| bottom \| left` | bottom | Which side the panel opens on. It flips on its own when there is no room. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/numberfield.html">
# NumberField

Numeric field with decrease and increase controls, for a quantity you nudge.

## Usage

```tsx
import {NumberField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<NumberField defaultValue={1} min={0} max={99} label="Quantity" />

<NumberField
  label="Price"
  name="price"
  defaultValue={1234.5}
  format={{style: "currency", currency: "BRL"}}
  locale="pt-BR"
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value / defaultValue` | `number \| null` | none | Controlled or uncontrolled. `null` means empty, which is not the same as zero. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: number \| null) => void` | none | Fires with the parsed number, or null when the field is cleared. |
| `min / max` | `number` | none | Bounds. The engine clamps and disables the control that would cross them. |
| `step` | `number` | 1 | How much each press moves the value. |
| `format` | `Intl.NumberFormatOptions` | — | Currency, percent or unit, formatted by the platform's Intl — {style: "currency", currency: "BRL"} replaces the money-formatting library a consumer would otherwise install for this alone. The engine formats when focus LEAVES the field, which is what accessibility guidance recommends and the opposite of a live mask. |
| `locale` | `string` | the browser's | Which locale formats the number. Pass it when the value's locale is a property of the data (a price in BRL) rather than of the reader. |
| `name` | `string` | — | Form field name. It is also what makes the engine render the hidden input carrying the RAW number, so what a form submits is 1234.5 and never the formatted text. |
| `label` | `string` | none | Accessible name of the field. Use with `Field` when there is a visible label. |
| `disabled / readOnly / required` | `boolean` | false | Standard form states, forwarded to the input and to both buttons. |
| `scrubbable / scrubDirection` | `boolean / 'horizontal' \| 'vertical'` | false / horizontal | Opt-in drag handle: pulling it changes the value, which beats forty clicks on + over a wide range. Purely additive — the two buttons, the arrow keys and Home/End are untouched, and the handle itself is aria-hidden because dragging is a pointer gesture with no keyboard equivalent to promise. The axis is a class, not a data attribute: the engine does not publish direction. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
| `id` | `string` | — | Id of the focusable control, which is what a <label htmlFor> has to point at. Generated when you do not pass one. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/otpfield.html">
# OTPField

One box per character, for a verification code the user types or pastes.

## Usage

```tsx
import {OTPField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<OTPField length={6} label="Verification code" />
<OTPField length={6} groupSize={3} label="Verification code, in two groups" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `length` | `number` | — | REQUIRED. How many characters the code has. Without it the field cannot know when it is complete. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `string` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. The whole code as one string, not one value per box. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` | — | Fires on every character, including when a full code is pasted at once. |
| `mask` | `boolean` | false | Hides the characters, the way a password does. |
| `groupSize` | `number` | — | The dash between groups: one every groupSize boxes (3 for a 6-digit code), as the reference's showcase. Drawing only — the screen reader goes box by box. |
| `variant` | `"primary" \| "secondary"` | "primary" | secondary gives the boxes the neutral background of the secondary Input, for a field inside a card. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the group — what the code is for. |
| `disabled / required` | `boolean` | false | Standard form states, forwarded to every box. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
| `id` | `string` | — | Id of the focusable control, which is what a <label htmlFor> has to point at. Generated when you do not pass one. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pagination.html">
# Pagination

Pagination moves between the pages of a list: the page numbers, with ellipses when there are many, previous and next. The current page has Aurea's light highlight. With href, every page is a real link a search engine can follow.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Pagination} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Pagination label="Search results" page={page} total={12} onPageChange={setPage} />
```

- Numbers by default: the first, the last, the current one and one on each side (siblings).

- summary puts a line on the left — "1 to 5 of 50 orders".

- href turns each page into a link (<a href>), with aria-current on the current one.

- variant="simple" keeps only previous and next; variant="compact" is the look up to 0.31.0.

- Each number is named "Page 3" for screen readers.

- label names the navigation landmark: with two paginations on one page, each says what it pages through.

## Examples

### With a summary

The line on the left says what the pages hold.

```tsx
<Pagination label="Orders" page={1} total={10} summary="1 to 5 of 50 orders" onPageChange={setPage} />
```

### Simple

Only previous and next — for an article split into parts.

```tsx
<Pagination variant="simple" label="Article parts" page={2} total={4} onPageChange={setPage} />
```

### Links

With href each page is a real link, which a search engine follows and a person can open in a new tab.

```tsx
<Pagination label="Blog posts" page={2} total={6} href={(p) => `/blog?page=${p}`} />
```

### Compact

The look up to 0.31.0, for a tight toolbar.

```tsx
<Pagination variant="compact" label="Log entries" page={3} total={12} onPageChange={setPage} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `page` | `number` | — | The current page, counting from 1. |
| `total` | `number` | — | How many PAGES there are, not how many rows. Previous and Next disable themselves at the ends. |
| `onPageChange` | `(page: number) => void` | — | Called with the new page. Optional with href: the page can just navigate. |
| `variant` | `numbers \| simple \| compact` | numbers | numbers: the page numbers, with ellipses (the default). simple: previous and next only. compact: Previous · 3 / 12 · Next, for a tight toolbar. |
| `summary` | `ReactNode` | — | The summary on the left — "1 to 5 of 50 orders". |
| `href` | `(page: number) => string` | — | The address of each page. With it, pages are real links a search engine follows. |
| `siblings` | `number` | 1 | How many pages show on each side of the current one. |
| `label` | `string` | strings.paginationLabel | The name of the navigation landmark. With two paginations on one page, each says what it pages through ("Orders", "Search results"); otherwise a screen reader hears two identical landmarks. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the nav, after the Aurea skin. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/paragraph.html">
# Paragraph

A paragraph of body text in one of three sizes.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Paragraph} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Paragraph>The weekly report is ready for review.</Paragraph>
<Paragraph size="sm">Generated by Writer at 09:40.</Paragraph>
<Paragraph size="xs" color="muted">Figures are rounded to the nearest unit.</Paragraph>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size` | `"base" \| "sm" \| "xs"` | "base" | Body text at 16, 14 or 12px, all with relaxed leading. The same three sizes the reference library's Paragraph has. |
| `color` | `"default" \| "muted"` | "default" | Two colours only, like the reference library: the text colour or the muted one. A closed list protects contrast — both pass AA on every Aurea surface. |
| `tone` | `"default" \| "muted" \| "subtle" \| "primary" \| "link" \| "danger" \| "success" \| "warning" \| "info"` | — | The text colour with the native package's name — the same names on web and native. link is the yellow made for text, readable on both themes; primary is the fill yellow and nearly disappears on the light theme. The state colours are the -400 pair. It wins over color when both are given. |
| `weight` | `"normal" \| "medium" \| "semibold" \| "bold" \| "extrabold"` | — (the role's own) | Overrides the weight of the role. Headings are semibold and body text is regular by default. "extrabold" (800, --weight-extrabold) is for a cover title; the default title weight is still semibold. |
| `align` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "justify"` | — (inherited) | Text alignment. start and end follow the writing direction, so the same value mirrors in RTL. |
| `truncate` | `boolean` | false | One line, cut with an ellipsis. Turns the element into a block so the cut has a width to measure against. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The text. |
| `numeric` | `boolean` | false | Tabular figures (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums) — for numbers that line up in a column (price, year, spec sheet) or change on screen. Off by default: in running text the narrow "1" is right. Native: the same prop sets fontVariant ["tabular-nums"]. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/passwordfield.html">
# PasswordField

A password field with a show/hide control that announces what it does.

## Usage

```tsx
import {PasswordField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Field label="Password">
  <PasswordField autoComplete="new-password" />
</Field>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step. It also picks the size of the show/hide button, so the two never disagree. |
| `defaultVisible` | `boolean` | false | Starts with the password showing. Uncontrolled — the component owns the state from there, because the toggle is a gesture, not application state. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/popover.html">
# Popover

Anchored floating surface with content or interaction.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Popover} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Popover
  title="Filters"
  arrow
  trigger={<Button variant="outline">Filters</Button>}
>
  <Checkbox label="Only mine" />
  <Checkbox label="Archived" />
</Popover>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trigger` | `ReactElement` | — | One element, and it becomes the trigger — the engine merges the ref and the ARIA into it instead of wrapping it, so your button stays your button. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Optional heading inside the panel, rendered as a <strong>. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The content. This is the overlay that may hold focus and interactive elements; a Tooltip may not. |
| `side` | `top \| right \| bottom \| left` | bottom | Preferred side. It flips on its own when there is no room, so this is a preference, not a promise. |
| `arrow` | `boolean` | false | The arrow, off by default as in the reference library. Our own curve, 12 × 6, with the surface fill and the border line. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/progress.html">
# Progress

Progress shows how far a task has gone. With a value it is determinate; without one it is indeterminate — the total is not known yet, and a piece runs across the track instead of a 0% that reads as stalled. The anatomy is the reference library's ProgressBar: the detail above, on the end side, and the track below.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Progress} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Progress value={64} label="Uploading" />
<Progress label="Counting files" />
```

- No value, no aria-valuenow: the bar never announces a 0% it does not mean.

- With reduced motion the indeterminate bar does not run — it fills and dims, and never stands still at 40%.

- A text detail is heard once, inside aria-valuetext ("64%, 2.3 MB/s").

- Tone uses Button's closed list: paused is neutral, failed is danger. Every tone keeps 3:1 against the track.

## Examples

### Detail

Speed, time left, bytes — small, muted, with figures of equal width so the numbers do not jitter.

```tsx
<Progress value={64} label="Uploading" detail="2.3 MB/s · 12 s left" />
<Progress label="Counting files" detail="1,204 files" />
```

### Tone

What the colour means. Paused is neutral; failed is danger.

```tsx
<Progress value={40} label="Paused" tone="neutral" detail="Paused" />
<Progress value={100} label="Done" tone="success" detail="Done" />
<Progress value={72} label="Disk" tone="warning" detail="72% full" />
<Progress value={58} label="Upload" tone="danger" detail="Failed at 58%" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | `number` | — | Percentage, 0 to 100. Clamped once and used for both the fill and aria-valuenow, so what is drawn and what is announced cannot drift apart. Without a value the bar is indeterminate: a piece two fifths wide runs across the track — the reference library's numbers, 1.5 s — instead of a 0% that reads as stalled. With reduced motion it does not run: the whole bar, dimmed, never a still piece that would read as 40% done. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the bar. Not drawn. Without it the screen reader announces a bare number with no subject. |
| `detail` | `ReactNode` | — | Supporting text above the track, on the end side — the reference library's ProgressBar.Output: speed, time left, bytes. Small, muted, tabular figures. As text it also becomes aria-valuetext; anything else (a link) stays where it is for the screen reader to reach. |
| `tone` | `brand \| neutral \| success \| warning \| danger \| info` | brand | What the fill colour means — the same closed list as Button's tone. Paused is neutral; failed is danger. Every tone keeps 3:1 against the track in both themes, except brand in the light theme (the brand gold is a fill, ADR-0054). |
| `showLabel` | `boolean` | false | shows the label above the bar, at the start (the reference library's progress bar). Without it, label only names the bar for screen readers. |
| `showValue` | `boolean` | false | shows the value ("60%") above the bar, at the end, when there is no detail. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg"` | "md" | The track: 4, 8 or 12 thick — the reference library's. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Goes on the outer box, the one that holds the detail and the track. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/progresscircle.html">
# ProgressCircle

ProgressCircle shows progress as a ring that fills from the top. Without a value it spins, because nobody knows how much is left. It needs a label, like every progress bar.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ProgressCircle} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ProgressCircle label="Uploading" value={60} size="sm" />
<ProgressCircle label="Uploading" value={60} />
<ProgressCircle label="Uploading" value={60} size="lg" />
```

- role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, min and max; indeterminate leaves the values out.

- Three sizes from the reference library: 20, 28 and 36.

- The same tones as Progress, with the brand yellow by default.

- With reduced motion, the indeterminate ring turns slower.

## Examples

### Tones and no value

The tone says how it is going; without a value, it spins.

```tsx
<ProgressCircle label="Backup" value={100} tone="success" />
<ProgressCircle label="Storage" value={92} tone="warning" />
<ProgressCircle label="Loading" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `string` | — | REQUIRED. What is in progress ("Uploading the file"). |
| `value` | `number` | — | From min to max. Left out, the ring spins: nobody knows how much is left. |
| `min` | `number` | 0 | The start. |
| `max` | `number` | 100 | The end. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg"` | "md" | 20, 28, 36 — the reference library's ring: a 4 stroke on a 36 frame, round cap. |
| `tone` | `"brand" \| "neutral" \| "success" \| "warning" \| "danger" \| "info"` | "brand" | The fill colour, the same tones as Progress. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Added to the ring. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/prose.html">
# Prose

The skin for long-form text. It is not the parser — that stays yours.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Prose} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Prose>
  <h2>The joke tax</h2>
  <p>The king thought long and hard, and finally came up with <a href="#">a plan</a>.</p>
  <blockquote>Everyone enjoys a good joke, so it is only fair that they pay.</blockquote>
  <ul><li>Puns: 5 coins</li><li>One-liners: 20 coins</li></ul>
</Prose>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The rendered article. Bring your own Markdown renderer — react-markdown, MDX, or the HTML your CMS already returns. Prose styles h1-h4, p, a, ul, ol, li, blockquote, code, pre, img, hr, figcaption, table, th and td, all scoped under .prose. |
| `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` | `{__html: string}` | — | Accepted because it is a div, and it is the most likely way to use this. SANITISE FIRST — with DOMPurify or your framework's sanitiser. Aurea styles the text; it cannot and must not decide what is safe to render. |
| `--prose-measure` | `CSS custom property` | 68ch | The reading measure. Long lines are hard to track back to the next one, so the text caps its own width rather than filling the container. Set it, or set it to none if the page already constrains the column. |
| `--font-editorial` | `CSS custom property` | not applied | IBM Plex Serif ships with the fonts package and Prose deliberately does NOT switch to it: serif body text is an appearance decision, and those go to the owner of the design system with a before and after, never into a component by default. Point font-family at this token on .prose if you want it. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/qrcode.html">
# QRCode

Scannable QR code rendered as a styled SVG with Aurea soft geometry.

## Usage

```tsx
import {QRCode} from "@aurea-uds/react/qrcode";
```

```tsx
<QRCode value="https://aureauds.dev" size="sm" />
<QRCode value="https://aureauds.dev" size="md" />
<QRCode value="https://aureauds.dev" size="lg" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | `string` | — | REQUIRED. What the code encodes. It is also what the default accessible name reads out, so a reader that cannot scan still gets the payload. |
| `size` | `sm \| md \| lg` | md | 7.5rem, 10rem or 15rem, quiet zone included (the box is border-box). A free number is deliberately gone — it forced raw pixels on you. For an odd size, such as print, override --qr-size in CSS. PICK BY SCANNING, NOT BY LAYOUT: what decides is how many pixels each module gets, and below roughly 4 an ordinary phone camera starts to miss it. Measured on a short URL (33 modules across, quiet zone included): sm gives 2.85 px per module, md 4.06, lg 6.48 — sm is already under the line, and a longer payload makes every one of them worse, because more data means more modules in the same box. |
| `ecc` | `low \| medium \| quartile \| high` | quartile | Error correction. Higher than the usual default on purpose: round dots cover less area than squares, so more correction is what keeps this skin scannable. |
| `quietZone` | `number` | 4 | Blank border in modules, not pixels — it is part of the matrix, not of the layout. Four is the specified minimum; below it, scanners start failing. |
| `label` | `string` | "QR code: {value}" | Accessible name. Replace the default when the value is a long opaque token and the purpose is what matters — "Ticket for row 12", not the token. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/radio.html">
# Radio

Radio is one-of-many: the options share a name, and choosing one releases the other. What groups them is the name attribute — without it every radio is its own group and two can be on at once, which is the most common bug with this control.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Radio} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Radio name="billing" label="Monthly" defaultChecked />
<Radio name="billing" label="Yearly" />
<Radio name="billing" label="Lifetime" />
```

- The shared name is what makes a group. Same name, one choice; different names, no group at all.

- The label is inside the <label>, so the words are part of the target.

- Native keyboard: the arrows move within the set and Tab leaves it — the browser's own behaviour.

- One of the options should start selected; a group with nothing chosen has no default to submit.

- For two options that apply immediately, consider SegmentedControl or Switch instead.

## Examples

### With a description

The muted line under each name, as the Checkbox has. For a named group with an error, use RadioGroup.

```tsx
<Radio name="plan" label="Basic" description="For one person" defaultChecked />
<Radio name="plan" label="Pro" description="For a small team" />
```

### With a disabled option

The unavailable choice keeps its place, so the list never reorders under the arrows.

```tsx
<Radio name="region" label="Europe" defaultChecked />
<Radio name="region" label="South America" disabled />
```

### Inside a Field

The Field names the question; each Radio names an answer.

```tsx
<Field label="Visibility" hint="Who can open this workspace">
  <div className="stack">…radios…</div>
</Field>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED. One radio per option, all sharing the same name. |
| `labelHidden` | `boolean` | false | Keeps the label in the DOM but out of sight, as the Checkbox does — for a row of bare controls, where the group names them. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | A muted line under the label, as the Checkbox and the reference — then the label is set in bold. |
| `name` | `string` | — | What groups the set. Without it every radio is its own group and two can be on. |
| `checked / defaultChecked` | `boolean` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled; the option keeps its place in the list. |
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/radiogroup.html">
# RadioGroup

RadioGroup is a set of radio options under one label, with a description and an error. It keeps the chosen value: each option says its own value, and the group hands it the checked state, the shared name and the change. The options are native radios, so Tab enters on the chosen one and the arrows move and choose.

## Usage

```tsx
import {RadioGroup, Radio} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<RadioGroup label="Plan" description="You can change it later" name="plan" defaultValue="pro">
  <Radio value="basic" label="Basic" description="For one person" />
  <Radio value="pro" label="Pro" description="For a small team" />
  <Radio value="business" label="Business" description="For the whole company" />
</RadioGroup>
```

- role="radiogroup" named by the label; the description and the error are read with it.

- value / defaultValue / onValueChange, the same names as the native RadioGroup.

- orientation: vertical (16 before each option) or horizontal (16 between them), as the reference.

- Each option can carry a description; with an error, every option is marked invalid.

## Examples

### Horizontal

The options in a row, 16 apart.

```tsx
<RadioGroup label="Size" orientation="horizontal" defaultValue="m">
  <Radio value="s" label="Small" />
  <Radio value="m" label="Medium" />
  <Radio value="l" label="Large" />
</RadioGroup>
```

### Disabled

No option can be chosen.

```tsx
<RadioGroup label="Delivery" disabled defaultValue="standard">
  <Radio value="standard" label="Standard" />
  <Radio value="express" label="Express" />
</RadioGroup>
```

### With an error

The error closes the group, and every option is marked invalid.

```tsx
<RadioGroup label="Payment" required error="Choose how to pay">
  <Radio value="card" label="Card" />
  <Radio value="pix" label="Pix" />
</RadioGroup>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED. The group's visible name — what the screen reader announces for the group. |
| `labelHidden` | `boolean` | false | Keeps the group name in the DOM but out of sight, as the Checkbox does: the options start at the top, without the 16 that separated them from the name. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | A line under the label, joined to the group by aria-describedby. |
| `error` | `ReactNode` | — | The error at the end; marks every option invalid. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `string` | — | The chosen option's value: controlled, or where it starts. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` | — | Called with the value of the option chosen. |
| `name` | `string` | the group's own | The name of every option, for a form. |
| `orientation` | `"vertical" \| "horizontal"` | "vertical" | vertical stacks the options with 16 before each; horizontal puts them in a row with 16 between them, as the reference. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | No option can be chosen. |
| `invalid` | `boolean` | false | Paints every option invalid, as the native invalid; error already does it. |
| `required` | `boolean` | false | The asterisk on the label, and required on the options. |
| `RadioGroup.Item` | `component` | — | The option: the Radio (value, label, description, disabled). |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/range.html">
# Range

Range is a value picked along a line: volume, opacity, a threshold. It is the native input, themed by tokens — the drag, the arrow keys and the touch behaviour are the platform's. Use it when the approximate value is the point; when the exact number matters, pair it with a field.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Range, Field} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Field label="Volume"><Range defaultValue={60} /></Field>
```

- For the drawn slider — label and value on top, the fill, a range of two thumbs, formatted values — use Slider. Range is the browser's own control, with the change event.

- Native input: dragging, arrow keys, Home and End all work without a line of our JS.

- The thumb and the track wear the tokens — the accent colour is the brand's, in both themes.

- min, max and step pass through; the browser enforces them.

- Show the number next to it when the value is meant to be read, not only felt.

- Two thumbs (a min–max band) is not this component: use two fields until a real demand appears.

## Examples

### With the number

When the exact value matters, the slider sets it and the field states it.

```tsx
<div className="cluster">
  <Range min={0} max={100} defaultValue={72} />
  <Input type="number" defaultValue={72} min={0} max={100} />
</div>
```

### Steps

A coarse step turns a continuous line into a small set of allowed values.

```tsx
<Range min={0} max={4} step={1} defaultValue={2} />
```

### Disabled

Locked value: still readable, not draggable.

```tsx
<Range defaultValue={30} disabled />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `min / max / step` | `number` | 0 / 100 / 1 | Native bounds. The thumb is themed by tokens; the behaviour is the browser's. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `number` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes. Pair it with a text field when the exact number matters. |
| `orientation` | `Responsive<RangeOrientation>` | horizontal | A vertical slider. The engine publishes the orientation and the arrow keys follow it, so this is not only a rotation. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/searchfield.html">
# SearchField

SearchField is an Input that carries the search glyph inside the pill. The icon is decorative — the accessible name still comes from the label, because a magnifier is not a word. Everything else is the native input: type, value, events.

## Usage

```tsx
import {SearchField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<SearchField size="sm" />
<SearchField />
<SearchField size="lg" />
```

- The glyph is inside the field and aria-hidden: decoration cannot be the accessible name.

- Native input underneath — value, onChange, onKeyDown and the rest behave as you expect.

- The icon is swappable (filter, catalog) for a field that filters rather than searches.

- For search that opens a list of results as you type, compose it with Combobox.

- Pair with a scope Select when the same query can run over different sets.

## Examples

### Plain search

One field, one placeholder saying what is searchable.

```tsx
<Field label="Search"><SearchField placeholder="Search components…" /></Field>
```

### Filter row

Search plus scope: the pair that heads most collections.

```tsx
<SearchField placeholder="Filter rows…" />
<Select aria-label="Category" defaultValue="all"><option value="all">All categories</option></Select>
```

### As a filter

Same control, different glyph: what it does to the list is filter, not search.

```tsx
<SearchField icon="funnel" placeholder="Filter by name…" />
```

### With an action

When the query costs something to run, give it an explicit button as well as Enter.

```tsx
<SearchField placeholder="Search the archive…" />
<Button variant="primary">Search</Button>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `icon` | `IconName` | search | The glyph inside the field. Decorative — the accessible name comes from the label. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | — | What can be searched, e.g. "Search components…". |
| `value / defaultValue` | `string` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. |
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step. The glyph shrinks with it. |
| `width` | `string` | — | The field width: "20rem" or "auto". Without it, 100% of the line as always. `size` changes height and type, never width. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/section.html">
# Section

An edge-to-edge band of a website page, with its own surface, site spacing and, optionally, its own theme. variant="footer" makes it the site's footer; variant="hero" makes it the page opening.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Section} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Section theme="dark" aria-labelledby="t-app">
  <Container>
    <Grid columns={12}>
      <Grid.Item span={{base: "12", viewport: {md: "7"}}}>
        <Heading id="t-app" level={2}>O app no seu bolso</Heading>
      </Grid.Item>
      <Grid.Item span={{base: "12", viewport: {md: "5"}}}>
        <Button tone="brand">Baixar</Button>
      </Grid.Item>
    </Grid>
  </Container>
</Section>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `surface` | `"background" \| "card" \| "inset"` | "background" | The band's background: the page's (the default), a card surface, or the recessed inset surface. |
| `spacing` | `"sm" \| "md"` | "md" | The space above and below: md is --space-16 (64) and --space-24 (96) from the md breakpoint up; sm is half of that. Aurea's choice from existing tokens: none of the references had a section to read. |
| `theme` | `"light" \| "dark"` | — | A theme for this band only: theme="dark" makes a dark band inside a light page, and the other way round. The background, the text and every piece inside follow the band's theme, and the page's light-theme rules do not leak into it. |
| `variant` | `"base" \| "footer" \| "hero"` | "base" | footer makes the band the website's footer: a <footer> with the brand, the link columns and the legal line, its content already in a Container. Surface, spacing and theme keep working — a dark footer on a light page is theme="dark". On a phone everything stacks in one column. `hero` is the opening of a page: eyebrow, title, text, buttons or an e-mail field, and an image beside them; on a phone, everything stacks. |
| `brand` | `ReactNode` | — | Footer only: the brand and a short line, top left. |
| `links` | `SectionFooterGroup[]` | — | Footer only: the link columns, each { title, items }. The items are SidebarItem (id, label, href, render), the same shape as the menus. From 768px the columns share the width, each at least 8rem. |
| `legal` | `ReactNode` | — | Footer only: the bottom line — rights, terms, privacy — under a hairline. |
| `layout` | `"columns" \| "inline"` | "columns" | Only on footer: columns is the large site footer; inline is ONE centred line, as the reference's home page footer — the legal sentence, the links (without the column titles) and the children (social icons). The brand does not go in. |
| `maxWidth` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl" \| "2xl" \| "docs" \| "full"` | "xl" | Footer only: how far the content grows, on the Container's scale. |
| `navLabel` | `string` | "Footer" | Footer only: the footer navigation's name for screen readers. Pass it in the page's language. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | — | Only on hero: the title of the opening, the page's h1. It grows with the width of the BAND, not of the window: --text-4xl (36), --text-6xl (60) from 768 and --text-7xl (72) from 1024. On the other variants a string here is still the HTML title attribute. |
| `titleAs` | `"h1" \| "h2"` | "h1" | Only on hero: the tag of the title. The opening is the start of the page, so h1; h2 when the band opens a section further down. |
| `eyebrow` | `ReactNode` | — | Only on hero: the line above the title — a badge, a short phrase, a link to what changed. 8 above the title, 16 from 1024. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | Only on hero: the text under the title, glued to it. 16/24, and 18/28 from 768, at most 672 wide. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` | — | Only on hero: the buttons, or a form with the e-mail field and its button (the form grows up to 480). 16 under the text. |
| `media` | `ReactNode` | — | Only on hero: the image, or the piece that proves what the text says. With align="start" it sits beside the text from 1024 and under it before that. It takes the width of its column: size a phone frame in the app. |
| `align` | `"start" \| "center"` | "start" | Only on hero: start puts the text on the left and the image beside it; center puts everything on the middle line, with the image under the text. What comes as children goes after the buttons. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The band's content, usually inside a Container. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the <section>. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/segmentedcontrol.html">
# SegmentedControl

SegmentedControl is one-of-many, always visible: two to five options in a track, the chosen one raised. It carries one value and one tab stop. Past five options this becomes a Select — a track that wraps to a second line stops being a segmented control.

## Usage

```tsx
import {SegmentedControl} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<SegmentedControl label="View" value={view} onChange={setView}
  items={[{value: "list", label: "List"}, {value: "board", label: "Board"}]} />
```

- One value, controlled by design: one-of-many always has an owner.

- Two to five options. More than that is a Select; many-of-many is a ButtonGroup of toggles.

- The selected option shows the system's selected language — raised capsule, brand label, yellow bar.

- The track keeps the pill; the options never fuse into a single bar.

- Switches the VIEW of the same data, never its meaning — that would be a filter.

## Examples

### Time range

Three spans over the same chart — the classic dashboard header.

```tsx
<SegmentedControl label="Range" value="7d" onChange={setRange}
  items={[{value: "24h", label: "24h"}, {value: "7d", label: "7 days"}, {value: "30d", label: "30 days"}]} />
```

### The ceiling

Five is the limit. At this width it already asks to become a Select — which is the signal to switch.

```tsx
// five options: still a track. six: use Select.
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `Array<{value, label}>` | — | The options. Two to five: past that it is a Select, not a segmented control. |
| `value` | `string` | — | The selected value. Controlled by design — one of many always has an owner. |
| `onChange` | `(v: string) => void` | — | Fires with the new value. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the set. |
| `fullWidth` | `boolean` | false | Fills the row: each segment grows from its own label and never shrinks below it, so no label wraps. When the options do not fit, the control scrolls, as without the prop. The name the reference library gives this prop on its toggle-button group; the same prop on native. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/select.html">
# Select

Select chooses a VALUE from a known list. A Menu executes an ACTION — that is the line between them, and it decides which one you need. This is the native element: the list is the platform's, which is why it works with a screen reader, on a phone, and with the keyboard you already know.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Select, Field} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Select size="sm">…</Select>
<Select>…</Select>
<Select size="lg">…</Select>
```

- Native <select>: the option list is the platform's own, on every device, with no JS to load.

- Choosing a value is Select; running a command is DropdownMenu. Never swap them for looks.

- <optgroup> works, so a long list can be sectioned without a custom widget.

- The chevron is drawn by the field and mirrors itself in RTL.

- When the user needs to type to find the option, that is Combobox — not a longer Select.

## Examples

### A plain choice

Short list, one value. The Field names the question.

```tsx
<Field label="Plan">
  <Select defaultValue="pro">
    <option value="free">Free</option>
    <option value="pro">Pro</option>
    <option value="scale">Scale</option>
  </Select>
</Field>
```

### Grouped options

optgroup sections a long list; the browser reads the group name before the options.

```tsx
<Select defaultValue="fra">
  <optgroup label="Europe"><option value="fra">Paris</option></optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Americas"><option value="gru">São Paulo</option></optgroup>
</Select>
```

### Disabled

The whole field, or a single option that exists but cannot be picked yet.

```tsx
<Select disabled defaultValue="pro">…</Select>
<option value="lifetime" disabled>Lifetime (soon)</option>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | <option> and <optgroup> elements, read the way the browser reads them: an option without value uses its text. Kept so code written for the native <select> keeps working; the list itself is drawn by the Aurea. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `string` | — | The chosen value, as a string. Without value, defaultValue or placeholder the first enabled option is chosen, which is what the native <select> did. |
| `items` | `SelectOption[] \| SelectOptGroup[]` | — | The list as data: { value, label, disabled? } or groups { label, items }. Use it instead of <option> children when the list comes from data. |
| `onChange` | `(e: { target: { value, name } }) => void` | — | Called with an event-shaped object, so handlers written for the native <select> (reading e.target.value) keep working. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string) => void` | — | Called with the chosen value directly. |
| `placeholder` | `ReactNode` | — | Shown in the trigger while nothing is chosen. Giving one also stops the first option from being chosen by default. |
| `name` | `string` | — | Form field name. The value is submitted through a hidden input, as the native element did. |
| `required` | `boolean` | false | The form will not submit without a value. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes. Choosing a VALUE is Select; executing an ACTION is a Menu. |
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step, NOT the HTML size attribute — that one is how many options show at once, and it is deliberately shadowed here. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/separator.html">
# Separator

Separator is the rule between things: a full-width hairline, or a 1px column between items in a row. It is what a sidebar puts between sections and what a row of actions puts between groups.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Separator} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <Stack>
    <p>Account</p>
    <Separator />
    <p>Billing</p>
  </Stack>
</Card>
```

- It is a native <hr> and ships NO JavaScript. The role comes from the element, not from an attribute — an <hr> already carries role="separator" implicitly, and writing it would be redundant ARIA. The APG's own warning is that no ARIA beats bad ARIA.

- aria-orientation appears ONLY on the vertical one. The separator role already defaults to horizontal, so writing it there would repeat the platform out loud for nothing.

- It draws with `background` on a 1px box, not with `border` — the thickness then does not depend on which border side someone wrote, and one class serves both orientations.

- The vertical one stretches to the tallest sibling AND carries a floor: inside a parent with no height of its own it would otherwise measure zero and disappear while still existing in the DOM. There is a test for exactly that case.

- Inside a Toolbar use ToolbarSeparator instead — that one takes part in the roving tabindex the engine manages. This one is for everything else.

## Examples

### Between items in a row

The vertical rule stretches to the tallest sibling. Useful between counts, authors, timestamps — the places a bullet would go.

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <span>12 open</span>
  <Separator orientation="vertical" />
  <span>4 closed</span>
  <Separator orientation="vertical" />
  <span>updated today</span>
</Cluster>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `orientation` | `Responsive<'horizontal' \| 'vertical'>` | horizontal | Horizontal is a full-width hairline; vertical is a 1px column that stretches to the tallest sibling, with a floor so it cannot measure zero inside a flex row. BEHAVIOURAL and not visual: the resolved value goes to the engine, which publishes data-orientation and, in the vertical case, aria-orientation — the horizontal one is role="separator"'s implicit default and announcing it would be noise. This is why the component is client-side: an attribute cannot come from a CSS class. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the separator element. |
| `spacing` | `"none" \| "tight" \| "normal" \| "loose"` | "none" | The space on both sides of the line, in the same three steps as the layout primitives' gap. On a vertical separator the space goes to the sides. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/sidebar.html">
# Sidebar

Sidebar is the <aside> the AppShell composes, and the navigation inside it. Pass `items` and it renders the list — icons, groups, one level of nesting, and the current item marked with aria-current. Pass children instead and the markup is entirely yours.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Sidebar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Sidebar
  label="Components"
  current="button"
  items={[
    {id: "button", label: "Button", icon: "plus", href: "../button.html", badge: <Badge variant="primary">12</Badge>},
    {id: "navlist", label: "NavList", icon: "list-bullets", href: "../navlist.html"},
    {id: "sidebar", label: "Sidebar", icon: "sidebar-simple", href: "../sidebar.html"},
  ]}
/>
```

- One item shape covers both: an item with `items` and no `href` is a group heading; with an href it is a parent with a sublist.

- The current item is marked with aria-current="page" — the same attribute the screen reader announces and the skin paints, so they cannot drift apart.

- Collapsed turns it into an icon rail. The labels stay in the DOM as screen-reader-only text. The panel narrows to --sidebar-rail; a floating shell track also preserves its two outer margins.

- It FLOATS by default — margin, card radius, its own surface. That is what this design system looks like everywhere. `variant="flush"` is the one exception it makes to that rule, and it is opt-in: against the edges, full height, separated from the content by a single rule. It was measured against four shipping admin dashboards. Aurea's own pages stay floating; flush is for the applications that want it.

- AppShell forwards it: `<AppShell sidebarVariant="flush">`. Without that the variant would be unreachable for anyone composing through the shell, which is the normal path.

- Below the lg breakpoint (1024px) the AppShell turns it into a drawer with the native popover — Escape and click-outside stay native, and the shell normalises focus across the three browser engines.

- No roving tabindex: site navigation has no APG pattern, and in a sidebar people expect Tab to walk the items one by one.

## Examples

### Groups and one level of nesting

A group has a label and no link of its own. A parent that navigates keeps its link and gains a sublist.

```tsx
<Sidebar
  label="Catalog"
  current="sidebar"
  items={[
    {id: "components", label: "Components", items: [
      {id: "button", label: "Button", icon: "plus", href: "../button.html"},
      {id: "navigation", label: "Navigation", icon: "list-bullets", href: "../navlist.html", items: [
        {id: "navlist", label: "NavList", href: "../navlist.html"},
        {id: "sidebar", label: "Sidebar", href: "../sidebar.html"},
      ]},
    ]},
    {id: "shells", label: "Shells", items: [
      {id: "appshell", label: "AppShell", href: "../appshell.html"},
    ]},
  ]}
/>
```

### Slim · floating — the icon rail

Same list, same DOM. The labels become screen-reader-only, so the rail never turns into a column of unnamed icons.

```tsx
<Sidebar collapsed label="Components" current="button" items={items} />
```

### Full · flush — the one exception

The variant that gives up the floating box: it sits against the edges, takes the full height and is separated from the content by a single rule instead of a gap. The rows inside keep the same radius in both variants — what changes is the panel, not the line.

```tsx
<Sidebar variant="flush" label="Components" current="button" items={items} />
```

### Slim · flush — the rail against the edge

The fourth combination: collapsed AND flush. The reference does the opposite of this one — their narrow column floats as a card while the wide one sits flush, measured on their own docs: 68px floating against 280px flush. Both pairings exist because the two props are separate axes.

```tsx
<Sidebar collapsed variant="flush" label="Components" current="button" items={items} />
```

### Bring your own navigation

children still works and is not legacy: when the list comes from a router or a CMS, the <nav> and its label are yours.

```tsx
<Sidebar>
  <nav aria-label="Project">
    <a href="../button.html" aria-current="page">Button</a>
    <a href="../sidebar.html">Sidebar</a>
  </nav>
</Sidebar>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `SidebarItem[]` | — | The navigation, as data. One shape covers grouping and nesting: an item with `items` and no href is a group heading; with an href it is a parent that also has a sublist. Each item is {id, label, href?, icon?, badge?, onClick?, items?}. An item may carry render (a ReactElement, your router's link) instead of href — it receives the item's skin, the current-page state and the item's content. |
| `variant` | `"floating" \| "flush" \| "plain"` | floating | floating is the default and it is what this design system looks like: the panel detaches from the edges, takes the card radius and a border all the way around. flush is the ONE exception this system makes to that rule, and it is opt-in: the sidebar sits against the edges, takes the full height and is separated from the content by a single rule instead of a gap. That is what four shipping admin panels do — the reference library's own dashboard among the ones measured. Aurea's own pages stay floating; flush is there for the applications that want it. plain is the sidebar with NO box — no fill, no line, no shadow — in the floating one's place and height: the items sit loose on the page, like a documentation page's "On this page" column. The 1px border stays, transparent, so switching variants moves nothing. |
| `current` | `string` | — | The id of the item you are on. It gets aria-current="page", which is also what the skin paints — one source for both, so they cannot drift apart. |
| `collapsed` | `boolean` | false | Icon rail. Labels stay in the DOM as screen-reader-only text, and the panel narrows to --sidebar-rail. In AppShell, a floating rail keeps its outer margins in the grid track; flush uses the token as the raw track width. Controlled by you: the sidebar never decides on its own when to collapse. |
| `label` | `string` | "Sidebar" | Accessible name of the <nav> that `items` renders. Two navigation landmarks with the same name fail axe, so name it when a page has more than one. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Escape hatch, not legacy: when the list comes from a router or a CMS, pass your own markup and the <nav> and its label are yours. Rendered after `items` when both are given. |
| `placement` | `left \| right` | left | Which side the sidebar lives on. On the right, the flush variant's line moves to the inner side. It is the AppShell's aside column. |
| `scrollbar` | `hover \| visible` | hover | hover is a light scrollbar that is invisible at rest and comes back with the pointer over the sidebar, with keyboard focus inside it, and always on a screen without hover (touch). It stays native and keeps its width, so nothing jumps when it shows. visible keeps the bar on screen all the time, for whoever needs it. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/skeleton.html">
# Skeleton

Placeholder shown while content loads.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Skeleton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Skeleton style={{height: "0.875rem", width: "70%"}} />
<Skeleton style={{height: "0.875rem", width: "90%"}} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `animation` | `"pulse" \| "none"` | "pulse" | the reference library's pulse, or none. Its shimmer is a gradient, which Aurea does not have. With reduced motion requested by the system, it never pulses. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Where the shape comes from. There is no size prop on purpose: a skeleton stands in for one specific piece of content, and only the page knows how big that is. |
| `style` | `CSSProperties` | — | The usual way to give it width and height for a one-off. Every other div attribute passes through as well. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/slider.html">
# Slider

Slider picks a number by dragging a thumb along a track: label and value on top, the track with its fill, a capsule thumb in the brand colour. One value or a range of two, horizontal or vertical, with the number written by the platform's Intl. It speaks numbers — onValueChange(value) — where Range speaks the browser's change event.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Slider} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Slider label="Volume" defaultValue={40} />
```

- The label names the thumbs; with two values, thumbLabels gives each one its own name.

- Arrows step, Page Up/Down and Shift + arrow take the large step, Home and End jump to the ends.

- onValueChange on every step; onValueCommitted when the thumb is released — the moment to save.

- format and locale write the value (percent, currency…) with Intl, as NumberField does.

- Range stays for the browser's own slider, with its change event.

- channel makes it a colour track — hue, saturation, brightness, lightness, red, green, blue or alpha: painted with the channel, the thumb in the colour.

- On a colour track the value is the colour (hex, rgb(), hsl(), hsb()), so several tracks share one colour; onValueChange gives the hex.

## Examples

### A range of two

Pass a list: two thumbs, and the fill between them. Each thumb has its own name.

```tsx
<Slider label="Price" defaultValue={[200, 800]} min={0} max={1000} step={50}
  thumbLabels={["Minimum", "Maximum"]} format={{style: "currency", currency: "BRL"}} locale="pt-BR" />
```

### Formatted

A percentage, written by Intl. The stored value stays the raw number.

```tsx
<Slider label="Discount" defaultValue={0.25} min={0} max={1} step={0.05} format={{style: "percent"}} />
```

### Vertical

Value on top, track in the middle, label below. The height is --range-vertical-size.

```tsx
<Slider label="Level" orientation="vertical" defaultValue={60} />
```

### Colour track

The hue, from 0 to 360 degrees. The screen reader hears the colour's name with the number.

```tsx
<Slider label="Hue" channel="hue" defaultValue="hsl(210, 100%, 50%)" />
```

### Colour track, disabled

Unavailable, not hidden.

```tsx
<Slider label="Hue" channel="hue" defaultValue="hsl(120, 100%, 40%)" disabled />
```

### Colour track, vertical

Standing up, like the number slider.

```tsx
<Slider label="Hue" channel="hue" orientation="vertical" defaultValue="hsl(280, 90%, 55%)" />
<Slider label="Brightness" channel="brightness" orientation="vertical" defaultValue="hsl(280, 90%, 55%)" />
```

### Colour track with the value

Controlled: the value is the colour, and onValueChange gives the hex.

```tsx
const [colour, setColour] = useState("hsl(30, 100%, 50%)");

<Slider label="Hue" channel="hue" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
<ColorSwatch color={colour} label="The colour" />
```

### HSL channels

Three tracks share one colour: each one is painted with the other two.

```tsx
const [colour, setColour] = useState("hsl(200, 80%, 50%)");

<Slider label="Hue" channel="hue" colorSpace="hsl" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
<Slider label="Saturation" channel="saturation" colorSpace="hsl" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
<Slider label="Lightness" channel="lightness" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
```

### Transparency

The alpha track, from transparent to solid, over a checkerboard. With transparency, the hex has eight digits.

```tsx
const [colour, setColour] = useState("rgba(4, 133, 247, 0.6)");

<Slider label="Alpha" channel="alpha" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
```

### RGB channels

Red, green and blue, from 0 to 255.

```tsx
const [colour, setColour] = useState("rgb(240, 194, 0)");

<Slider label="Red" channel="red" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
<Slider label="Green" channel="green" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
<Slider label="Blue" channel="blue" value={colour} onValueChange={setColour} />
```

### Disabled

Unavailable, not hidden.

```tsx
<Slider label="Brightness" defaultValue={70} disabled />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED. Names the thumbs. labelHidden keeps it for screen readers only. |
| `labelHidden` | `boolean` | false | Hides the label from the screen, keeps it as the accessible name. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `number \| number[]` | — | A number, or a list of two for a range (two thumbs). With channel, the colour (hex or rgb()/hsl()/hsb()). |
| `onValueChange` | `(value) => void` | — | Called on every step with the number (or the list). |
| `onValueCommitted` | `(value) => void` | — | Called when the thumb is released — the moment to save. |
| `min / max / step` | `number` | 0 / 100 / 1 | The scale. |
| `largeStep` | `number` | 10 | The step for Page Up/Down and Shift + arrow. |
| `orientation` | `horizontal \| vertical` | horizontal | Vertical stacks value, track and label; its height is --range-vertical-size. |
| `format / locale` | `Intl.NumberFormatOptions / string` | — | How the value is written (currency, percent…), by the platform's Intl. |
| `showValue` | `boolean` | true | Shows the value next to the label. |
