| `thumbLabels` | `string[]` | — | With two values, each thumb's name, in order ("Minimum", "Maximum"). |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Disables the slider. |
| `name` | `string` | — | For the form: the engine renders the hidden input with the raw value. |
| `channel` | `ColorChannel` | — | The colour track (ADR-0069), a variation of this Slider: hue, saturation, brightness, lightness, red, green, blue or alpha. The value becomes the COLOUR (hex), as in the reference, so several tracks share one colour; the track is painted with the channel, the thumb shows the colour, alpha has the checkerboard, and the screen reader hears the channel and the colour's name. |
| `colorSpace` | `"hsb" \| "hsl" \| "rgb"` | "hsb" | With channel: the space of hue and saturation. The other channels already say theirs (red, green and blue are rgb), so one colorSpace serves every track of a picker; with hue or saturation, rgb reads as hsb. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin. |
| `id` | `string` | — | The id of the slider root. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/sortablelist.html">
# SortableList

Reorder by dragging — and by keyboard, which is the reason it may exist at all.

## Usage

```tsx
import {SortableList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [items, setItems] = useState([
  {id: "a", label: "Draft"},
  {id: "b", label: "In review"},
  {id: "c", label: "Published"},
]);

<SortableList
  label="Pipeline stages"
  items={items}
  onReorder={(from, to) => setItems(prev => {
    const next = [...prev];
    next.splice(to, 0, ...next.splice(from, 1));
    return next;
  })}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `Array<{id, label}>` | — | The rows, in the order they are shown. Data and not children, the same idiom as Timeline, Stepper and Sidebar. |
| `onReorder` | `(from: number, to: number) => void` | — | Called with the two indexes. The list is controlled and keeps no order of its own — the keyboard path and the pointer path call this same callback, so there are never two sources of truth about the order. |
| `label` | `string` | Sortable list | Accessible name of the list. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/spinner.html">
# Spinner

Indeterminate activity indicator for a wait with no known end.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Spinner} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Spinner size="sm" />
<Spinner label="Loading results" />
<Spinner size="lg" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl"` | "md" | 16, 24, 32, 40 — the reference library's scale. The component default is md, 24; the bare glyph inside a button stays 16. |
| `label` | `string` | the provider's "Loading" | What is being waited for. Announced by screen readers. |
| `decorative` | `boolean` | false | Hides it from assistive tech. Use only inside a control that already announces the wait — a Button with `loading` does. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/stack.html">
# Stack

Vertical spacing/layout primitive.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stack} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stack>
  <Card>First</Card>
  <Card>Second</Card>
</Stack>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Vertical flow: a column with --space-4 between items. The gap has three steps and no others (ADR-0051) — a layout primitive that takes any spacing is how a system stops having spacing. |
| `gap` | `"tight" \| "normal" \| "loose"` | "normal" | Three steps and no others (ADR-0051): tight is --space-2, normal is --space-4, loose is --space-6. The old rule still holds against ANY spacing; these two extra steps exist for the two measured cases — a note under its value, and a grid of filters. |
| `align` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "stretch"` | "stretch" | The cross axis. The default stretches children to the column width, as always; `start` keeps each child at its own width. |
| `className` | `string` | — | For alignment or width that this one job needs. Every other div attribute passes through. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/status.html">
# Status

Status shows the operational condition of a thing — online, busy, offline. It is not a Badge: a Badge is a short metadata pill, Status says what state something is in, as a coloured dot plus a readable label.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Status} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Status variant="online">Online</Status>
<Status variant="busy">Busy</Status>
<Status variant="away">Away</Status>
<Status variant="offline">Offline</Status>
```

- The colour is never the only signal — the label states the condition (WCAG 1.4.1); the dot is decorative.

- offline is a hollow dot, so it never collapses onto neutral in the light theme.

- Operational names (online/busy/away) and semantic names (success/warning/danger) map to the same theme-aware tokens.

## Examples

### Status vs Badge

A Badge is a pill of metadata; a Status is a state on the line.

```tsx
<Status variant="online">Deployed</Status>
<Badge variant="success">v1.7.0</Badge>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `neutral \| online \| offline \| busy \| away \| running \| success \| warning \| danger \| info` | neutral | Which condition, and therefore which dot. The operational names (online/busy/away) and the semantic ones (success/warning/danger) map to the same theme-aware tokens — pick the vocabulary of your domain. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The label, and it is not optional in practice: it is what carries the meaning when the colour cannot. |
| `state` | `waiting_user \| waiting_approval \| waiting_dependency \| offline \| stale \| partial \| degraded` | — | Universal state (Part J) — an axis of its own alongside `variant`: the variant is the colour of the dot, the state is the condition. It sets `data-state` and, when no `variant` is given, derives one: `offline` keeps the hollow dot it has always had, the other six fall back to severity. With no children the label comes from the shared string table, so the same condition reads the same on every screen. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/stepper.html">
# Stepper

Progress through numbered steps, for a task that happens in a fixed order.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stepper} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stepper label="Publishing" items={[
  {label: "Configure", state: "done"},
  {label: "Permissions", state: "done"},
  {label: "Validation", state: "error"},
  {label: "Publish", optional: "Optional"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `StepItem[]` | none | REQUIRED. One entry per step: label, state, optional note, and an optional handler. The number comes from the position, so it can never drift. |
| `items[].state` | `"default" \| "active" \| "done" \| "error"` | "default" | `done` shows a check, `error` shows the error glyph in the danger colour, `active` is the one announced as current. |
| `items[].optional` | `ReactNode` | none | A note under the label, for a step that may be skipped. |
| `items[].onClick` | `() => void` | none | Makes the step a real button, for a flow the user may enter at any point. Without it the step is not interactive. |
| `label` | `string` | the provider's "Steps" | Accessible name of the whole list. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/switch.html">
# Switch

Switch applies now. Flip it and the setting is on — no Save button in between. That is the whole difference from Checkbox, which changes a value the form will submit later. It carries role="switch", so the screen reader says "on" and "off" instead of "checked".

## Usage

```tsx
import {Switch} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Switch label="Email notifications" defaultChecked />
<Switch label="Weekly digest" />
<Switch label="Mentions only" />
```

- role="switch": announced as on/off, which is what an immediate setting is.

- The label is required and part of the target — the words toggle it too.

- Effect is immediate. If the change needs a Save button, the control is a Checkbox.

- Never use it for a destructive setting without confirmation: there is no submit step to think in.

## Examples

### On a surface

Inside a Card, with the section title above: the setting reads as part of that area.

```tsx
<Card>
  <strong>Notifications</strong>
  <Switch label="Email" defaultChecked />
  <Switch label="Push" />
</Card>
```

### With a description, and the switch at the end

The muted line under the name, and indicatorPlacement="end" to put the switch after the text — the reference's notification setting.

```tsx
<Switch label="Allow notifications" description="Receive push notifications" defaultChecked />
<Switch label="Allow notifications" description="Receive push notifications" defaultChecked
  indicatorPlacement="end" />
```

### Without a visible label

When the name is already on screen beside it, labelHidden keeps it for the screen reader only.

```tsx
<Switch label="Dark mode" labelHidden defaultChecked />
```

### Disabled

Locked by the plan or by permission — the state stays visible, the control does not.

```tsx
<Switch label="Audit log" disabled />
<Switch label="SSO" defaultChecked disabled />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED. A switch with no label is a mystery toggle. |
| `labelHidden` | `boolean` | false | Keeps the label in the DOM but out of sight, as the Checkbox does — for a switch whose name is already on screen beside it. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | A muted line under the label, as the Checkbox and the reference — then the label is set in bold. |
| `indicatorPlacement` | `"start" \| "end"` | "start" | Where the switch sits: before the label (the default) or after it, with the label and description on the left — the same name as the native RadioGroup. |
| `checked / defaultChecked` | `boolean` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. role="switch" is set for you. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes. Switch applies immediately; a Checkbox waits for the form to be submitted. |
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/table.html">
# Table

Presents rows and columns of data — also a comparison table: groups of rows, the row's name pinned while scrolling sideways, the header pinned while scrolling down, the best value marked and a 'differences only' switch. Every cell has tabular figures, so price and year columns line up.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Table} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Table caption="Team">
  <thead><tr><th>Name</th><th>Role</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Messenger</td><td>Owner</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Analyst</td><td>Editor</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</Table>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `caption` | `ReactNode` | — | Rendered as a real <caption>, and when it is a string it also becomes the accessible name of the scroll region around the table. Without it the region falls back to "Table". |
| `stickyHeader` | `boolean` | false | The header stays at the top of the table's box while the body scrolls inside it — the same name and mechanism as DataGrid. The box gets a ceiling, `--table-max-h` (60vh by default), set in CSS: a box with no ceiling never scrolls inside itself. It pins to the box, not to the page: the box also scrolls sideways, and a sticky element only sticks to its nearest scroll container. |
| `stickyFirstColumn` | `boolean` | false | The first column — the name of each row — stays put while the table scrolls sideways, on an opaque background so the rest slides under it, with a hairline at its end. With stickyHeader too, the corner stays above both. |
| `fit` | `boolean` | false | The table fits its box, without the 720px minimum that makes a wide table scroll sideways. This is what lets a comparison of TWO items fit a 360px phone with no sideways scroll; which two is the page's choice (a Select above the table). |
| `differencesOnly` | `boolean` | false | The 'differences only' view — hides the rows the page marked as identical with <tr data-same>. The table does not compare cells itself; the page knows which rows are equal and owns the switch. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The <thead> and <tbody>, written by you. This is the presentational table; the one that sorts, filters and pages is DataGrid. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the <table>. The wrapper around it is focusable (tabIndex 0) so a table wider than the screen can be scrolled with the keyboard, not only by dragging. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/tableofcontents.html">
# TableOfContents

In-page index of a document's sections. Sticky beside the content, marks the section in view.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TableOfContents} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TableOfContents label="On this page" current="preview" items={[
  {id: "preview", label: "Preview"},
  {id: "installation", label: "Installation"},
  {id: "reference", label: "Reference"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `TocItem[]` | — | The entries: {id, label, sub?}. `sub` indents one level and there is no level below that — a contents list that mirrors five heading levels is a second document. |
| `current` | `string` | — | The id of the section you are in; it gets aria-current. Which one that is depends on scroll, and scroll is the page's business, not the component's. |
| `label` | `string` | "On this page" | Both the visible heading and the accessible name of the <nav> — one string, so they cannot say different things. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/tabs.html">
# Tabs

Tabs switch between views of the same thing. The arrows move between tabs, and the panel follows. Two looks, like the reference's: the capsule track, and the secondary tabs with a line under them.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tabs} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tabs label="Report" value={tab} onChange={setTab} tabs={tabs} />
```

- The track has 4 of padding; each tab is 32 high, 16 on each side, medium weight.

- The chosen tab is the raised capsule; in the secondary look, the Aurea selected line.

- orientation="vertical" stacks the tabs beside the panel; panel="plain" removes the box.

- activateOnFocus switches as the arrow moves; turn it off when a panel costs a network call.

## Examples

### Secondary

No track: a line under the list, and the chosen tab marked by the selected line.

```tsx
<Tabs variant="secondary" label="Report" value={tab} onChange={setTab} tabs={tabs} panel="plain" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tabs` | `Array<{id: string; label: ReactNode; content: ReactNode}>` | — | Tab and panel together, because they are one thing: a tab with no panel is a button. |
| `value` | `string` | — | The id of the open tab. Controlled. |
| `onChange` | `(id: string) => void` | — | Fires on click and on arrow keys. |
| `label` | `string` | "Tabs" | Accessible name of the tab list. |
| `orientation` | `Responsive<'horizontal' \| 'vertical'>` | horizontal | Resolved at runtime and handed to the engine, which publishes data-orientation/aria-orientation and adapts the arrow keys. |
| `activateOnFocus` | `boolean` | true | Automatic activation: the arrow switches the panel along with focus. Set false for the APG's manual pattern — the arrow moves focus and Enter/Space activates. Use false when switching a tab is expensive. |
| `loopFocus` | `boolean` | true | Whether the arrow wraps from the last tab back to the first. |
| `panel` | `'card' \| 'plain'` | card | The panel. `card` is an inset card. `plain` drops the box, like the reference library's panel: the content starts on the same line as what is outside the Tabs, with only the space-3 gap above it. Use it when the content already has a frame (Table, DataGrid, a list of cards), which would otherwise be a box inside a box. The same prop on native. |
| `variant` | `primary \| secondary` | primary | secondary is the reference's secondary tabs: no track, a hairline under the list, the chosen tab marked by the Aurea selected line. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/taggroup.html">
# TagGroup

TagGroup is a wrapping row of tags under one label. None, one or several can be selected, and each can be removed. The group is one Tab stop; the arrows move between the tags.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TagGroup} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TagGroup label="Topics" selectionMode="multiple" defaultSelectedKeys={["travel"]}
  items={[{id: "news", label: "News"}, {id: "travel", label: "Travel"},
    {id: "gaming", label: "Gaming"}, {id: "shopping", label: "Shopping"}]} />
```

- selectionMode none, single or multiple; the selected tag is in the light yellow wash.

- onRemove adds the X; Delete or Backspace remove the active tag, and the focus moves to the next.

- One Tab stop for the group; arrows, Home and End move between the tags.

- description and errorMessage under the tags, read with the group.

- Three sizes — 20, 24 and 32 high — and a variant for grey surfaces.

## Examples

### Removable

The X removes; so does Delete on the active tag.

```tsx
<TagGroup label="Filters" items={filters} onRemove={(ids) => setFilters(f => f.filter(x => !ids.includes(x.id)))}
  description="Remove a filter to widen the search" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | REQUIRED. The group's name. labelHidden keeps it for screen readers only. |
| `labelHidden` | `boolean` | false | Hides the label from the screen, not from screen readers. |
| `items` | `TagItem[]` | — | REQUIRED. {id, label, textValue?, icon?, disabled?}. |
| `selectionMode` | `"none" \| "single" \| "multiple"` | "none" | none: a list. single/multiple: each tag toggles (aria-pressed); the selected one is in the light yellow wash. |
| `selectedKeys / defaultSelectedKeys` | `string[]` | — | The selected ids, controlled or not. |
| `onSelectionChange` | `(keys: string[]) => void` | — | Called with the new list. |
| `onRemove` | `(ids: string[]) => void` | — | With it each tag gets the X, and Delete/Backspace remove the active one; the focus goes to the neighbour. |
| `description` | `ReactNode` | — | Help under the tags, in aria-describedby. |
| `errorMessage` | `ReactNode` | — | The error under the tags, in aria-describedby. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg"` | "md" | 20, 24, 32 high — the reference library's tag. |
| `variant` | `"default" \| "surface"` | "default" | The neutral fill, or the card fill (for a tag on a grey surface). |
| `className` | `string` | — | Added to the group. |
| `id` | `string` | — | The group's id. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/taskqueue.html">
# TaskQueue

The work queue: what is waiting, what is running, what failed.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TaskQueue} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TaskQueue tasks={[
  {id: "1", title: "Index the archive", state: "running", progress: 0.4},
  {id: "2", title: "Rebuild the sitemap", state: "queued", priority: "high"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tasks` | `QueueTask[]` | — | The queue. Six states and three priority steps, measured from the reference. The reference's task carries 15 fields and five of them belong to OTHER components in this same family — token and cost are ModelUsage and CostMeter, checkpoints are TraceTimeline, assignee is AgentCard. Absorbing them here would make the queue answer for four contracts and none of them properly. |
| `label` | `string` | "Task queue" | Accessible name of the list. |
| `onRetry` | `(task: QueueTask) => void` | — | Shows a retry button on failed tasks only. Without it a failure is reported and cannot be acted on. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the list. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/text.html">
# Text

Text in one of a closed list of roles — a heading level, body text or code — never a loose size. The reference library's Typography model.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Text} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Text>Body text</Text>
<Text type="body-sm" color="muted">Supporting text</Text>
<Text type="h4">Looks like a heading, reads as text</Text>
<Text weight="semibold">Semibold</Text>
<Text weight="extrabold">Extrabold, for a cover title</Text>
<Text numeric>$ 41,118.00</Text>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | `"body" \| "body-sm" \| "body-xs" \| "code" \| "h1" … "h6"` | "body" | The role. The list is closed on purpose, like the reference library's: pick "h2" or "body-sm", never a pixel size. Only the look changes — the element stays a span, so a visual h2 is not a heading for a screen reader (use Heading for that). |
| `color` | `"default" \| "muted"` | "default" | Two colours only, like the reference library: the text colour or the muted one. A closed list protects contrast — both pass AA on every Aurea surface. |
| `tone` | `"default" \| "muted" \| "subtle" \| "primary" \| "link" \| "danger" \| "success" \| "warning" \| "info"` | — | The text colour with the native package's name — the same names on web and native. link is the yellow made for text, readable on both themes; primary is the fill yellow and nearly disappears on the light theme. The state colours are the -400 pair. It wins over color when both are given. |
| `weight` | `"normal" \| "medium" \| "semibold" \| "bold" \| "extrabold"` | — (the role's own) | Overrides the weight of the role. Headings are semibold and body text is regular by default. "extrabold" (800, --weight-extrabold) is for a cover title; the default title weight is still semibold. |
| `align` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end" \| "justify"` | — (inherited) | Text alignment. start and end follow the writing direction, so the same value mirrors in RTL. |
| `truncate` | `boolean` | false | One line, cut with an ellipsis. Turns the element into a block so the cut has a width to measure against. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | The text. |
| `numeric` | `boolean` | false | Tabular figures (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums) — for numbers that line up in a column (price, year, spec sheet) or change on screen. Off by default: in running text the narrow "1" is right. Native: the same prop sets fontVariant ["tabular-nums"]. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/textarea.html">
# Textarea

Textarea is the control for text that runs long: several lines, resizable by the user, with the same skin as Input. Same rule as Input — no state of its own, every native attribute passes through, and the label belongs to Field.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Textarea, Field} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Textarea size="sm" />
<Textarea />
<Textarea size="lg" />
```

- rows sets the visible height; the user can still drag it taller and we do not fight that.

- Native attributes pass through: maxLength, required, readOnly, spellCheck, wrap.

- Same radius family as the other surfaces — a text area is not a pill, it is a panel of text.

- For code use CodeEditor: it brings a language, gutters and highlighting, which a textarea has not.

## Examples

### With hint

Three visible lines and a note about what belongs there.

```tsx
<Field label="Description" hint="Shown to every member.">
  <Textarea rows={3} />
</Field>
```

### With a limit

maxLength is enforced by the browser; say the number in the hint so it is not a surprise.

```tsx
<Field label="Summary" hint="Up to 140 characters">
  <Textarea rows={2} maxLength={140} />
</Field>
```

### With error

Rejected content: the message is the accessible description and marks the field invalid; the label stays the name.

```tsx
<Field label="Reason" error="Tell us a bit more."><Textarea rows={2} /></Field>
```

### Read-only

Selectable and copyable, not editable — for a log or a generated snippet you must not lose.

```tsx
<Textarea rows={3} readOnly defaultValue={log} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rows` | `number` | 2 | Visible height in lines. The user can still resize it; the field does not fight that. |
| `value / defaultValue` | `string` | — | Controlled or uncontrolled. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | — | An example of the content, not the label. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Native disabled. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes. Every native attribute of the element passes through: name, required, autoComplete, pattern, min/max, and the rest. |
| `size` | `Responsive<FieldSize>` | md | The system's size step, NOT the HTML rows/cols. Height still grows with the content. |
| `variant` | `primary \| secondary` | primary | secondary is the neutral fill with no visible border, for a field inside a card. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/themetoggle.html">
# ThemeToggle

The light/dark switch, with colour in the glyph: a dark moon in the light theme, the brand yellow sun in the dark one.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ThemeToggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ThemeToggle />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `"light-dark" \| "light-dark-system"` | "light-dark" | light-dark is the button that flips the theme. light-dark-system is the reference's three-way switch — light, dark and system (follow the computer, and change with it): a radio group of three icon options, the chosen one filled. |
| `size` | `"xs" \| "sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl"` | "md" | The IconButton size. The button is round, like every icon-only button (ADR-0052). |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Blocks the switch. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Added to the button. |
| `pressed` | `boolean` | — | Inherited from IconButton, where it is deprecated. The toggle's state is the document theme, not this prop. |
| `grow` | `boolean` | false | Inherited from Button: the button takes the free space of its row. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/timeline.html">
# Timeline

Chronological sequence of events.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Timeline} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Timeline items={[
  {title: "Created", description: "by Curator", time: "09:00"},
  {title: "Shipped", time: "14:20"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `Array<{title: ReactNode; description?: ReactNode; time?: ReactNode}>` | — | The events, rendered as an <ol> because the order IS the information. `time` is a node, so an absolute date and a relative one are equally welcome. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toggle.html">
# Toggle

Toggle is a button that stays on. It is the Aurea component for a two-state control that is not a form field: bold in a text toolbar, list-or-grid, mute. The state is aria-pressed, so a screen reader announces it as a toggle button and says whether it is pressed.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toggle defaultPressed>Bold</Toggle>
<Toggle>Italic</Toggle>
<Toggle>Underline</Toggle>
```

- It OWNS the state. Uncontrolled with defaultPressed, controlled with pressed plus onPressedChange — the Base UI engine handles keyboard, focus and aria-pressed.

- THE LABEL MUST NOT CHANGE between the two states. If the text turns from "Mute" into "Unmute", or "Play" into "Pause", this is the wrong component: use a Button. A screen reader reads the new label and the state at the same time, and the listener cannot tell whether the button describes what it IS or what it WILL DO. The rule is the APG's and one of the references', and it is the one rule that decides between the two components.

- Icon only needs a name: pass label. Without visible children and without label the component writes to the console, because an anonymous button is a dead end for a screen reader.

- It is not a Switch and not a Checkbox. A switch is a setting that applies immediately; a checkbox is a form field that gets submitted; a toggle is an action that stays on.

- `Button` also accepts a `pressed` prop. It is DEPRECATED since 0.4.0 and goes away in 1.0 — it only paints and announces, and you keep the state. Twelve reference libraries were read in August 2026 and none of them puts the pressed state on the plain button.

## Examples

### Icon only, with a name

No visible text means label is required — it becomes the accessible name. Note the name says what the control IS ("Mute"), not what pressing it will do.

```tsx
<Toggle icon="speaker-slash" label="Mute" />
```

### Ghost

The default has the neutral fill; ghost has none, for a quiet row. Pressed looks the same on both.

```tsx
<Toggle variant="ghost" icon="text-b" label="Bold" defaultPressed />
<Toggle variant="ghost" icon="text-italic" label="Italic" />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pressed / defaultPressed` | `boolean` | none | Controlled or uncontrolled. The engine keeps aria-pressed in sync; you never set it. |
| `onPressedChange` | `(pressed: boolean) => void` | none | Fires with the new state. Pair with `pressed` for the controlled form. |
| `icon` | `IconName` | none | Glyph shown before the label, or alone when there are no children. |
| `label` | `string` | none | REQUIRED and non-blank when there is no visible text: an icon-only toggle with no name is unusable by screen reader. Since 2026-08-12 the ToggleProps union rejects omitted, boolean and nullish children unless label is present. Blank labels, empty strings, arrays, Fragments and decorative-only elements need a runtime guard because TypeScript/ReactNode cannot encode whether arbitrary content will render text; they emit console.error too. A custom child that receives apparently visible children but discards them remains the consumer's responsibility (AUD-0003). |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg"` | "md" | Matches the button scale, so a toggle sits level with the controls beside it. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Ignores interaction and dims the control. |
| `children` | `ToggleChildren \| never` | — | What the toggle shows. With children you may omit label; with no children label is REQUIRED, because a bare icon with no accessible name is a control nobody can announce. The type enforces it — the form without a name does not compile. |
| `id` | `string` | — | Id of the focusable control, which is what a <label htmlFor> has to point at. Generated when you do not pass one. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
| `value` | `string` | — | What identifies this toggle inside a ToggleGroup — without it the group cannot tell which button changed. Standalone, it makes no difference. |
| `variant` | `default \| ghost` | default | default has the neutral fill; ghost has none. Pressed uses Aurea's selected language on both. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/togglegroup.html">
# ToggleGroup

Several toggles sharing one state, with arrow-key navigation between them.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ToggleGroup} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ToggleGroup label="Text style" multiple defaultValue={["bold"]}>
  <Toggle value="bold">Bold</Toggle>
  <Toggle value="italic">Italic</Toggle>
  <Toggle value="underline">Underline</Toggle>
</ToggleGroup>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | — | The Toggles that share the state. |
| `value` | `string[]` | — | Controlled selection. An array even in single mode, which is the engine's shape. |
| `defaultValue` | `string[]` | — | Seeds the selection without controlling it. |
| `onValueChange` | `(value: string[]) => void` | — | Fires with the new selection. |
| `multiple` | `boolean` | false | More than one toggle pressed at a time. |
| `orientation` | `Responsive<Orientation>` | horizontal | Stacks the toggles, and the arrow keys follow the axis. Responsive. |
| `label` | `string` | — | Accessible name of the group. Without it the group is a set of buttons with no subject. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Turns every toggle off at once. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Merged onto the outermost element, after the Aurea skin — your class wins on a tie. |
| `size` | `sm \| md \| lg` | — | The size of every toggle inside; a toggle may set its own. |
| `fullWidth` | `boolean` | false | Fills the parent's width, and the toggles share it equally. |
| `detached` | `boolean` | false | Loose toggles with a 4 gap, instead of joined in one capsule. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toolbar.html">
# Toolbar

Toolbar is a set of actions with ONE tab stop: Tab enters and leaves the whole set, and the arrows move between the buttons inside it. That roving tabindex is the difference from ButtonGroup, where every button is its own tab stop. A formatting bar with twelve actions must not cost twelve presses of Tab to walk past.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarButton, ToolbarSeparator} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Formatting">
  <ToolbarGroup label="Style">
    <ToolbarButton pressed>Bold</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton>Italic</ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarGroup label="Align">
    <ToolbarButton>Left</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton>Center</ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
</Toolbar>
```

- Roving tabindex from Base UI: Tab in and out, arrows within — the APG toolbar pattern.

- Horizontal or vertical; the orientation decides which arrows navigate and turns the separator.

- Named by aria-label: two toolbars on one page must not answer to the same name.

- ToolbarGroup labels a sub-set; ToolbarSeparator draws the divide without claiming a tab stop.

- Buttons are ghost by default — the toolbar surface already frames them.

## Examples

### Vertical

Stacked for a side rail. Up and down navigate, and the separator turns with the axis.

```tsx
<Toolbar orientation="vertical" label="Tools">
  <ToolbarButton>Select</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton>Draw</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarButton>Erase</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

### Icon only

Glyph actions still need names: each one carries its label, the bar carries its own.

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Canvas">
  <ToolbarButton render={<IconButton icon="arrow-counter-clockwise" label="Undo" />} />
</Toolbar>
```

### With a disabled action

Unavailable but still counted: it keeps its place in the roving order, so the set never shifts under the arrows.

```tsx
<Toolbar label="History">
  <ToolbarButton disabled>Undo</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton>Redo</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `orientation` | `horizontal \| vertical` | horizontal | Vertical stacks the buttons and swaps which arrows navigate. |
| `label` | `string` | Toolbar | Accessible name of the toolbar. Two toolbars on a page must not share one. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | ToolbarButton, ToolbarGroup and ToolbarSeparator. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the surface. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toolbarbutton.html">
# ToolbarButton

ToolbarButton is the Button that belongs to a Toolbar. Same API, same skin — what changes is that it joins the roving tabindex of the bar instead of owning a tab stop of its own. Outside a Toolbar it has nothing to roam, so use Button there.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Style">
  <ToolbarButton pressed>Bold</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton>Italic</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton>Underline</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

- Accepts every Button prop: variant, size, icons, loading, pressed, disabled.

- Ghost by default — inside a toolbar the surface already frames the action.

- Reachable by arrow keys, not by Tab: the bar owns the single tab stop.

- pressed makes it a toggle (bold, italic) with aria-pressed, the same state as Button.

- Disabled buttons stay in the arrow order so the row does not renumber under the user.

## Examples

### With icons

Glyph plus word: in a dense bar the icon speeds the scan and the label keeps the meaning.

```tsx
<ToolbarButton leadingIcon="arrow-counter-clockwise">Undo</ToolbarButton>
<ToolbarButton leadingIcon="arrow-clockwise">Redo</ToolbarButton>
```

### A destructive action in the bar

Even here the tone carries weight: ghost destructive reads as available, not as the main move.

```tsx
<ToolbarButton>Duplicate</ToolbarButton>
<ToolbarSeparator />
<ToolbarButton variant="danger-ghost" leadingIcon="trash">Delete</ToolbarButton>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `ButtonVariant \| danger-soft` | ghost | Ghost by default: inside a toolbar the surface already frames the action. `secondary` is the neutral fill with the brand-coloured label; `tertiary` the neutral fill with the plain label (the default). |
| `appearance` | `solid \| outline \| ghost \| link \| nav \| soft` | ghost | Inherited from Button. How much weight the box carries; the default here is ghost. |
| `tone` | `neutral \| brand \| danger \| success \| warning \| info` | neutral | Inherited from Button. What the colour means; every combination exists. |
| `pressed` | `boolean` | — | Toggle inside the toolbar (bold, italic). aria-pressed, not a variant. |
| `leadingIcon` | `AureaIcon` | — | Same icon API as Button; every Button prop is accepted. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | false | Stays in the roving order but is not activatable, so the set does not shift. |
| `size` | `Responsive<ComponentSize>` | md | The system's size step, shared with Button. Responsive. |
| `href` | `string` | — | Renders an <a> instead of a <button>: a toolbar item that NAVIGATES has to be a link, or middle-click and open-in-new-tab stop working. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | false | Shows the spinner and sets aria-busy. |
| `trailingIcon` | `AureaIcon` | — | A glyph after the label. |
| `kbd` | `string \| string[]` | — | Shows the shortcut and announces it with aria-keyshortcuts. A list (["Ctrl", "K"]) shows one key cap per key and announces the combination (Control+K). |
| `fullWidth` | `boolean` | false | Fills the width of the container. |
| `grow` | `boolean` | false | In a row (Cluster), takes an equal share with the other buttons that also grow. `fullWidth` asks for the whole line instead. |
| `target` | `HTMLAttributeAnchorTarget` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `rel` | `string` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `download` | `boolean \| string` | — | Link attribute, only with `href`. |
| `render` | `ReactElement` | — | Inherited from Button: the element that renders the button — the router's link, for example — receiving the Aurea skin and the content. |
| `quiet` | `boolean` | false | Less weight: muted text one step smaller — the Button's quiet. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toolbargroup.html">
# ToolbarGroup

ToolbarGroup names a sub-set inside a Toolbar. Without it a bar of twelve buttons is one flat list; with it a screen reader can say "Align, three items" before reading them. It changes the announcement and the spacing — never the tab order, which belongs to the Toolbar.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarGroup, ToolbarButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Formatting">
  <ToolbarGroup label="Style">
    <ToolbarButton pressed>Bold</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton>Italic</ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarGroup label="Align">
    <ToolbarButton>Left</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton>Center</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton>Right</ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
</Toolbar>
```

- Groups by intent — style, align, history — so a long bar reads as a few short lists.

- The label is the announcement; a group with no label is only visual spacing.

- Does not create a tab stop: the arrows still cross the whole toolbar in one sweep.

- Pairs with ToolbarSeparator: the group carries the meaning, the separator the line.

## Examples

### Vertical rail

In a vertical toolbar the groups stack and the separator turns with the axis.

```tsx
<Toolbar orientation="vertical" label="Tools">
  <ToolbarGroup label="Draw">…</ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarGroup label="View">…</ToolbarGroup>
</Toolbar>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `string` | — | Names the sub-group. Without it the group is only visual. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Buttons that belong together inside the toolbar. |
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes on the group. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toolbarseparator.html">
# ToolbarSeparator

ToolbarSeparator draws the divide between sets of actions in a Toolbar. It is one hairline and nothing else: no tab stop, no action, no name to announce. The meaning of the division belongs to ToolbarGroup; the line only makes it visible.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarSeparator} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Formatting">
  <ToolbarButton>Bold</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarButton>Left</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

- Reads the toolbar's orientation: a vertical line between columns, a horizontal one between rows.

- Never focusable — arrow keys skip it, so it costs the keyboard nothing.

- One hairline of --border, the same the surfaces use; no shadow, no double rule.

- Use with ToolbarGroup: the group says what the sets are, the separator shows where they split.

## Examples

### Turned by the axis

The same component in a vertical toolbar: it becomes a horizontal rule, without a prop.

```tsx
<Toolbar orientation="vertical" label="Tools">
  <ToolbarButton>Select</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarButton>Erase</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `className` | `string` | — | Extra classes. Orientation is read from the toolbar, not passed in. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/toolpermission.html">
# ToolPermission

What each tool may do, without asking again.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ToolPermission} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ToolPermission tools={[
  {id: "1", name: "read", scope: "/docs", permission: "always"},
  {id: "2", name: "write", scope: "/docs", permission: "ask"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tools` | `ToolPermissionEntry[]` | — | One row per tool. `scope` sits NEXT TO the name, never hidden: "read" and "read /etc" are different permissions, and granting the second thinking it is the first is the defect this component exists to prevent. |
| `onChange` | `(id: string, permission: PermissionLevel) => void` | — | Fires when a permission changes. The three-way choice is a SegmentedControl, so arrows move AND select, with Home and End — writing three toggle buttons here would redo by hand the pattern ADR-0016 rejected. |
| `label` | `string` | "Tool permissions" | Accessible name of the region. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the region. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/tooltip.html">
# Tooltip

Brief label revealed on hover or focus.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tooltip} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Copy to clipboard" side="top">
  <IconButton icon="copy" label="Copy" />
</Tooltip>

// with the arrow; on plain text the trigger becomes focusable by itself
<Tooltip content="Monthly recurring revenue" arrow>
  <span>MRR</span>
</Tooltip>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `ReactElement` | — | The trigger, as a single element. It receives aria-describedby pointing at the popup — that reference is what makes the hint exist for a screen reader instead of only for the eye. When the element is not focusable on its own (a <span>, a Badge), it becomes focusable, as a button — as in the reference library — so the tip opens from the keyboard too. |
| `content` | `ReactNode` | — | The hint. Short, and never the only place the information lives: a tooltip is a description, and it must hold nothing focusable. |
| `side` | `top \| right \| bottom \| left` | top | Preferred side; it flips when there is no room. |
| `arrow` | `boolean` | false | The arrow, off by default as in the reference library. Our own curve, 12 × 6, with the surface fill and the border line. |
| `delay` | `number` | 1500 | Milliseconds the pointer rests before it opens — the reference library's 1.5 s (the engine's own is 0.6 s). From the keyboard it opens at once, and once one is open its neighbours open without waiting. |
| `closeDelay` | `number` | 500 | Milliseconds before it closes after the pointer leaves — the reference library's 0.5 s. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/topbar.html">
# Topbar

The old name of Header. Same component, still works the same; use Header.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Topbar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Topbar variant="floating" brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}>
  <Button variant="primary" size="sm">New</Button>
</Topbar>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `variant` | `floating \| flush \| pill` | floating | The skin. floating is a detached card; flush merges into the background so the bar frames the window; pill is a centred capsule for a site header — not for a shell, because search plus density plus theme plus command do not fit in a capsule. |
| `brand` | `ReactNode` | — | The lockup. It lives here and not in the sidebar: the top crosses the full width and the side panel starts below it. Inside a shell this is also where the drawer toggle sits, injected before what you pass. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Everything beside the brand: sections, search, actions, account. Presentational — the bar never decides what collapses. It wraps by content, so text at 200% breaks it to a second line instead of overflowing; hide what is secondary with hide-below-md/lg. |
| `divider` | `boolean` | false | Only on `flush`: a hairline under the bar. flush has the page's background and sticks to the top, so without a line the content scrolls under it with nothing saying where the bar ends. |
| `items` | `SidebarItem[]` | — | The website's links — the same list the Sidebar and the BottomNav take, so the app keeps one menu. Uses id, label, href and render (the router link); sub-items, icon and onClick are ignored: the bar is flat. Below 768px they leave the bar and drop into the menu panel. |
| `current` | `string` | — | The id of the current page's item: it gets aria-current="page", the highlight colour and the medium weight, in the bar and in the menu panel. |
| `actions` | `ReactNode` | — | What sits on the right: search, a call to action, the account. It stays in the bar on a phone too. |
| `maxWidth` | `"sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl" \| "2xl" \| "docs" \| "full"` | — | How far the bar's content grows, on the Container's scale, so the bar lines up with the page below it. Without it, the bar keeps its own padding. docs is the documentation block, 1400 (--docs-width), with 24 of padding from 768 up. |
| `itemsJustify` | `"start" \| "end"` | "end" | Where the links sit: end (just before the actions, at the other end from the brand) or start (right after the brand, with the actions at the other end — the reference's home page). |
| `size` | `"md" \| "sm"` | "md" | The bar's height: md is 64 (the reference's bar guide), sm is 56 (the reference's home page), with 6 between the actions instead of 8. |
| `blurred` | `boolean` | false | Only on flush: a transparent background that blurs what scrolls under it, as the reference's home page. With reduced transparency asked by the system, or a browser without backdrop blur, the background is solid. |
| `menuActions` | `ReactNode` | — | What only the phone menu carries, under the links (the GitHub link, the account). Not shown in the wide bar. |
| `navLabel` | `string` | "Main" | The navigation's name for screen readers. Pass it in the page's language. |
| `menuLabel` | `string` | "Menu" | The phone menu button's name for screen readers. Pass it in the page's language. In an app with client-side routing the panel does not close by itself on a page change: give the Header a key that changes with the route. |
| `menuId` | `string` | "aurea-header-menu" | The id of the phone menu panel, which the button points at with popovertarget. Change it only when a page has two website headers: each one needs its own. |
| `tabs` | `HeaderTab[]` | — | A second row: the site's areas, each with an optional icon, like the area row of the reference documentation. The row is 40 tall, the areas sit at its bottom, 12 apart (4 on a phone), and it scrolls sideways when they do not fit. The current one gets aria-current="page" and a 2px bar in the accent color. It comes last in the Tab order, after the actions. With tabs the bar is exactly its height and the divider line hangs just below it. |
| `currentTab` | `string` | — | The id of the current area in the second row. |
| `tabsLabel` | `string` | "Sections" | The accessible name of the second row. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/tracetimeline.html">
# TraceTimeline

How long each step took, as a waterfall.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TraceTimeline} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TraceTimeline spans={[
  {id: "1", label: "invoke", start: 0, end: 900},
  {id: "2", label: "retrieve", start: 40, end: 380, depth: 1, kind: "tool"},
]} />
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `spans` | `TraceSpan[]` | — | Each bar is offset by (start-min)/(max-min) and sized by (end-start)/(max-min) — the maths of the reference. This is NOT the Timeline component: that one is a column of moments, this is a waterfall of DURATIONS, where position and width are the data. `depth` indents to show who called whom. `kind` is TEXT: the reference paints eleven span categories in eleven colours, and colour-per-category on a locked palette is unreadable for anyone who does not separate them. |
| `label` | `string` | "Trace" | Accessible name of the list. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the list. |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/treeview.html">
# TreeView

Hierarchical, expandable tree of items.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TreeView} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TreeView
  label="Files"
  defaultExpandedIds={["src"]}
  onSelect={node => open(node.id)}
  items={[
    {id: "src", label: "src", children: [
      {id: "index", label: "index.tsx"},
      {id: "tokens", label: "tokens.css"},
    ]},
    {id: "readme", label: "README.md"},
  ]}
/>
```

## API Reference

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `items` | `TreeNode[]` | — | The tree: {id, label, icon?, children?, hasChildren?}. Nesting is by containment — the group lives inside its treeitem, with no aria-owns to keep in sync. `hasChildren: true` makes a node openable before its children exist (one of the references calls it hasChildItems); the children arrive later through `items`. |
| `defaultExpandedIds` | `string[]` | — | Which nodes start open. Only the initial value: after that the tree owns its own expansion. |
| `onSelect` | `(node: TreeNode) => void` | — | The whole node, not just the id — you rarely want only the id. |
| `onExpand` | `(node: TreeNode) => void \| Promise<unknown>` | — | Called every time a node opens (never when it closes). If it returns a promise and the node has no children yet, the node shows the spinner where the caret was and is aria-busy until the promise settles. A rejected promise closes the node again, so opening it retries. |
| `selectedId` | `string \| null` | — | Controls which node is selected, as in DependencyGraph. `null` means none. Without it the tree keeps the selection itself, as before. |
| `label` | `string` | "Tree" | Accessible name of the root. |
| `className` | `string` | — | On the root <ul>, which is the element with role="tree". |
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/useaureatheme.html">
# useAureaTheme

Read theme and density straight from the document, and set them — for a host that owns the <html> attributes.

## Usage

```tsx
import {useAureaTheme} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const {theme, density, setTheme, setDensity, toggleTheme} = useAureaTheme();

// Lê direto do <html> e acompanha quem mudar o atributo por fora.
// Use este quando a APLICAÇÃO é dona do data-theme; use useTheme quando
// quem guarda a escolha é o AureaProvider.
<IconButton
  icon={theme === "light" ? "moon" : "sun"}
  label={theme === "light" ? "Switch to dark" : "Switch to light"}
  onClick={toggleTheme}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/usedensity.html">
# useDensity

Read the current density and switch it, from anywhere inside AureaProvider.

## Usage

```tsx
import {useDensity} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const {density, setDensity} = useDensity();

<SegmentedControl
  value={density ?? "comfortable"}
  onChange={setDensity}
  items={[
    {value: "compact", label: "Compact"},
    {value: "comfortable", label: "Comfortable"},
    {value: "spacious", label: "Spacious"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/useportalcontainer.html">
# usePortalContainer

The node every Aurea popup is mounted into, as configured once on AureaProvider.

## Usage

```tsx
import {usePortalContainer} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
// Configurado UMA vez, no provider — não é prop de componente.
<AureaProvider portalContainer={ref.current}>…</AureaProvider>

// E lido por quem monta um popup próprio, para cair no mesmo lugar:
const container = usePortalContainer();
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/usereorder.html">
# useReorder

The accessible drag-and-drop reordering protocol, shared by SortableList and BlockEditor.

## Usage

```tsx
import {useReorder} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const {itens, aoSoltar, propsDoItem} = useReorder(lista, setLista);

// Reordenar sem ponteiro: pegar (Space), mover (setas), soltar (Space),
// cancelar (Escape) — e cada passo é anunciado por live region.
<ul>{itens.map((it, i) => <li key={it.id} {...propsDoItem(i)}>{it.label}</li>)}</ul>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/usetoast.html">
# useToast

Raise a transient notification from anywhere inside AureaProvider.

## Usage

```tsx
import {useToast} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const toast = useToast();

<Button onClick={() => toast.add({title: "Saved", type: "success"})}>
  Save
</Button>

// with a line under the title and an action
toast.add({title: "Conversation deleted", actionProps: {children: "Undo", onClick: restore}});

// a promise: spins while it runs, then success or error
toast.promise(send(), {loading: "Sending…", success: "Sent", error: "Could not send"});

// where the stack lives (the default is the bottom middle)
<AureaProvider toastPlacement="top-end">…</AureaProvider>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-accordion-questions-on-a-marketing-page.html">
# Questions on a marketing page

The title is the question in the reader's own words, not a category. An accordion earns its place when the reader wants one answer, not all of them — otherwise plain headings read faster.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Accordion} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Accordion items={[
  {id: "ship", title: "How do I ship it?",
   content: "Install the three packages and import the CSS. Nothing to configure."},
  {id: "theme", title: "Can I match my brand?",
   content: "Every visual value is a token. Override the ones you need."},
  {id: "a11y", title: "Is it accessible?",
   content: "Keyboard and ARIA come from the engine; contrast is gated in CI."},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-accordion-advanced-options-folded-away.html">
# Advanced options, folded away

The defaults are enough for most people, so the rest starts closed. Folding is not hiding: the summary line says what is inside, so nobody has to open it to find out.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Accordion} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Accordion items={[
  {id: "retry", title: "Retries and timeouts", content: <RetryForm />},
  {id: "net", title: "Network and proxy", content: <NetworkForm />},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-appshell-the-frame-of-a-whole-application.html">
# The frame of a whole application

Brand and global actions on the topbar, the sections on the sidebar, the screen in the middle. It is the only component that owns page landmarks — one per document, never nested — and it emits the skip link for free, which is what closes WCAG 2.4.1 without the consumer writing anything.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AppShell, Button, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AppShell
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  navigation={<nav aria-label="Sections"><a href="/inbox" aria-current="page">Inbox</a><a href="/archive">Archive</a></nav>}
  topbar={<><IconButton icon="bell" label="Notifications" /><Button variant="primary" size="sm">New</Button></>}
>
  <h1>Inbox</h1>
  <p>Nothing needs your attention.</p>
</AppShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-appshell-a-topbar-joined-to-the-page.html">
# A topbar joined to the page

`topbarVariant="flush"` drops the floating surface and welds the bar to the top edge. Pick one of the two per application and hold it: floating on one screen and flush on the next reads as two products, not as two screens.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AppShell, SearchField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AppShell
  topbarVariant="flush"
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  navigation={<nav aria-label="Sections">…</nav>}
  topbar={<SearchField aria-label="Search" placeholder="Search…" />}
>
  <h1>Reports</h1>
</AppShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-appshell-the-sidebar-out-of-the-way.html">
# The sidebar out of the way

`sidebarCollapsed` is controlled by the consumer, like `open` on the palette: the shell never decides on its own that the navigation should disappear. The toggle in the brand slot is emitted by the shell and drives the same sidebar on small screens, where it opens as a popover instead of a column.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AppShell, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [collapsed, setCollapsed] = useState(true);

<AppShell
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  navigation={<nav aria-label="Sections">…</nav>}
  sidebarCollapsed={collapsed}
  topbar={<Button size="sm" variant="ghost" onClick={() => setCollapsed(c => !c)}>Toggle</Button>}
>
  <h1>Editor</h1>
</AppShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-aspectratio-a-media-slot-that-reserves-its-space.html">
# A media slot that reserves its space

The box holds the shape before the image arrives, so nothing below it jumps when it does. That is the whole job: not cropping the picture, but stopping the layout from shifting under the reader — the failure a card grid makes most visibly.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AspectRatio, Card} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <AspectRatio ratio={16 / 9}>
    <img src={cover} alt="" style={{width: "100%", height: "100%", objectFit: "cover"}} />
  </AspectRatio>
  <strong>Design tokens, end to end</strong>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-aspectratio-one-ratio-held-across-a-grid.html">
# One ratio held across a grid

Cards of different image heights read as a broken grid even when every card is correct. Fixing the ratio in one place is what makes the row line up, and it survives a source image nobody checked.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AspectRatio} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="grid">
  {items.map(i => (
    <AspectRatio key={i.id} ratio={4 / 3}>
      <img src={i.cover} alt="" />
    </AspectRatio>
  ))}
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-aspectratio-a-square-for-identity.html">
# A square, for identity

`ratio={1}` is the default because the square is the shape identity uses — an avatar, a logo, a QR code. Naming it explicitly in the code is still worth it: a reader who sees `ratio={1}` knows the square was chosen, not inherited.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AspectRatio, QRCode} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AspectRatio ratio={1}>
  <QRCode value="https://aureauds.dev" />
</AspectRatio>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-avatar-initials-when-there-is-no-picture.html">
# Initials when there is no picture

The fallback is not a placeholder, it is the normal case: most people in most systems have no photo. Initials come from the name so two rows never look alike by accident.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Avatar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Avatar fallback="AN" alt="Analyst" />
<Avatar src="/people/curator.jpg" alt="Curator" size="lg" />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-avatargroup-who-is-on-this-run.html">
# Who is on this run

Overlapping faces plus a count for the rest. The cutoff exists because a row of twelve avatars stops being information and becomes texture — the number carries what the faces no longer can.

## Usage

```tsx
import {AvatarGroup, Avatar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<AvatarGroup max={3} total={9} label="Participants">
  <Avatar fallback="ME" alt="Messenger" />
  <Avatar fallback="AN" alt="Analyst" />
  <Avatar fallback="CU" alt="Curator" />
  <Avatar fallback="WR" alt="Writer" />
</AvatarGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-badge-version-tag.html">
# Version tag

Short metadata next to a title — the release the page documents.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Badge variant="primary">v1.7.0</Badge>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-badge-maturity-scale.html">
# Maturity scale

The whole maturity ladder in one row, so a reader places an item at a glance.

# Badge next to Status

Badge classifies, Status reports a condition. Together they answer what and how.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-badge-categories-not-statuses.html">
# Categories, not statuses

Eight colour names mark a group — a section, a kind of item — and say nothing about health, so they never compete with success or danger. Yellow is left out: it belongs to the brand. The word and the icon carry the meaning; the colour only helps the eye find the group again.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Badge, Icon} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Badge variant="blue" leading={<Icon name="code" />}>Engineering</Badge>
<Badge variant="violet" leading={<Icon name="palette" />}>Design</Badge>
<Badge variant="orange" leading={<Icon name="megaphone" />}>Marketing</Badge>
<Badge variant="green" leading={<Icon name="coins" />}>Finance</Badge>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-badge-one-category-in-three-emphases.html">
# One category in three emphases

The categories take the same three emphases as every other badge: soft for a list, solid for the one that must stand out, outline (since 0.34.0 a light tint, no line) when the surface is already busy.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Badge variant="teal">Research</Badge>
<Badge variant="teal" emphasis="solid">Research</Badge>
<Badge variant="teal" emphasis="outline">Research</Badge>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-banner-something-that-affects-the-whole-page.html">
# Something that affects the whole page

A banner spans the region it is about; an alert sits inside it. Dismissible only when the message is genuinely optional — a banner about degraded service that can be closed is a banner nobody sees twice.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Banner} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Banner variant="warning" title="Reduced capacity">
  Runs are queueing. Scheduled jobs may start late until 18:00 UTC.
</Banner>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-banner-the-cookie-notice.html">
# The cookie notice

variant="consent" asks before setting cookies that are not necessary: reject them, accept all, or choose by category in a window. Rejecting is as easy to see as accepting — same weight, same place —, the optional categories start off, and after the choice the confirmation takes the focus. Put the notice at the top of the page, before the skip link, and do not fix it to the screen. To change the choice later, show it again from a link in the footer, with value set to what you stored. On this static page the buttons do not answer; in your app they do.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Banner, Dialog, Switch, Link} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Banner
  variant="consent"
  categories={[
    {id: "necessary", label: "Necessary", description: "Sign-in, the cart, your cookie choice.", required: true},
    {id: "analytics", label: "Analytics", description: "Visits counted without saying who you are."},
    {id: "marketing", label: "Marketing", description: "Ads for what you saw here, on other sites."},
  ]}
  value={stored}
  onConsent={(choice) => store(choice)}
  onDismiss={() => setShown(false)}
>
  <p>We use necessary cookies to make this site work and, if you allow it, others to measure visits and show ads. <Link href="/privacy">Privacy policy</Link>.</p>
</Banner>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-breadcrumb-where-this-page-sits.html">
# Where this page sits

Every level is a link except the last, which is the page itself and carries aria-current. A breadcrumb whose last item is also a link tells the screen reader that the user can navigate to where they already are.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Breadcrumb} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Breadcrumb items={[
  {label: "Components", href: "./index.html"},
  {label: "Actions", href: "./index.html#actions"},
  {label: "Button"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-the-two-axes.html">
# The two axes

Appearance is how much weight the box has; tone is what the colour means. The old names are shortcuts for pairs — variant="danger-outline" and appearance/tone below render the same button.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button appearance="outline" tone="danger">Delete</Button>
<Button variant="danger-outline">Delete</Button>  {/* o mesmo */}
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-confirming-a-safe-outcome.html">
# Confirming a safe outcome

Success tone for an action that lands somewhere good — publishing, approving, marking done. Filled, because tone and weight are independent: choosing green does not force the button to be quieter.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button appearance="solid" tone="success" leadingIcon="check">Approve</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-warning-is-not-the-brand.html">
# Warning is not the brand

Amber, not the Aurea yellow. Until August 2026 the warning token resolved to the brand colour in dark theme — same pixels, two different meanings — so warning was not a tone at all. It has its own identity now, picked by measuring perceptual distance from both neighbours: the brand on one side, the destructive red on the other.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button appearance="solid" tone="warning" leadingIcon="warning">Revoke access</Button>
<Button variant="primary">Publish</Button>  {/* a marca, ao lado */}
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-informational-action-in-running-text.html">
# Informational action in running text

Info tone on the link appearance: a pointer to context that is neither a warning nor a commitment.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button appearance="link" tone="info">Why is this blocked?</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-the-same-tone-across-appearances.html">
# The same tone across appearances

One tone, four weights — and every cell exists. A tone never loses its filled form: each one owns a colour and the text colour that goes on top of it, chosen per theme and verified for AA contrast, exactly as the destructive tone always had.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button appearance="solid" tone="success">Approve</Button>
<Button appearance="outline" tone="success">Approve</Button>
<Button appearance="ghost" tone="success">Approve</Button>
<Button appearance="link" tone="success">Approve</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-stacked-actions.html">
# Stacked actions

A vertical group for a menu of actions on a card or in a side panel. The buttons all measure the same width — without that the column comes out ragged, which is the one defect a vertical group cannot have. It stays role="group" and announces no orientation: it does not navigate by arrow, and promising keyboard that does not exist is worse than staying quiet.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ButtonGroup, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ButtonGroup orientation="vertical" label="Item actions">
  <Button variant="outline">Duplicate</Button>
  <Button variant="outline">Archive item</Button>
  <Button variant="danger-outline">Delete</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-the-same-button-in-three-container-widths.html">
# The same button in three container widths

One button, one value, one viewport — three container widths. The step comes from the space the component was placed in, not from the size of the window, so a sidebar and a main column can show the same component at different steps at the same time. This is the proof that separates the two mechanisms: if the three measured the same, what existed would be a media query under another name. The parent needs `container-scope`, which names the container — an unnamed one matches the nearest ancestor that happens to be a container, including one somebody else declared for another reason.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="container-scope">
  <Button size={{base: "xs", container: {xs: "sm", sm: "md", md: "lg"}}}>
    Publish
  </Button>
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-reacting-to-the-window-instead.html">
# Reacting to the window instead

The other mechanism, for when the decision really does belong to the application and not to the slot: the step follows the viewport. Same axis, same scale, and the prefix in the emitted class says which of the two is measuring — `md` is always 768px, and never means two things depending on where you read it. Resize the window to see it move; the example above will not move, because its containers have fixed widths.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button size={{base: "xs", viewport: {sm: "md", lg: "xl"}}}>Publish</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-button-every-family-follows-its-own-scale.html">
# Every family follows its own scale

The same three containers, now with one piece from each family. Control, mark and avatar come from the control height and step together; the icon inside the button comes from the glyph scale and does NOT follow the button — a large button with a huge glyph is not a larger button, it is a different drawing. The two behaviours in one picture are the point: sharing a step is measured, never assumed.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button, Checkbox, Switch, Avatar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="container-scope">
  <Button leadingIcon="plus" size={{base: "xs", container: {xs: "sm", sm: "md", md: "lg"}}}>Add</Button>
  <Checkbox label="Include drafts" size={{base: "sm", container: {sm: "md", md: "lg"}}} />
  <Switch label="Live" size={{base: "sm", container: {sm: "md", md: "lg"}}} />
  <Avatar fallback="AB" size={{base: "sm", container: {sm: "md", md: "lg"}}} />
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-buttongroup-time-range.html">
# Time range

Day, week, month over the same chart — the label names the set, the buttons the spans.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-calendar-date-picker.html">
# Date picker

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-calendar-booking-with-days-closed.html">
# Booking with days closed

The reason this component exists. A native date input cannot say "not before Thursday, and never a Sunday" — everything else about a plain date, it does better.

```tsx
  mode="range"

/>
```

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-calendar-when-the-native-input-wins.html">
