<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-card-a-summary-at-the-top-of-an-article.html">
# A summary at the top of an article

Three short points before the long text, for the reader who has thirty seconds. It is a card with a short title and a list, not an alert: an alert interrupts, a summary waits to be read. The check icon is decoration; the list is announced as a list.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Stack, Cluster, Icon} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <Stack gap="tight">
    <h2>In 30 seconds</h2>
    <Stack gap="tight" role="list">
      <Cluster role="listitem" gap="tight" align="start" wrap={false}>
        <Icon name="check" />The new model arrives in March.
      </Cluster>
      <Cluster role="listitem" gap="tight" align="start" wrap={false}>
        <Icon name="check" />It costs 6% more than the current one.
      </Cluster>
      <Cluster role="listitem" gap="tight" align="start" wrap={false}>
        <Icon name="check" />Orders open next week.
      </Cluster>
    </Stack>
  </Stack>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-card-the-card-that-stands-out.html">
# The card that stands out

The main card of a screen. In the light theme it is the dark theme's card; in the dark theme, the regular card (the yellow outline went with the lines in 0.34.0). Inside it the whole dark theme applies, so text, badges and buttons adjust by themselves. Not for a list of choices: in the dark theme its outline is close to `selected`.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card variant="contrast">
  <div className="cluster" style={{justifyContent:"space-between"}}>
    <strong>Main vehicle</strong>
    <Badge size="xs" variant="success">UP TO DATE</Badge>
  </div>
  <p>18,420 km</p>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-card-a-colour-stroke-on-top.html">
# A colour stroke on top

A stroke on the top edge in the tone's fill colour, the same in both themes. It is decoration: the title already says the subject.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card accent="success">
  <span className="muted">Fuel</span>
  <strong>3 days ago</strong>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-chart-one-series-over-time.html">
# One series over time

Chart is the frame, not the drawing: it carries the accessible name, the sizing and the surface, and the series comes in as a child of the chart library. That split is what lets the drawing engine be swapped without touching the page.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs per month">
  <AreaChart data={data}>
    <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Area dataKey="runs" name="Runs" stroke="var(--chart-2)" fill="var(--chart-2)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
  </AreaChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-chart-two-series-read-together.html">
# Two series, read together

Two bars side by side answer a question one bar cannot: not how many runs, but how many of them failed. The legend is required here — with two series the colours stop being decoration and start carrying meaning.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartLegend} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs and errors">
  <BarChart data={data}>
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <YAxis width={32} tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Bar dataKey="runs" name="Runs" fill="var(--chart-2)" />
    <Bar dataKey="errors" name="Errors" fill="var(--chart-4)" />
    <ChartLegend />
  </BarChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-chart-the-whole-reading-surface.html">
# The whole reading surface

Grid, axis, legend and tooltip on one chart — the assembled form, so the pieces are seen doing their jobs together instead of one at a time. `defaultIndex` pins the tooltip because a static page has no pointer; in an application it is not needed.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartLegend, ChartTooltip} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs and errors per month">
  <AreaChart data={data}>
    <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Area dataKey="runs" name="Runs" stroke="var(--chart-2)" fill="var(--chart-2)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
    <Area dataKey="errors" name="Errors" stroke="var(--chart-4)" fill="var(--chart-4)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
    <ChartTooltip />
    <ChartLegend />
  </AreaChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-chartlegend-naming-the-colours-of-a-stacked-series.html">
# Naming the colours of a stacked series

Stacking hides which band is which, so the legend stops being optional: it is the only place the reader learns that the darker band is the failures. It sits under the drawing by default, where it does not compete with the axis for the first read.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartLegend} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs by outcome">
  <BarChart data={data}>
    <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Bar dataKey="runs" name="Succeeded" stackId="a" fill="var(--chart-2)" />
    <Bar dataKey="errors" name="Failed" stackId="a" fill="var(--chart-4)" />
    <ChartLegend />
  </BarChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-chartlegend-legend-above-the-drawing.html">
# Legend above the drawing

`verticalAlign="top"` reads the names before the shapes, which is what a dashboard tile wants when the drawing is short and the reader is scanning several tiles at once. Everything else stays: the component still takes the series from the engine, never a hand-written list.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartLegend} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs and errors">
  <BarChart data={data}>
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <YAxis width={32} tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Bar dataKey="runs" name="Runs" fill="var(--chart-2)" />
    <Bar dataKey="errors" name="Errors" fill="var(--chart-4)" />
    <ChartLegend verticalAlign="top" />
  </BarChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-charttooltip-the-exact-value-under-the-pointer.html">
# The exact value under the pointer

An area chart shows a shape, not a number; the tooltip is where the number lives. It reuses the same `.tooltip` surface as the rest of the system, so a value read on a chart looks like a value read anywhere else.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartTooltip} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs per month">
  <AreaChart data={data}>
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Area dataKey="runs" name="Runs" stroke="var(--chart-2)" fill="var(--chart-2)" fillOpacity={0.15} />
    <ChartTooltip />
  </AreaChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-charttooltip-every-series-at-one-point-in-time.html">
# Every series at one point in time

With more than one series the tooltip becomes a small table: the label is the point on the axis, and each row is a series with its colour swatch. This is the comparison the drawing cannot make, because two bars of different heights do not tell you their difference.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Chart, ChartTooltip} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Chart label="Runs and errors">
  <BarChart data={data}>
    <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
    <XAxis dataKey="month" tickLine={false} axisLine={false} />
    <Bar dataKey="runs" name="Runs" fill="var(--chart-2)" />
    <Bar dataKey="errors" name="Errors" fill="var(--chart-4)" />
    <ChartTooltip />
  </BarChart>
</Chart>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-checkbox-one-box-that-gates-the-action.html">
# One box that gates the action

The label is the whole sentence and it is clickable — a checkbox whose label is not part of the target is a 16px hit area, which fails on touch. Never pre-checked when it grants permission.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Checkbox} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Checkbox
  label="Send me release notes"
  description="About once a month. You can turn this off any time."
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-checkbox-a-set-where-several-answers-are-right.html">
# A set where several answers are right

Checkbox, not radio, is the difference between 'pick any' and 'pick one'. The rule is the answer, not the look: if zero selected is a legitimate state, it is a checkbox.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Checkbox} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<fieldset>
  <legend>Notify me about</legend>
  <Checkbox label="Failed runs" />
  <Checkbox label="New members" />
  <Checkbox label="Weekly summary" />
</fieldset>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-cluster-a-row-of-actions-that-wraps-instead-of-overflowing.html">
# A row of actions that wraps instead of overflowing

Buttons side by side with the gap of the system, and a wrap that happens before anything is pushed off screen. Writing `display:flex` by hand gets the row right and the wrap wrong, which is only visible on the narrow viewport nobody tested.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Cluster, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <Button variant="primary">Save changes</Button>
  <Button variant="secondary">Save as draft</Button>
  <Button variant="ghost">Discard</Button>
</Cluster>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-cluster-tags-under-a-heading.html">
# Tags under a heading

A cluster of badges is the shape a filter list and a tag list share. The primitive is what keeps the vertical rhythm right when the second row appears — the case a hand-written flex row almost always gets wrong.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Cluster, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Cluster>
  {tags.map(t => <Badge key={t}>{t}</Badge>)}
</Cluster>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-cluster-metadata-beside-a-title.html">
# Metadata beside a title

Title, status and time on one line, aligned on their centres rather than their boxes. The alignment is the point: three elements of different heights on a hand-written row sit on three different baselines.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Cluster, Status, Avatar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <strong>Nightly sweep</strong>
  <Status variant="success">Succeeded</Status>
  <span className="muted">1m 48s</span>
</Cluster>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-codeblock-the-install-line.html">
# The install line

The shortest useful block: one command, one button. `copyable` is what makes it a block instead of a paragraph — a reader who has to select the text by hand will select the prompt with it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CodeBlock} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<CodeBlock language="bash" copyable>pnpm add @aurea-uds/react @aurea-uds/core</CodeBlock>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-codeblock-a-snippet-under-a-heading.html">
# A snippet under a heading

The shape every documentation page repeats: a sentence that says what the code does, then the code. The block keeps its own horizontal scroll, so a long line never widens the page around it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, CodeBlock} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <h3>Set the theme from the server</h3>
  <p className="muted">Write it on the root element so the first paint is already right.</p>
  <CodeBlock language="tsx" copyable>{snippet}</CodeBlock>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-codeblock-output-not-source.html">
# Output, not source

`language="text"` is the default for a reason: not everything in a block is code. A stack trace or a command's output is quoted verbatim, and pretending it is a language would colour tokens that are not tokens.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CodeBlock} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<CodeBlock>{stderr}</CodeBlock>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-codeeditor-a-snippet-the-reader-can-change.html">
# A snippet the reader can change

An editor, not a code block: the reader types. Use it where the change is the point — a query, a config, a rule — and use CodeBlock everywhere else, because a read-only editor costs a bundle it does not earn.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CodeEditor} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<CodeEditor defaultValue={`select count(*)
from runs
where status = 'failed'`} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-collapsible-advanced-options-folded-away.html">
# Advanced options, folded away

The default answer for a form section most people never open. `defaultOpen` is left off and the state stays inside the component — a consumer that does not need to read the state should not have to hold it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Collapsible, Field, Input, Switch} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Collapsible trigger="Advanced">
  <Field label="Timeout (ms)"><Input defaultValue="30000" inputMode="numeric" /></Field>
  <Switch label="Retry on failure" defaultChecked />
</Collapsible>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-collapsible-a-detail-already-unfolded.html">
# A detail already unfolded

`defaultOpen` starts unfolded but leaves the reader in charge of folding it back. Use it when the content is the point of the screen and the fold is a courtesy, not a filter.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Collapsible, DataList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Collapsible trigger="Run details" defaultOpen>
  <DataList items={[
    {term: "Started", value: "09:12:04"},
    {term: "Duration", value: "1m 48s"},
    {term: "Exit code", value: "0"},
  ]} />
</Collapsible>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-collapsible-fold-driven-from-outside.html">
# Fold driven from outside

`open` plus `onOpenChange` when something else in the screen decides — a "expand all" button, a deep link, a search that has to reveal the match it found. Passing `open` without `onOpenChange` freezes it, which is a legitimate read-only state and not a bug.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Collapsible, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

<Button size="sm" variant="ghost" onClick={() => setOpen(o => !o)}>
  {open ? "Collapse all" : "Expand all"}
</Button>
<Collapsible trigger="Environment" open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <CodeBlock>{env}</CodeBlock>
</Collapsible>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-collapsible-a-section-that-cannot-be-opened-yet.html">
# A section that cannot be opened yet

`disabled` keeps the row in place while the content is unavailable, instead of removing it. A section that disappears and comes back renumbers everything around it; a section that stays says the same thing without moving anything.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Collapsible} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Collapsible trigger="Billing history" disabled>
  <p>Available once the first invoice is issued.</p>
</Collapsible>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-combobox-picking-one-out-of-many.html">
# Picking one out of many

A select stops working somewhere around twenty options — the eye cannot scan them. A combobox lets the user type what they already know instead of hunting for it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Combobox} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [zone, setZone] = useState(null);

<Combobox
  label="Time zone"
  placeholder="Start typing a city…"
  value={zone}
  onValueChange={setZone}
  items={[
    {value: "sao_paulo", label: "America/Sao_Paulo"},
    {value: "lisbon", label: "Europe/Lisbon"},
    {value: "tokyo", label: "Asia/Tokyo"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-combobox-options-that-belong-to-sections.html">
# Options that belong to sections

A flat list of forty time zones is a wall; the same forty under continents is a map. Pass groups — `{label, items}` — in the same `items` prop, and the engine's filter runs inside each section, dropping a section that has nothing left to show. `empty` writes what appears when nothing matches, which is where a list stops saying No results and starts saying what the user can do about it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Combobox} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Combobox
  label="Time zone"
  placeholder="Start typing a city…"
  empty="No zone by that name — try the city, not the country."
  value={zone}
  onValueChange={setZone}
  items={[
    {label: "Americas", items: [
      {value: "sao_paulo", label: "America/Sao_Paulo"},
      {value: "new_york", label: "America/New_York"},
    ]},
    {label: "Europe", items: [
      {value: "lisbon", label: "Europe/Lisbon"},
      {value: "berlin", label: "Europe/Berlin"},
    ]},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-commandpaletteshell-every-command-on-one-keystroke.html">
# Every command on one keystroke

The palette is the keyboard route to anything the application can do. The field takes focus on open and the list narrows as you type, so the whole interaction is one gesture — never a menu you have to find first.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CommandPaletteShell, Kbd} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<CommandPaletteShell open={open} query={query} onQueryChange={setQuery}>
  <div className="menu">
    <button className="menu-item" type="button">Go to Button<Kbd>G B</Kbd></button>
    <button className="menu-item" type="button">Toggle theme<Kbd>T</Kbd></button>
    <button className="menu-item" type="button">Open settings<Kbd>,</Kbd></button>
  </div>
</CommandPaletteShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-commandpaletteshell-results-narrowed-by-what-was-typed.html">
# Results narrowed by what was typed

Filtering is the consumer's job, not the shell's: it holds `query` and decides what matches. Keeping it outside is what lets the same palette search components, files or an API — the shell never assumes the shape of what it is searching.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CommandPaletteShell, Kbd} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const shown = commands.filter(c => c.label.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()));

<CommandPaletteShell open={open} query={query} onQueryChange={setQuery}>
  <div className="menu">
    {shown.map(c => (
      <button key={c.id} className="menu-item" type="button" onClick={c.run}>{c.label}</button>
    ))}
  </div>
</CommandPaletteShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-commandpaletteshell-nothing-matched.html">
# Nothing matched

The one state a palette must not skip. A list that simply vanishes reads as a broken palette; EmptyState says the search ran and found nothing, which is a different fact and the one the reader needs.

## Usage

```tsx
import {CommandPaletteShell, EmptyState} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<CommandPaletteShell open={open} query={query} onQueryChange={setQuery}>
  {shown.length
    ? <div className="menu">{shown.map(renderCommand)}</div>
    : <EmptyState icon="magnifying-glass" title="No command matches" description="Try a shorter word." />}
</CommandPaletteShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-contextmenu-right-click-on-an-item.html">
# Right-click on an item

The menu the mouse expects on an item, and the keyboard reaches with Shift+F10. It never replaces a visible control: everything here has another way in.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ContextMenu, Card} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ContextMenu label="Item actions" items={[
  {label: "Rename", leadingIcon: "pencil-simple"},
  {label: "Move to…", leadingIcon: "folder"},
  "separator",
  {label: "Delete", leadingIcon: "trash"},
]}>
  <Card>Right-click this card, or focus it and press Shift+F10.</Card>
</ContextMenu>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-datagrid-a-list-you-act-on-in-bulk.html">
# A list you act on in bulk

Selection turns a table into a work surface: pick the rows, then act once. The header checkbox selects the page, never the whole dataset — a promise a static table cannot keep.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DataGrid} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DataGrid
  label="Members"
  selectable
  filterable
  pageSize={10}
  onSelectionChange={setSelected}
  getRowId={row => row.name}
  data={members}
  columns={[
    {accessorKey: "name", header: "Name"},
    {accessorKey: "role", header: "Role"},
    {accessorKey: "runs", header: "Runs"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-datalist-the-facts-about-one-record.html">
# The facts about one record

A definition list is the honest markup for "this thing has these properties". Every value here belongs to the same run; nothing on the list compares it to another run.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DataList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DataList items={[
  {term: "Status", value: "Succeeded"},
  {term: "Started", value: "21 Aug 2026, 09:12"},
  {term: "Duration", value: "1m 48s"},
  {term: "Triggered by", value: "Curator"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-datalist-values-that-are-components.html">
# Values that are components

`value` takes any node, so a status reads as a status and an identity reads as an identity. The alternative — spelling "Succeeded" as text — loses the one thing the reader scans for when the list is long.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DataList, Status, Avatar, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DataList items={[
  {term: "Result", value: <Status variant="success">Succeeded</Status>},
  {term: "Owner", value: <Avatar fallback="AN" size="sm" />},
  {term: "Version", value: <Badge>v1.4.0</Badge>},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-datalist-inside-a-card-under-a-heading.html">
# Inside a card, under a heading

The shape a detail panel repeats: a title that names the record and the list that describes it. The card supplies the surface; the list supplies the structure — neither tries to do the other's job.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, DataList, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <h3>Invoice AU-2026-0184</h3>
  <DataList items={fields} />
  <Button variant="secondary" size="sm" leadingIcon="download">Download PDF</Button>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-datalist-a-spec-sheet-in-groups.html">
# A spec sheet in groups

A long list of facts reads better cut by subject. Each group is a card with its own title and its own list; the grid lays the cards side by side and stacks them on a phone. No group component to learn — the parts already exist.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Grid, Card, DataList} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Grid min="sm">
  <Card>
    <h3>Engine</h3>
    <DataList items={engine} />
  </Card>
```

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dependencygraph-a-network-map-top-to-bottom.html">
# A network map, top to bottom

The internet on top and each layer below. The kind of device is a word with an icon beside it; badges carry the count and the status; ports name the ends of the lines; the line's drawing says what kind of link it is without colour — double for fibre — and its state comes apart, as a colour, a word and a cross when down. The legend builds itself in two parts: the kind of link and the state. Repeated links between the same two devices collapse into one with their count.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DependencyGraph} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DependencyGraph
  orientation="vertical"
  layout="layered"      // needs the optional peer elkjs
  rootId="internet"
  edgeShape="step"
  groupParallel
  legend
  nodes={[
    {id: "internet", label: "Internet", kind: "Cloud", icon: "globe"},
    {id: "fw", label: "Firewall", kind: "Firewall", icon: "shield", detail: "10.0.0.1"},
    {id: "core", label: "Core", kind: "Layer 3 switch", icon: "network",
      ports: [{id: "p1", side: "bottom"}, {id: "p2", side: "bottom"}]},
    {id: "floor", label: "Floor 1", kind: "Access switch", icon: "network",
      count: 20, countLabel: "20 workstations"},
    {id: "cam", label: "Gate camera", kind: "IP camera", icon: "security-camera",
      status: {label: "Unreachable", tone: "danger"}},
  ]}
  edges={[
    {from: "internet", to: "fw", legend: "Copper"},
    {from: "internet", to: "fw", legend: "Copper"},
    {from: "fw", to: "core", pattern: "double", legend: "Fibre"},
    {from: "core", to: "floor", fromPort: "p1", sourceLabel: "port 1", legend: "Copper"},
    {from: "core", to: "cam", fromPort: "p2", sourceLabel: "port 2", legend: "Copper",
      status: {label: "Down", tone: "danger", mark: "cross"}},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dialog-destructive-confirmation.html">
# Destructive confirmation

The pause before something irreversible. The title asks the question, the body says what is lost, and the confirming button carries the danger tone — never the cancel.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Dialog, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

<Button appearance="outline" tone="danger" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Delete project</Button>

<Dialog
  open={open}
  onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
  title="Delete this project?"
  footer={<>
    <Button variant="ghost" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>Cancel</Button>
    <Button appearance="solid" tone="danger" onClick={remove}>Delete</Button>
  </>}
>
  Every run, dataset and share link goes with it. This cannot be undone.
</Dialog>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dialog-short-form-in-a-dialog.html">
# Short form in a dialog

A dialog is the right home for a form only when it is short enough to fit without scrolling. The primary action repeats the verb of the title, so the user never has to re-read what they are confirming.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Dialog, Field, Input, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Dialog
  open={open}
  onClose={close}
  title="Invite a teammate"
  footer={<>
    <Button variant="ghost" onClick={close}>Cancel</Button>
    <Button variant="primary" type="submit" form="invite">Send invite</Button>
  </>}
>
  <form id="invite" onSubmit={send}>
    <Field label="Email" hint="They get access to this workspace only">
      <Input type="email" name="email" required />
    </Field>
  </form>
</Dialog>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-drawer-detail-panel-beside-the-list.html">
# Detail panel beside the list

The row stays on screen and the detail slides in beside it — the reason to pick a drawer over a dialog is exactly this: the context does not disappear.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Drawer, Button, Field} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Drawer open={open} onClose={close} side="right" title="Run #4821">
  <Field label="Status"><Input readOnly value="waiting_approval" /></Field>
  <Field label="Started"><Input readOnly value="14:31" /></Field>
</Drawer>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-drawer-filters-that-stay-open-while-you-read.html">
# Filters that stay open while you read

Filters on the left, results on the right. A dialog would cover the results the filters are changing, which is the one thing a filter panel must not do.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Drawer, Select, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Drawer open={open} onClose={close} side="left" title="Filters">
  <Field label="Status"><Select>…</Select></Field>
  <Field label="Owner"><Select>…</Select></Field>
  <Button variant="primary" fullWidth onClick={apply}>Apply</Button>
</Drawer>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dropdownmenu-the-overflow-menu-of-a-table-row.html">
# The overflow menu of a table row

Three dots at the end of the row. Destructive items sit last, after a separator, so the pointer never lands on Delete while reaching for Rename.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DropdownMenu, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DropdownMenu
  label="Row actions"
  trigger={<IconButton icon="dots-three" label="Row actions" />}
  items={[
    {label: "Rename", leadingIcon: "pencil-simple"},
    {label: "Duplicate", leadingIcon: "copy"},
    "separator",
    {label: "Delete", leadingIcon: "trash"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dropdownmenu-a-primary-action-with-variants-behind-it.html">
# A primary action with variants behind it

The button does the common thing; the chevron opens the rest. The label of the button is the action itself, never the word More.

## Usage

```tsx
import {DropdownMenu, Button, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ButtonGroup label="Export">
  <Button variant="primary">Export CSV</Button>
  <DropdownMenu
    label="Other formats"
    trigger={<IconButton variant="primary" icon="caret-down" label="Other formats" />}
    items={[{label: "Export JSON"}, {label: "Export Parquet"}]}
  />
</ButtonGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-dropdownmenu-a-menu-that-holds-state-not-just-commands.html">
# A menu that holds STATE, not just commands

The View menu of any application: things that toggle, things that are mutually exclusive, and a section label that names the group instead of pretending to be an item. Until 28/08/2026 the Aurea menu could express none of these — `items` had a single shape, and the engine underneath had five (G-API-02).

## Usage

```tsx
import {DropdownMenu, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<DropdownMenu
  label="View"
  trigger={<Button variant="ghost">View</Button>}
  items={[
    {kind: "checkbox", label: "Sidebar", defaultChecked: true,
      onCheckedChange: (on) => setSidebar(on)},
    {kind: "checkbox", label: "Ruler"},
    "separator",
    {kind: "radiogroup", label: "Sort by", defaultValue: "name",
      onValueChange: setSort, items: [
        {value: "name", label: "Name"},
        {value: "date", label: "Date modified"},
      ]},
    "separator",
    {kind: "submenu", label: "Export", leadingIcon: "download", items: [
      {label: "PDF"},
      {label: "CSV"},
    ]},
    {kind: "link", label: "Documentation", href: "/docs"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-emptystate-nothing-here-yet-and-one-way-forward.html">
# Nothing here yet, and one way forward

The empty state of a new account is not an error: it says what will appear and offers the one action that fills it. Never the same copy as a search with no results — those are different situations wearing the same layout.

## Usage

```tsx
import {EmptyState, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<EmptyState
  icon="rocket"
  title="No runs yet"
  description="Start one and it will show up here with its logs and timings."
  action={<Button variant="primary">Start a run</Button>}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-emptystate-the-filter-matched-nothing.html">
# The filter matched nothing

Different from an empty account: here there IS data, the query just missed it. The action clears the filter instead of creating something — offering Create here sends people down the wrong path.

## Usage

```tsx
import {EmptyState, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<EmptyState
  icon="magnifying-glass"
  title="No members match “curator”"
  description="Check the spelling, or clear the filter to see all 9 members."
  action={<Button variant="outline" onClick={clear}>Clear filter</Button>}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-fileinput-dropping-files-with-a-limit.html">
# Dropping files with a limit

The limits are written before the mistake, not after it: type and size are on the field, so the refusal never surprises. Dropping and clicking reach the same input, because a drop zone that is not also a button is unusable by keyboard.

## Usage

```tsx
import {FileInput} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<FileInput
  label="Attachments"
  hint="PDF or PNG, up to 5 MB each"
  accept=".pdf,.png"
  maxSize={5 * 1024 * 1024}
  multiple
  onFilesChange={setFiles}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-header-the-bar-that-carries-the-brand-and-the-global-actions.html">
# The bar that carries the brand and the global actions

Brand on the left, actions on the right, and nothing in between that belongs to a single page. The floating variant sits on the content; flush joins the page — pick one per application, not per screen.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Header, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Header brand={<strong>Aurea UDS</strong>}>
  <SearchField aria-label="Search" placeholder="Search…" />
  <IconButton icon="sun" label="Switch to light" onClick={toggleTheme} />
</Header>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-header-a-website-header-with-the-current-page-marked.html">
# A website header, with the current page marked

The same list the Sidebar and the BottomNav take goes in items, and current marks the page you are on. Below 768px the links leave the bar and drop into the menu panel; the actions stay in the bar. maxWidth lines the bar up with the Container of the page.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Header, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Header
  variant="flush"
  divider
  maxWidth="xl"
  brand={<strong>Acme</strong>}
  items={items}
  current="pricing"
  navLabel="Main"
  menuLabel="Menu"
  actions={<Button variant="primary" size="sm">Sign up</Button>}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-hovercard-who-this-person-is-without-leaving-the-sentence.html">
# Who this person is, without leaving the sentence

A name in running text is an identifier, not an identity. The card answers "who?" in place, and the profile page it previews stays one click away — the preview is a shortcut, never the only route.

## Usage

```tsx
import {HoverCard, Avatar, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<HoverCard trigger={<a href="/people/analyst">Analyst</a>}>
  <div className="cluster">
    <Avatar fallback="AN" />
    <div>
      <strong>Analyst</strong>
      <p className="muted">Data · joined March 2026</p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <Badge variant="success">Available</Badge>
</HoverCard>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-hovercard-previewing-what-a-link-leads-to.html">
# Previewing what a link leads to

`side="top"` when the trigger sits low in the viewport and a card below it would be cut off. The rest is unchanged: the preview saves a navigation, it does not replace one.

## Usage

```tsx
import {HoverCard, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<HoverCard side="top" trigger={<a href="/runs/8814">Run #8814</a>}>
  <strong>Nightly sweep</strong>
  <p className="muted">Finished 09:13 · 1m 48s · 0 errors</p>
  <Badge variant="success">Succeeded</Badge>
</HoverCard>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-input-settings-row.html">
# Settings row

Label on the left, control on the right — the line every settings screen is made of. Until August 2026 this only came out of Aurea with ad-hoc CSS. It is a grid and not a row for one reason: in a row the error message would become a third column beside the control, and the error is about the value, so it belongs under it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Field, Select} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Field label="Time zone" hint="used in reports" orientation="horizontal" error="Unknown zone">
  <Select aria-label="Time zone">…</Select>
</Field>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-input-composer-with-a-toolbar-below.html">
# Composer with a toolbar below

One box, text on top and controls underneath. The addon takes a whole line instead of sitting beside the field, and the frame drops the pill radius for the panel radius — a group with a block addon is no longer a line, it is a surface. Measured: at 999px on a tall box the sides become half-circles and the field text collides with the curve.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, Textarea, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <Textarea rows={2} placeholder="Ask anything…" aria-label="Prompt" />
  <InputGroupAddon side="end" layout="block">
    <Button variant="ghost" size="sm">Attach</Button>
    <Button variant="primary" size="sm">Send</Button>
  </InputGroupAddon>
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-inputgroup-a-unit-that-belongs-to-the-value.html">
# A unit that belongs to the value

The suffix is not a label and not a hint: it is part of reading the number. Putting "ms" inside the group keeps it welded to the field at every width, where a paragraph beside it would wrap away on a phone.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, Input} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <Input aria-label="Timeout" defaultValue="30000" inputMode="numeric" />
  <InputGroupAddon side="end" layout="inline">ms</InputGroupAddon>
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-inputgroup-a-prefix-that-cannot-be-typed-away.html">
# A prefix that cannot be typed away

The scheme and host are fixed; only the path is the user's. Showing them as an addon instead of pre-filling the field means the reader can never delete them by holding backspace, and the value you read back is only ever the part you asked for.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, Input} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <InputGroupAddon side="start" layout="inline">aureauds.dev/</InputGroupAddon>
  <Input aria-label="Path" defaultValue="components/button" />
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-inputgroup-both-ends-at-once.html">
# Both ends at once

A currency on one side and a unit on the other, with the field between them. Two addons is the ceiling: a third leaves less room for the value than for the frame around it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, Input} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <InputGroupAddon side="start" layout="inline">€</InputGroupAddon>
  <Input aria-label="Budget" defaultValue="1240.00" inputMode="decimal" />
  <InputGroupAddon side="end" layout="inline">/ month</InputGroupAddon>
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-inputgroup-a-toolbar-over-the-field.html">
# A toolbar over the field

`block-start` takes the whole line above the control, which is the only place a row of actions fits without stealing width from the value. This is the shape a composer wants: the field is the work, the bar is what you do to it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, Textarea, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <InputGroupAddon side="start" layout="block">
    <IconButton icon="text-b" label="Bold" size="sm" />
    <IconButton icon="text-italic" label="Italic" size="sm" />
    <IconButton icon="link" label="Link" size="sm" />
  </InputGroupAddon>
  <Textarea aria-label="Notes" rows={3} defaultValue="" />
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-inputgroup-a-counter-under-the-field.html">
# A counter under the field

`block-end` for what the reader consults while typing, not before. The count belongs to the control, so it travels with it — unlike a hint on the Field, which describes the input before anyone has touched it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {InputGroup, InputGroupAddon, Textarea} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <Textarea aria-label="Summary" rows={3} value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
  <InputGroupAddon side="end" layout="block">{text.length} / 280</InputGroupAddon>
</InputGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kpi-a-number-with-its-comparison.html">
# A number with its comparison

The delta only means something next to a period, so the trend line carries both. A KPI without a comparison is a number on a wall — true, and useless for deciding anything.

## Usage

```tsx
import {KPI} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<KPI label="Runs" value="1,284" trend="+12% vs last week" />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kpi-the-direction-not-just-the-sign.html">
# The direction, not just the sign

`trend` takes a node, so the comparison can carry a status of its own. Colour alone would fail WCAG 1.4.1 — the arrow and the words are what make the direction readable without it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {KPI, Status} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<KPI
  label="Failed runs"
  value="17"
  trend={<Status variant="danger">up 6 since Monday</Status>}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kpi-a-row-of-tiles-across-the-top-of-a-dashboard.html">
# A row of tiles across the top of a dashboard

Three or four side by side is the shape a dashboard opens with: the numbers that decide whether to keep reading. Past four they stop being a summary and become a table that forgot it was one.

## Usage

```tsx
import {KPI} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="grid">
  <KPI label="Runs" value="1,284" trend="+12%" />
  <KPI label="Success rate" value="98.7%" trend="+0.4pt" />
  <KPI label="P95 latency" value="1.8s" trend="−4%" />
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kpi-a-trend-with-a-direction.html">
# A trend with a direction

`direction` draws the arrow, colours the trend and gives screen readers a word before it — up is success and down is danger by default. When going up is bad news, `tone` turns it around. The trend text stays the domain's own words.

## Usage

```tsx
import {KPI} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<KPI label="Revenue" value="$12,400" trend="+8% this month" direction="up" />
<KPI label="Churn" value="2.1%" trend="−0.3pt" direction="down" tone="success" />
<KPI label="Support cost" value="$3,200" trend="+12%" direction="up" tone="danger" />
<KPI label="Active seats" value="148" trend="same as last month" direction="flat" />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kpi-numbers-inside-a-card-that-already-exists.html">
# Numbers inside a card that already exists

A KPI is a card, so three of them inside a panel would be boxes inside a box. `variant="plain"` drops the card and keeps the column: the panel is the surface, and the numbers sit on it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, KPI, Grid} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <Grid min="xs">
    <KPI variant="plain" label="Runs" value="1,284" trend="+12%" direction="up" />
    <KPI variant="plain" label="Success rate" value="98.7%" trend="+0.4pt" direction="up" />
    <KPI variant="plain" label="P95 latency" value="1.8s" trend="−4%" direction="down" tone="success" />
  </Grid>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kbd-a-shortcut-inside-a-sentence.html">
# A shortcut inside a sentence

Prose is where the keyboard is taught. Marking the keys instead of quoting them means a screen reader announces them as keys, and the reader can tell `Esc` the key from "esc" the word.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Kbd} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<p>Press <Kbd>Esc</Kbd> to close, or <Kbd>⌘</Kbd> <Kbd>K</Kbd> to search.</p>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kbd-one-key-per-element-in-a-chord.html">
# One key per element in a chord

`⌘ ⇧ P` is three elements, not one string. Split like this the keys line up with the physical keys the reader is looking for, and a chord never renders as a single wide pill that reads like one impossible key.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Kbd} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<span className="cluster">
  <Kbd>⌘</Kbd><Kbd>⇧</Kbd><Kbd>P</Kbd>
</span>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kbd-the-shortcut-column-of-a-menu.html">
# The shortcut column of a menu

A menu that lists its shortcuts teaches the keyboard without a separate page. The keys sit at the end of the row so the labels stay left-aligned and scannable — the shortcut is the second read, never the first.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Kbd} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="menu">
  <button className="menu-item" type="button">New run<Kbd>N</Kbd></button>
  <button className="menu-item" type="button">Search<Kbd>/</Kbd></button>
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-kbd-on-the-button-that-performs-it.html">
# On the button that performs it

The one case where the keys must NOT be a bare Kbd: `kbd` on the Button both draws the shortcut and emits `aria-keyshortcuts`, so the shortcut is announced and not only seen. A Kbd dropped inside a button would be the decoration without the promise.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" kbd="⌘ Enter">Send</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-logstream-the-tail-of-a-running-job.html">
# The tail of a running job

Time, level and message in three fixed tracks, so the eye can find the level column without reading the lines. It is a live region: a line that arrives while the reader is elsewhere is announced, not silently appended.

## Usage

```tsx
import {LogStream} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<LogStream lines={[
  {time: "14:32:01", level: "info", text: "task#4821 accepted"},
  {time: "14:32:02", level: "info", text: "model loaded"},
  {time: "14:32:04", level: "warn", text: "external tool requires approval"},
  {time: "14:32:08", level: "error", text: "scope invoke:external denied"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-logstream-lines-with-no-level-of-their-own.html">
# Lines with no level of their own

Program output is not levelled, and forcing a level on it would be inventing information. The three cells stay in place even when two are empty — that is what keeps the message in its own track instead of sliding left.

## Usage

```tsx
import {LogStream} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<LogStream lines={stdout.map(text => ({text}))} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-logstream-the-log-under-the-thing-it-describes.html">
# The log under the thing it describes

A log beside a status is the shape an operations panel repeats: the badge says what happened, the stream says why. Neither answers the other's question, which is why both are here.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Status, LogStream, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <div className="cluster">
    <strong>Nightly sweep</strong>
    <Status variant="danger">Failed</Status>
  </div>
  <LogStream lines={lines} />
  <Button size="sm" variant="secondary" leadingIcon="arrow-counter-clockwise">Run again</Button>
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-mediaplayer-a-clip-with-its-title-on-the-frame.html">
# A clip with its title on the frame

Title and subtitle ride on the player instead of above it, so the frame is self-contained wherever it is embedded. Every control is reachable by keyboard and announced from the string dictionary, which is what makes the player translatable.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayer} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayer
  kind="video"
  title="Aurea in ninety seconds"
  subtitle="Product tour · 1:30"
  poster="/poster.jpg"
  src="/tour.mp4"
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-mediaplayer-an-episode-without-the-video-frame.html">
# An episode, without the video frame

The same player with kind="audio": no picture area, the controls carry the whole component. Reaching for a second component here would double the keyboard surface for no gain.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayer} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayer kind="audio" title="Episode 12 · Design tokens" subtitle="42:10" src="/ep12.mp3" />
```

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-mediaplayershell-a-stream-with-its-own-controls.html">
# A stream with its own controls

The frame gives the surface, the aspect ratio and the dark canvas that holds in both themes; everything inside is yours. This is the shape to reach for when the engine is not a <video> — a remote screen, a canvas, a live socket.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayerShell, Badge, Icon} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayerShell>
  <div className="media-overlay-title">

      <button type="button" className="media-control" aria-label="Stop"><Icon name="stop" /></button>
      <button type="button" className="media-control" aria-label="Mute"><Icon name="speaker-high" /></button>
    </div>
  </div>
</MediaPlayerShell>
```

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-mediaplayershell-waiting-for-a-source.html">
# Waiting for a source

The state a player spends more time in than anyone plans for. Saying nothing reads as broken; the frame with a placeholder says the surface is ready and the source is not, which is the fact the reader needs while they wait.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayerShell, Spinner} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayerShell>
  <div className="media-placeholder">
    <Spinner />
    <strong>Connecting…</strong>
  </div>
</MediaPlayerShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-mediaplayershell-the-source-failed.html">
# The source failed

A dead stream is not an empty one: it needs the reason and a way out. Keeping the failure inside the frame instead of replacing the frame with an alert holds the layout still — the page does not jump when a tile drops.

## Usage

```tsx
import {MediaPlayerShell, Icon, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<MediaPlayerShell>
  <div className="media-placeholder">
    <Icon name="warning" />
    <strong>Stream unavailable</strong>
    <Button size="sm" variant="secondary" onClick={retry}>Try again</Button>
  </div>
</MediaPlayerShell>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-menubar-the-menu-row-of-an-editor.html">
# The menu row of an editor

One row, and the arrow keys walk from an open menu straight into the next — that is what separates a menubar from three dropdowns side by side. It belongs to applications, not to websites.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Menubar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Menubar label="Main" menus={[
  {label: "File", items: [
    {label: "New file", kbd: "⌘N"}, {label: "Open…", kbd: "⌘O"},
    "separator", {label: "Close", kbd: "⌘W"},
  ]},
  {label: "Edit", items: [{label: "Undo", kbd: "⌘Z"}, {label: "Redo", kbd: "⇧⌘Z"}]},
  {label: "View", items: [{label: "Zoom in"}, {label: "Zoom out"}, {label: "Reset zoom"}]},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-menubar-the-menu-bar-as-a-column.html">
# The menu bar as a column

`orientation="vertical"` stacks the bar and the menus open to the side — down would put them on top of the next item of the bar itself. The side is logical (`inline-end`), so in Arabic the column sits on the right and the menus open left without anyone writing a second rule.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Menubar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Menubar label="Tools" orientation="vertical" menus={[
  {label: "File", items: [{label: "New file"}, {label: "Open…"}]},
  {label: "Selection", items: [{label: "Select all"}, {label: "Expand"}]},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-messagecomposer-the-line-you-type-into.html">

One field and one send. The icon is optional and the field does not reserve space for one that is not there — a defect this component actually shipped with, and the reason the InputGroup exists.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-messagelist-a-thread-between-a-person-and-an-agent.html">
# A thread between a person and an agent

Author, time and body, with the delivery state on the message that has one. The list is a log: it does not reorder, and a failed message stays where it was written so the retry lands in context.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-multicombobox-labelling-something-with-several-tags.html">

Each choice stays visible as a chip, so the user reads the whole selection without opening the list again. Backspace removes the last one — the keyboard shape people already expect from an email To: field.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-notificationcenter-the-bell-in-the-top-bar.html">

Grouped by day, unread first, and one control that clears the badge without opening every item. The count on the trigger is the only thing most people ever read.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-numberfield-a-quantity-with-a-floor-and-a-ceiling.html">
# A quantity with a floor and a ceiling

The steppers are for small corrections and the keyboard is for big ones — both hit the same bounds. Bounds on the field, not in a message after submit: the refusal should never be a surprise.

## Usage

```tsx
import {NumberField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<NumberField label="Retries" defaultValue={3} min={0} max={10} step={1} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-numberfield-a-wide-range-you-drag-instead-of-clicking-forty-times.html">
# A wide range you drag instead of clicking forty times

Opacity 0–100, a width in pixels: ranges where the steppers are the wrong instrument. `scrubbable` adds a handle that changes the value as you pull it — the gesture every drawing tool has in a numeric field. It is opt-in and strictly additive: the buttons, the arrow keys and Home/End are untouched, and the handle is hidden from assistive technology because dragging is a pointer gesture with no keyboard equivalent to promise. Use `scrubDirection="vertical"` when the fields are stacked, as in a width/height pair.

## Usage

```tsx
import {NumberField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<NumberField label="Opacity" defaultValue={80} min={0} max={100} scrubbable />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-otpfield-the-six-digits-from-the-email.html">
# The six digits from the email

One box per character, and paste fills all of them — because nobody types a code they can copy. Masking is for a secret; a verification code is not one, and hiding it only makes it harder to check.

## Usage

```tsx
import {OTPField} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<OTPField label="Verification code" length={6} onValueChange={check} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-pagination-walking-a-long-result-set.html">
# Walking a long result set

The current page is announced, not just highlighted. Previous and Next keep their labels for screen readers even when they show only a chevron — a nameless arrow is a dead end.

## Usage


```tsx
<Pagination page={page} total={12} onPageChange={setPage} />
```

</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-passwordfield-a-password-the-user-can-check.html">

The reveal exists because typing a password blind is how people get locked out. The button says the action, not the state — Show password, then Hide password — so a screen reader announces what will happen.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-popover-the-definition-behind-a-number.html">
# The definition behind a number

A popover, not a tooltip: the content is rich, it stays open, and the pointer can travel into it to select text. A tooltip that needs a second sentence should have been this.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-section-the-page-opening-text-beside-the-proof.html">
# The page opening, text beside the proof

variant="hero" is the opening of a page: an eyebrow, the title (the page's h1), a line of text, the buttons, and the image beside it. The title grows with the width of the band, not of the window — 36, then 60 from 768 and 72 from 1024 — and the image sits beside the text from 1024; below that, it goes under. The image takes the width of its column: size it in the app.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Section, Badge, Button, Image} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Section
  variant="hero"
  eyebrow={<Badge tone="primary" emphasis="flat">New in 2.0</Badge>}
  title="Plan the week in one screen"
  description="Tasks, people and dates side by side, on the web and on the phone."
  actions={<>
    <Button variant="primary" href="/start">Get started</Button>
    <Button variant="outline" href="/tour">Take the tour</Button>
  </>}
  media={<Image src="/week.png" alt="The app's week view" ratio="4/3" />}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-section-the-page-opening-centred.html">
# The page opening, centred

align="center" puts everything on the middle line, with the image (if any) under the text. What comes inside the Section goes after the buttons: a short note, a link.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Section, Badge, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Section
  variant="hero"
  align="center"
  eyebrow={<Badge tone="primary" emphasis="flat">Version 2.0 is out</Badge>}
  title="One design system. Web and native."
  description="The same look on both sides, made for people who see little."
  actions={<>
    <Button variant="primary" href="/start">Get started</Button>
    <Button variant="outline" href="/components">View components</Button>
  </>}
>
  <Link href="/github">Open source on GitHub</Link>
</Section>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-section-the-page-opening-with-an-e-mail-field.html">
# The page opening with an e-mail field

actions takes anything: here, the e-mail field with its button, inside a form. The field keeps its name for the screen reader (aria-label), because the placeholder is not a label.

## Usage

```tsx

```

```tsx
<Section
  variant="hero"
  title="Get the monthly notes"
  description="One e-mail a month with what changed. No spam."
  actions={
    <form onSubmit={subscribe}>
      <InputGroup>
        <Input type="email" name="email" autoComplete="email" aria-label="E-mail address" placeholder="you@example.com" required />
        <InputGroupAddon side="end" layout="inline">
          <Button type="submit" variant="primary" size="sm">Subscribe</Button>
        </InputGroupAddon>
      </InputGroup>
    </form>
  }
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-section-the-website-footer-dark-on-a-light-page.html">

variant="footer" turns the band into the footer: brand, link columns and the legal line, already inside a Container. It keeps the band's theme, so a dark footer on a light page is theme="dark". On a phone everything stacks.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-segmentedcontrol-switching-the-window-of-a-chart.html">
# Switching the window of a chart

One dimension, few values, and one is always chosen — that is what separates a segmented control from a button group. Zero selected is not a state it can express, so never use it for a filter that can be cleared.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-select-a-short-closed-list-of-options.html">
# A short, closed list of options

The native select is the right answer more often than it gets used: it is the control the platform already knows how to render on a phone, and it needs no portal, no listbox and no keyboard code. Reach for a Combobox when typing beats scrolling.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-separator-between-items-on-one-line.html">
# Between items on one line

`orientation="vertical"` for metadata that shares a row and does not share a meaning. It stretches to the line, so it never reads as a stray character the way a typed pipe does at a different font size.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Cluster, Separator} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Cluster>
  <span>12 components</span>
  <Separator orientation="vertical" />
  <span>186 patterns</span>
  <Separator orientation="vertical" />
  <span>Apache-2.0</span>
</Cluster>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-separator-grouping-a-menu-without-labelling-it.html">
# Grouping a menu without labelling it

The line groups the destructive action away from the rest so it is not reached by accident. Note what it is not doing: a screen reader hears one flat list, and that is correct — the separation is a pointer affordance, and the wording of the item is what carries the warning.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Separator, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<div className="menu">
  <button className="menu-item" type="button">Rename</button>
  <button className="menu-item" type="button">Duplicate</button>
  <Separator />
  <button className="menu-item" type="button">Delete permanently</button>
</div>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-sidebar-the-main-navigation-of-an-application.html">
# The main navigation of an application

Collapsing keeps the icons and drops the labels — it narrows the column, it does not hide the navigation. On a narrow screen the AppShell turns the same sidebar into a drawer, so there is one navigation, not two.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Sidebar} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Sidebar
  label="Main"
  current="runs"
  items={[
    {id: "overview", label: "Overview", icon: "squares-four", href: "#"},
    {id: "runs", label: "Runs", icon: "play", href: "#"},
    {id: "members", label: "Members", icon: "users", href: "#"},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-skeleton-the-shape-of-the-content-that-is-coming.html">
# The shape of the content that is coming

A skeleton only helps when it matches the layout it replaces — otherwise the page jumps when the data lands, which is the exact flicker it was meant to avoid. Use it for content, never for a control.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Skeleton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <Skeleton style={{height: 20, width: "40%"}} />
  <Skeleton style={{height: 14}} />
  <Skeleton style={{height: 14, width: "80%"}} />
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-spinner-waiting-inside-a-button.html">
# Waiting inside a button

The label stays while the spinner runs — replacing it with a bare spinner loses what the user is waiting for. Decorative here, because the button already announces itself busy.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Spinner, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Button variant="primary" loading>Saving…</Button>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-status-the-state-of-a-service-in-a-row.html">
# The state of a service, in a row

A coloured dot plus a word. The word is mandatory: colour alone fails for a third of readers, and green and amber are the pair people confuse most.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Status} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Status variant="online">Running</Status>
<Status variant="offline">Stopped</Status>
<Status>Unknown</Status>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-stepper-where-you-are-in-a-sequence.html">
# Where you are in a sequence

Three states in one row: what is done, what you are on, what is left. The current step carries `aria-current="step"`, so the position is announced and not only drawn — a stepper that only draws is a decoration.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stepper} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stepper label="Checkout" items={[
  {label: "Cart", state: "done"},
  {label: "Address", state: "active"},
  {label: "Payment"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-stepper-a-step-that-can-be-skipped.html">
# A step that can be skipped

`optional` says out loud what a greyed-out label only implies. Marking it is what lets a reader decide to move on, instead of hunting for the field they think they missed.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stepper} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stepper label="Onboarding" items={[
  {label: "Account", state: "done"},
  {label: "Team", state: "done", optional: "Skipped"},
  {label: "Import data", state: "active", optional: "Optional"},
  {label: "Finish"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-stepper-a-step-that-failed.html">
# A step that failed

`state: "error"` keeps the failure in the sequence instead of replacing it with an alert somewhere else. The reader sees which step broke and how far they had got, which is the pair of facts they need to decide whether to fix or restart.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stepper, Alert} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stepper label="Deploy" items={[
  {label: "Build", state: "done"},
  {label: "Test", state: "error"},
  {label: "Release"},
]} />
<Alert variant="danger" title="Tests failed">Two suites did not pass.</Alert>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-stepper-going-back-to-a-finished-step.html">
# Going back to a finished step

`onClick` turns a step into a real button — but only where going back is allowed. Leaving the unreached steps inert is the point: a stepper whose every step is clickable is a tab list wearing the wrong clothes.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Stepper} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Stepper label="Checkout" items={[
  {label: "Cart", state: "done", onClick: () => goTo(0)},
  {label: "Address", state: "done", onClick: () => goTo(1)},
  {label: "Payment", state: "active"},
  {label: "Review"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-switch-notification-settings.html">
# Notification settings

Flip and it is done. No Save button — that is what makes it a Switch and not a Checkbox.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Switch} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <strong>Notifications</strong>
  <Switch label="Email" defaultChecked />
  <Switch label="Push" />
  <Switch label="Weekly digest" defaultChecked />
</Card>
```

The switch sets it; a Status reports what the system did with it.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-switch-gated-by-plan.html">
# Gated by plan

Visible so the value is known, disabled so it cannot be flipped — with the reason next to it.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-switch-when-it-waits-it-is-a-checkbox.html">
# When it waits, it is a Checkbox

Same yes-or-no, different moment: this one only takes effect when the form is submitted.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-with-caption.html">
# With caption

The caption names the table for a screen reader and for the eye — a table with no name is a grid of noise.

# Operational state

A Status per row instead of a coloured cell: the condition is spelled out, not encoded in a fill.

# With pagination

The full collection composition: filter above, selection in the first column, pagination below.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-view-switch.html">
# View switch

Table or cards for the same data — SegmentedControl switches the view, never the meaning.

```tsx
import {SegmentedControl, Table} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<SegmentedControl label="View" value="table"
  items={[{value:"table",label:"Table"},{value:"cards",label:"Cards"}]} onChange={setView} />
```

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-row-actions.html">
# Row actions

Actions live at the end of the row, ghost so they do not shout over the data.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Table, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<td className="cluster">
  <Button variant="ghost" size="sm">Edit</Button>
  <Button variant="ghost" size="sm">Remove</Button>

```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-a-comparison-with-groups-and-the-best-value.html">
# A comparison with groups and the best value

Items are columns, specs are rows. Each group of rows is a <tbody> that opens with a band; each row is named by a <th scope="row">. The name column stays put when the table scrolls sideways, and the header stays at the top of the box when it scrolls down. The best value is bold and also says so in text — a Badge, because colour alone tells nothing to someone who cannot see it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Table, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Table caption="Compare models" stickyHeader stickyFirstColumn>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">Spec</th><th scope="col">Model A</th>…</tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="rowgroup" colSpan={4}>Engine</th></tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Power</th>
      <td>120 hp</td>
      <td data-best>150 hp <Badge>Best</Badge></td>
      <td>110 hp</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</Table>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-two-at-a-time-on-a-phone.html">
# Two at a time on a phone

On a narrow screen the page shows two items, picked with two selects above the table, and `fit` drops the 720px minimum so the two fit with no sideways scroll. Which two is the page's choice; the table only has to fit.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Table, Field, Select, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Field label="Compare"><Select value={a} onValueChange={setA}>…</Select></Field>
<Field label="With"><Select value={b} onValueChange={setB}>…</Select></Field>
<Table caption="Compare models" fit>…two columns…</Table>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-table-differences-only.html">
# Differences only

A switch hides the rows that are the same for every item — the page marks them <tr data-same>, and `differencesOnly` hides them. Removing what does not differ is what makes a long comparison readable.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Table, Switch, Badge} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Switch label="Differences only" checked={only} onChange={e => setOnly(e.target.checked)} />
<Table caption="Compare models" differencesOnly={only}>
  …<tr data-same><th scope="row">Fuel</th><td>Flex</td><td>Flex</td><td>Flex</td></tr>…
</Table>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tableofcontents-an-index-that-follows-the-reading.html">
# An index that follows the reading

It marks the section in view by itself — pass current only when something else owns that state. Sub-items are one level deep and no more: an index that needs three levels is a document that needs splitting.

## Usage

```tsx
import {TableOfContents} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<TableOfContents items={[
  {id: "install", label: "Installation"},
  {id: "usage", label: "Usage"},
  {id: "props", label: "Props", sub: true},
  {id: "a11y", label: "Accessibility"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tabs-two-readings-of-the-same-thing.html">
# Two readings of the same thing

Tabs are for alternative views of one subject, never for steps — a step has an order and a tab does not. If the user must visit all of them, it was a form, not a tab set.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tabs} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
const [tab, setTab] = useState("preview");

<Tabs
  label="Component view"
  value={tab}
  onChange={setTab}
  tabs={[
    {id: "preview", label: "Preview", content: <Preview />},
    {id: "code", label: "Code", content: <Code />},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tabs-a-column-of-sections-beside-the-content.html">
# A column of sections beside the content

`orientation="vertical"` when the labels are words rather than one-word nouns, or when there are more of them than a row can hold without scrolling. The root becomes a grid and not a row: on a row the panel and the list share a line, and a tall panel would stretch the label column with it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tabs} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tabs
  orientation="vertical"
  label="Settings"
  value={section}
  onChange={setSection}
  tabs={[
    {id: "profile", label: "Profile", content: <Profile />},
    {id: "notifications", label: "Notifications", content: <Notifications />},
    {id: "billing", label: "Billing and invoices", content: <Billing />},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tabs-when-switching-a-tab-costs-a-request.html">
# When switching a tab costs a request

With the default, the arrow key switches the panel along with focus — right when the panel is already there. When each tab fetches, that means crossing five tabs fires five requests. `activateOnFocus={false}` is the APG's manual pattern: the arrow only moves focus, and Enter or Space commits. The choice belongs to the panel's cost, not to taste.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tabs} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tabs
  label="Report"
  activateOnFocus={false}
  value={tab}
  onChange={setTab}
  tabs={[
    {id: "summary", label: "Summary", content: <Summary />},
    {id: "runs", label: "Runs", content: <Runs />},
    {id: "audit", label: "Audit log", content: <AuditLog />},
  ]}
/>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-textarea-a-description-field-that-grows.html">
# A description field that grows

Rows set the starting height, not the limit. The field keeps the pill radius of every other control, because a text area is still a field — the shape changes only when it becomes a composition box with its own toolbar.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Textarea, Field} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Field label="Description" hint="Markdown is supported">
  <Textarea rows={4} placeholder="What does this project do?" />
</Field>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-timeline-what-happened-to-this-record.html">
# What happened to this record

An ordered list because the order carries meaning: a screen reader announces "item 2 of 5" and the reader knows where in the story they are. A stack of divs would say the same words and lose that.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Timeline} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Timeline items={[
  {title: "Created", time: "09:02", description: "Drafted by Writer."},
  {title: "Reviewed", time: "10:41", description: "Two comments resolved."},
  {title: "Published", time: "11:15"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-timeline-entries-that-carry-their-own-outcome.html">
# Entries that carry their own outcome

`title` takes a node, so an entry can say what it was and how it went in one line. This is the difference between a log the reader has to interpret and an audit trail they can scan.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Timeline, Status} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Timeline items={[
  {title: <>Deploy <Status variant="success">succeeded</Status></>, time: "03:14"},
  {title: <>Rollback <Status variant="warning">manual</Status></>, time: "04:02"},
]} />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-timeline-the-activity-panel-of-a-detail-page.html">
# The activity panel of a detail page

Beside the record, not under it: the timeline answers "what has been done to this" while the page answers "what is this". Putting it in a card of its own is what keeps the two questions from running together.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Card, Timeline} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Card>
  <h3>Activity</h3>
  <Timeline items={activity} />
</Card>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-toggle-a-button-that-stays-pressed.html">
# A button that stays pressed

Two states the user flips and reads back from the button itself. It is not a Switch: a switch applies a setting, a toggle marks the thing under the cursor.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toggle icon="text-b" label="Bold" defaultPressed />
<Toggle icon="text-italic" label="Italic" />
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-togglegroup-the-alignment-row-of-an-editor.html">
# The alignment row of an editor

Arrow keys walk the group and only one alignment can be true at a time. With multiple it becomes a filter bar where none selected is legitimate — the same component, a different contract.

## Usage

```tsx
import {ToggleGroup, Toggle} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<ToggleGroup label="Alignment" defaultValue={["left"]}>
  <Toggle value="left" icon="text-align-left" label="Align left" />
  <Toggle value="center" icon="text-align-center" label="Center" />
  <Toggle value="right" icon="text-align-right" label="Align right" />
</ToggleGroup>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-toolbar-undo-and-redo.html">
# Undo and redo

History with the unavailable step kept in place, so the arrows never renumber the set.

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-toolbarbutton-a-toggle-that-stays-pressed.html">
# A toggle that stays pressed

`pressed` emits `aria-pressed`, so the state is announced and not only shaded. This is the whole reason a formatting bar uses ToolbarButton instead of a styled div: bold-is-on has to be a fact, not an appearance.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Formatting">
  <ToolbarButton pressed leadingIcon="text-b">Bold</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton leadingIcon="text-italic">Italic</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-toolbarbutton-an-unavailable-step-kept-in-place.html">
# An unavailable step kept in place

`disabled` on the step that cannot run — never removing it. A bar whose buttons come and go renumbers itself under the reader's hand, and the muscle memory that a toolbar exists to build never forms.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="History">
  <ToolbarButton leadingIcon="arrow-counter-clockwise" disabled>Undo</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton leadingIcon="arrow-clockwise">Redo</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-toolbarbutton-the-one-action-that-is-not-a-tool.html">
# The one action that is not a tool

A toolbar is mostly ghost buttons because they are peers; the moment one of them is the point of the screen it takes a tone of its own. One per bar — a bar of primaries has no primary.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Toolbar, ToolbarButton, ToolbarSeparator} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Toolbar label="Draft">
  <ToolbarButton leadingIcon="floppy-disk">Save</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton leadingIcon="eye">Preview</ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarButton variant="primary">Publish</ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tooltip-naming-an-icon-only-control.html">
# Naming an icon-only control

The IconButton already carries its accessible name; the tip is what shows that name to everyone else. Two mechanisms, one string — which is why the label and the tip must say the same thing, never two different things.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tooltip, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Export as CSV">
  <IconButton icon="download" label="Export as CSV" />
</Tooltip>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tooltip-why-a-control-is-unavailable.html">
# Why a control is unavailable

A disabled button says no and not why, and a disabled element does not receive focus — so the tip goes on a wrapper that does. Without that the explanation exists only for a mouse, which is the failure this pattern is here to avoid.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tooltip, Button} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Tooltip content="Add a payment method first">
  <span tabIndex={0}>
    <Button variant="primary" disabled>Publish</Button>
  </span>
</Tooltip>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-tooltip-spelling-out-an-abbreviated-column.html">
# Spelling out an abbreviated column

`side="right"` when the trigger sits in a narrow column and a tip above would cover the row being read. The header still has to make sense without the tip: P95 is the label, the tip only expands it.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Tooltip} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<th>
  <Tooltip side="right" content="95th percentile over the last 7 days">
    <abbr>P95</abbr>
  </Tooltip>
</th>
```
</page>

<page url="https://aureauds.dev/pattern-topbar-the-bar-that-carries-the-brand-and-the-global-actions.html">
# The bar that carries the brand and the global actions

Brand on the left, actions on the right, and nothing in between that belongs to a single page. The floating variant sits on the content; flush joins the page — pick one per application, not per screen.

## Usage

```tsx
import {Topbar, IconButton} from "@aurea-uds/react";
```

```tsx
<Topbar brand={<strong>Aurea UDS</strong>}>
  <SearchField aria-label="Search" placeholder="Search…" />
  <IconButton icon="sun" label="Switch to light" onClick={toggleTheme} />
</Topbar>
```
</page>
